#111741. A Gigantic Stellar Eruption Spreads Planetary Material Into Space

A Gigantic Stellar Eruption Spreads Planetary Material Into Space

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1593 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that highly-evolved stars spread the material for new planets and stars into space with their stellar winds.
  • The material is first emitted in pulses of gas, and eventually that gas cools into dust and the star's radiation pressure pushes it away with its stellar wind.
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers at Chalmers University in Sweden have been observing Mira, an AGB star about 300 light years away.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that highly-evolved stars spread the material for new planets and stars into space with their stellar winds. These stars are called aysmptotic giant branch (AGB) stars, and they're cool, luminous stars that are running out of hydrogen and leaving the main sequence behind. As they age, they can shed as much as 30 Earth masses of material per year into the interstellar medium (ISM).

The material is first emitted in pulses of gas, and eventually that gas cools into dust and the star's radiation pressure pushes it away with its stellar wind. Carbon and silica are key parts of what's emitted, and silica is the main building block for rocky planets, while carbon feeds into organic particles. So these stellar winds from AGB stars clearly play an important role in the formation of planets, other stars, and even potential life.

Recent findings suggest that researchers at Chalmers University in Sweden have been observing Mira, an AGB star about 300 light years away. It's the prototype and namesake of what are called Mira variables, pulsating AGB stars that are oxygen-rich. Their results are challenging the long-held understanding that stellar winds driven by radiation pressure are what spread heavy elements into the interstellar medium (ISM).

Industry observers note that the research is "A giant magnetic eruption from the asymptotic-giant-branch star Mira A," and it's published in Astronomy and Astrophysics. The lead author is Wouter Vlemmings, Professor in the department of Physics and Astronomy at Chalmers University of Technology in Gothenburg, Sweden.

"Mass loss during the advanced evolutionary stages of low- and intermediate-mass stars is traditionally attributed to dust-driven winds, whereas the influence of magnetic fields remains poorly constrained," the authors write. "This mass-loss process is crucial for the chemical enrichment of the Universe.".

It has been revealed that since this type of mass-loss is so fundamental, it's attracted a lot of attention and is the subject of a huge amount of research. In this work, the researchers used the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) observations to study how Mira's magnetic fields might shape its mass loss. ALMA can't directly observe magnetic fields; instead it observes them indirectly through their polarizing effect on radio emissions.

âFor decades, astronomers have believed that the winds from stars like this must be powered by starlight. Light from the star shines on grains of dust in the starâs outer atmosphere, and that gives them a push. But this star is showing us something different: that strong magnetic fields can also shape and power stellar winds. That changes a fundamental part of the origin story of the atoms we ourselves are made of," lead author Vlemmings explained in a press release.

This schematic demonstrates the structure of an AGB star, from its degenerate core to its circumstellar envelope. It shows it during its thermal pulse stage, when pulses drive gas outward, where it cools and forms dust in the envelope. Radiation pressure generates the stellar wind that drives the dust away into the ISM. Image Credit: Lu et al. Front. Astron. Space Sci., 23 July 2025. Sec. Astrostatistics.

Astrophysicists have detected strong magnetic fields in the circumstellar envelopes of AGB stars like Mira, and researchers have suggested that they may play a role in driving their mass loss. But the researchers explain that there's been no empirical evidence of the role magnetic fields play in the process, and that wind-driven mass loss models don't include magnetic fields.

According to recent reports, recent observations, however, are challenging the overall understanding of the wind-driven mass loss scenario. Some AGB stars show mass-loss but also show insufficient dust to explain it. These stars are oxygen-rich AGB stars like Mira. Since Mira is the nearest of its type of dusty, pulsation-driven O-rich AGB stars, it makes sense to study it.

Sources indicate that both ALMA and the Very Large Array recently observed Mira A, the AGB star, and its companion Mira B, a white dwarf, in August 2025. But observations go back ten years, and both sets of data combine to reveal dramatic changes on Mira A's surface.

"During the past decade, high-angular-resolution observations of Mira A at visible, millimetre, and submillimetre wavelengths have revealed several unexpected phenomena related to the stellar atmosphere and mass-loss process," the authors write.

This ten-year study of Mira's surface is the longest study of any star other than the Sun.

This time-lapse indicates ten years of changes on the surface of Mira A. Credit: W. Vlemmings et al. 2026. Astronomy and Astrophysics.

According to recent reports, âWe were astonished to see how the starâs surface is constantly changing. The brightest areas were different every time we looked, and the brightest patches are amazingly bright. We realised that star is flaring, releasing vast amounts of energy each time," noted study co-author Miora Andriantsaralaza, a postdoctoral researcher in the department of Physics and Astronomy at Chalmers University of Technology.

Industry observers note that some of the hotspots in the video have brightness temperatures of 8,000 Kelvin. That's far higher than the average 2,000 K brightness temperature.

But the main finding is what researchers call SiO (silicon monoxide) masers. They're often found in the circumstellar envelopes of AGB stars, just inside the dust formation zone. But Mira A's masers are at a much greater distance, where the gas is too thin for a strong SiO maser to form. So the researchers say the masers trace a shock moving outward, and that it has much higher density than expected. In short, a flare that expanded into a huge loop of expelled material.

According to recent reports, âIn 2023, we saw one of these flares appear on the starâs surface, but it didnât stop there. Over the next two years, this eruption on the surface created a vast, expanding loop of gas around the star, which we captured in an image in 2025. The loop was much bigger than the star, extending as far out as the distance of Saturn from the Sun. We hadnât seen anything like that before," said co-author Behzad Bojnordi Arbab, a doctoral student at Chalmers University.

Masers aren't always polarised, but these ones are linearly and circularly polarized. Linearly polarised means its polarisation is organized, and the polarising is shaping it. Circular means it rotates in a corkscrew pattern. Taken together, the astronomers used those features to map Mira's magnetic field geometry. That in turn let them understand how the magnetism is shaping its wind and its mass loss.

The loop and its polarisation is the key in this work.

âIn the loop, thereâs a strong magnetic field, which must also influence the starâs wind. That revealed us a connection between the flare and the loop, and reminded us also of phenomena we can see on our Sun," remarked Vlemmings.

This figure from the research shows a three-dimensional representation of the adopted magnetic-loop ejection model anchored to the surface of Mira. The structure is colour coded according to line-of-sight velocity. Image Credit: W. Vlemmings et al. 2026. Astronomy and Astrophysics.

For now, the source of these magnetic fields isn't entirely clear. "The origin of the magnetic fields responsible for the observed ejections remains uncertain, although several mechanisms have been proposed," the authors write. A turbulent dynamo deep in Mira's convective envelope could be responsible, or differential rotation between the star's core and envelope could be behind them. Making progress understanding how the magnetic fields drive mass loss will depend on understanding how they're generated.

Recent findings suggest that the flares and magnetic fields are evidence of a new element in mass-loss. On our Sun, flares are generated by magnetic fields, and they're associated with coronal mass ejections, where material is sent speeding away from the Sun. But our Sun is young, and isn't an aged AGB star experiencing the same level of mass loss. Still, these findings draw a parallel between the two.

Recent findings suggest that âNow we see that magnetic storms on Miraâs surface are continually creating bright flares. Even more surprisingly, each of these is strong enough to lift parts of the starâs outer layers and launch them into interstellar space,â said Andriantsaralaza.

This research demonstrates that our understanding of AGB mass-loss has to take into account magnetic fields, not just radiation-driven stellar winds.

Sources indicate that "The discovery of coronal-mass-ejection-style eruptions from an AGB star redefines our understanding of late-stage stellar evolution," the authors write. They can help explain some of the features of AGB mass-loss, like clumpiness, asymmetry, and time variability. They can also help explain some of the morphologies of planetary nebulae, the beautiful shells of ionized gas ejected by aged stars.

According to recent reports, "Consequently, magnetic activity must be integrated into models as a dynamically dominant force in initiating mass loss and shaping circumstellar environments," the authors conclude in their study. And since AGB mass loss spreads the stuff of planets into the ISM, that could explain, at least partly, why we're here.

âOur study has consequences for our understanding of the whole of the galaxyâs ecosystem. Perhaps, Earth wouldnât be here if it wasnât for magnetic storms on a red giant star, billions of years ago before the Sun was born," remarked Vlemmings.

Scientists Discover a Potential New Way To Treat Diabetes – No Insulin Required

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (789 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A discovery in animal muscle suggests that the body’s natural ability to absorb sugar without insulin could be harnessed to develop new diabetes treatments.
  • It has been revealed that for people with diabetes or insulin resistance, controlling blood sugar can be difficult because their muscles do not respond effectively to insulin, the hormone that helps move glucose from the bloodstream into cells.
  • According to recent reports, scientists at the University of Cincinnati (UC) College of Medicine have identified a previously unknown pathway that allows skeletal muscles to absorb glucose independently of insulin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A discovery in animal muscle suggests that the body’s natural ability to absorb sugar without insulin could be harnessed to develop new diabetes treatments.

It has been revealed that for people with diabetes or insulin resistance, controlling blood sugar can be difficult because their muscles do not respond effectively to insulin, the hormone that helps move glucose from the bloodstream into cells. Muscles, however, have another way of absorbing glucose that does not require insulin. Understanding how this process works could give researchers an entirely latest way to treat high blood sugar.

According to recent reports, scientists at the University of Cincinnati (UC) College of Medicine have identified a previously unknown pathway that allows skeletal muscles to absorb glucose independently of insulin. Their findings, published in the Nature Portfolio journal Communications Biology, could provide a newly introduced target for treating diabetes, hyperglycemia, and insulin resistance.

It has been revealed that skeletal muscle makes up about 40% of the human body and plays a major role in regulating blood sugar. After a meal, rising insulin levels stimulate muscles to absorb and store up to 90% of ingested glucose through a transport protein called GLUT4, which helps glucose enter muscle cells.

Recent findings suggest that during exercise or stress, insulin levels drop, yet working muscles can absorb glucose at rates up to 100 times higher than after a meal to meet the energy demands of contraction. How muscles manage this without insulin has remained a mystery despite decades of research.

According to recent reports, to investigate, the researchers developed a way to measure glucose uptake independently of insulin. They used glucose derivatives that could be carried by a family of transport proteins known as SGLTs but not by GLUT4. The team tested these derivatives in isolated muscles from animal models, using electrical stimulation to reproduce the contractions of working muscles.

Recent findings suggest that “We showed that if we stimulate muscle to contract in insulin-free conditions, it can take up a lot of glucose from a pathway that’s not GLUT4,” mentioned Judith A. Heiny, PhD, the study’s co-corresponding author and professor emerita in the Division of Neurobiology and Integrative Physiology in UC’s Department of Biomedical Sciences, whose laboratory led the research.

It has been revealed that the researchers named the newly identified pathway mSGLT. It shares properties with SGLT2, a glucose transporter in the kidneys that is already targeted by widely used diabetes medications such as Jardiance. These drugs lower blood sugar by increasing the amount of glucose expelled through urine. Targeting a similar transport mechanism in muscles could offer another way to remove excess glucose from the bloodstream.

Industry observers note that “This insulin-independent process uses a glucose transport protein in skeletal muscle and may offer a drug target for controlling blood sugar,” stated Heiny. “The skeletal musculature is the natural depot for glucose. It has a huge capacity to regulate blood sugar, which can be a struggle for those with diabetes and insulin resistance.”.

Industry observers note that “A therapy that targets glucose uptake by skeletal muscles could be as impactful as SGLT2 inhibitors that lower blood sugar by stimulating the kidneys to excrete excess glucose in the urine,” stated Natalie Norman, PhD, the study’s first author. Norman contributed to the research as a UC graduate student and is now a postdoctoral researcher at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden.

Working with collaborators at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, the team also developed a latest technique for measuring glucose uptake using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS), an analytical technique that could have applications beyond diabetes research.

“I expect our method will be ideal for studying biological processes that require simultaneous tracking of multiple molecules,” stated Julio Landero, PhD, the study’s co-corresponding author and associate professor and director of a trace metals lab at Mount Sinai.

Although the researchers have established how the pathway behaves in isolated animal muscles, they have yet to identify the specific transport protein responsible or determine whether targeting it can improve blood sugar regulation.

In a recent development, “This study defines the core properties of mSGLT in muscle. Studies are underway to identify the gene and protein at the molecular level,” said Heiny.

Industry observers note that reference: “Insulin-independent glucose uptake into mouse skeletal muscle by a sodium/glucose linked transporter” by Natalie J. Norman, Tatiana L. Radzyukevich, Peter W. Chomczynski, Michal Rymaszewski, Izabela D. Fokt, Waldemar Priebe, Lucas Schmidt, Tiffany Zhu, Bryan Mackenzie, Julio A. Landero and Judith A. Heiny, 19 November 2026, Communications Biology. DOI: 10.1038/s42003-026-10848-y.

The National Institutes of Health, the UC College of Medicine and private philanthropy funded this research.

Breaking: A Brief-ish History of METI. Part IV: Millennial METI Experiments

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that welcome back to our ongoing series on the Brief-ish History of Messaging Extraterrestrial Intelligence (METI).
  • It has been revealed that today, we'll look at experiments conducted since the end of the Space Age and the turn of the century.
  • Industry observers note that this era also saw revitalized efforts to search for signs of past (and maybe present) life on Mars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that welcome back to our ongoing series on the Brief-ish History of Messaging Extraterrestrial Intelligence (METI). In our previous installments, we examined the inspiration and earliest experiments in this field. We then looked at how it co-evolved with the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI), leading to the first true attempt to send a message of greeting to the stars (the Arecibo Message). We followed up with a look at two of the brightest minds in the business (Frank Drake and Carl Sagan), the brains behind the first interstellar messages (the Pioneer Plaques and the Voyager Golden Records).

It has been revealed that today, we'll look at experiments conducted since the end of the Space Age and the turn of the century. And just like SETI, the number of experiments has grown considerably, thanks to renewed interest in space exploration following new efforts to explore Mars and the Solar System. This included the first orbital observatory, the venerable Hubble Space Telescope, and deep space probes like the Galileo, Cassini-Huygens, Magellan, and Venus Express missions.

Industry observers note that this era also saw revitalized efforts to search for signs of past (and maybe present) life on Mars. These included orbiters like the Mars Odyssey and Mars Express missions, and rovers and landers like Mars Pathfinder and Sojourner, as well as Spirit and Opportunity. These experiments also reflected the changing nature of space exploration, which included missions from emerging space agencies, non-profits, and private entities.

All of these experiments built on the legacy of the Arecibo Message, adding additional information and personal touches where the creators desired.

Recent findings suggest that an explanatory diagram of a message transmitted in 1983 by Masaki Morimoto and Hisashi Hirabayashi to Altair. Credit: ShizuShizu/Wikimedia.

In 1983, astronomers Masaaki Morimoto and Hisashi Hirabayashi used the Stanford Dish radio telescope at Stanford University to transmit the Message to Altair (or the Call to the Cosmos 83'). The message was produced in collaboration with the Japanese publication Weekly Shonen Jump and transmitted on August 15th, 1983, to commemorate the publication's 15th anniversary. The destination was Altair, an A-type blue-white giant star located 16.7 light-years from Earth, which represents the Shinto deity Hikoboshi in the Tanabata legend.

Recent findings suggest that like the Arecibo Message, the content was a symbolic, graphic message meant to convey information about humanity, life on Earth, and peace. Unlike the Arecibo message, the Message to Altair consisted of several pages rather than a single, long pictograph, each dealing with a different subject. The first page included mathematical information, such as the numbers 1 to 12, prime numbers, powers of 3, formulas for indicating addition and multiplication, and chemical elements essential to life.

Industry observers note that for this, Morimoto and Hirabayashi chose hydrogen, helium, carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen, the building blocks of stars and planetary systems. Several other molecules were included, including hydroxide, water, nitrous oxide, formaldehyde, hydrogen cyanide, and their respective wavelengths. All of these chemicals play a central role in prebiotic chemistry and the formation of organic molecules that give rise to life.

Sources indicate that page two included information on the Solar System, including (from top to bottom) the Sun, the planets in order of distance, some of the larger moons, and their equatorial radii and mean distances from the Sun. Pages three and four included the chemical formulae for DNA compounds, as well as showing DNA structure and replication. This was followed by a series of drawings that showed different types of life forms on Earth, and they were arranged to convey the process of biological evolution.

They begin with pictures of early primitive life, followed by jellyfish, fish, amphibians, lizards, early mammals, apes, and then humans. Like the Pioneer Plaques, this image shows a man and a woman with two children between them. This was followed by a close-up illustration of the woman's face waving hello. The last page highlighted the transmission parameters: the total number of bits, the transmission wavelength, and the radius of the radio telescope that beamed the message.

It also contained the Japanese and English spelling for the word "toast," followed by the chemical formula for ethanol alcohol - in short, the message concludes with the raising of a toast with an alcoholic drink.

The thirteen pictures that make up the Message to Altair, listed in order (left to right, top to bottom). Credit: Shinya Nurasawa.

As Altair is approximately 17 light-years distant, the message would have arrived around 2000, and the window for a reply would open by 2017. In 2023, Hyogo University astronomer Shin-ya Narusawa (who knew Morimoto before his death) asked the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) to help search for a possible reply. JAXA obliged and used the radio antenna at the Usuda Space Observatory to observe Altair for an hour at 10 p.m. on August 22nd, 2023.

It has been revealed that the date was significant because it also fell on Tanabata in the old Japanese calendar and is the only day of the year when the deities Orihime and Hikoboshi (represented by Vega and Altair, respectively) are allowed to meet. The observations detected no signals, but Narusawa said he intends to continue observing and collaborating with other research institutions.

Between 1999 and 2003, three METI experiments were conducted using the Evpatoria Planetary Radar (EPR), a Soviet-era facility located in the Crimea for deep-space communications and radio astronomy. All four projects were organized with help from famed Soviet-Russian radio engineer, astronomer, and SETI researcher Alexander Zaitsev. As we addressed in part I of the series, he coined the term METI in his 2006 paper, Messaging to Extra-Terrestrial Intelligence.

The first project to use the EPR RT-70 radio telescope was the Cosmic Call, which included two broadcasts, one sent in 1999 and the other in 2003. The venture was a crowdsourced effort by Texas-based startup Team Encounter, Canadian astrophysicist Yvan Dutil, Russian scientists (including Zaitsev), and Eastern European radio engineers.

The message included contributions by Dutil and his fellow physicist StÃ©phane Dumas. Their primer was inspired by Hans Freudenthal's 1960 book Lincos: Design of a Language for Cosmic Intercourse, which describes a language designed to be understandable to an extraterrestrial intelligence (ETI). Using Lincos, Dutil and Dumas' message (DDM) was carefully structured to include pictograms showing mathematics, physics (the hydrogen spectrum), and related concepts.

According to recent reports, the second part consisted of a series of pictograms created by Richard Braastad of Team Encounter, the Braastad Message (DM). It used mathematical symbols to describe a solar sail (another project Team Encounter was working on), including its dimensions, payload, trajectory, and projected launch time. This was followed by the original Arecibo Message (AM), the company's Team Encounter 2001 Staff Message (ESM), and a message composed with input from the public - the Public Part (PP).

The second page of the primer prepared by Dutil and Dumas, denoting mathematical concepts (part of the Cosmic Call). Credit: Dumas, S.

The broadcast was broken into four sessions, lasting a total of 40 hours, with each session targeting a different Sun-like (G-type) star system. These included 16 Cygni A on May 24th, 1999, a G-type star in a triple-star system located 69 light-years from Earth. On June 30th, 1999, the target was 15 Sagittae, another G-type star about 58 light-years from Earth in the Sagittarius Constellation. Lastly, and again on June 30th, 1999, the team transmitted to HD 178428, a G-type star located 69 light-years away, also in the Sagittarius Constellation.

Industry observers note that each session of Cosmic Call 1 transmitted the scientific parts (DDM, BM, AM, and ESM) three times at 100 bits per second, followed by the Public Part (PP), sent once at 2000 bits/s. The full message was structured as:.

DDM â BM â AM â ESM â DDM â BM â AM â ESM â DDM â BM â AM â ESM â PP.

It has been revealed that the second Cosmic Call, in 2003, followed a similar structure. For this message, Dutil and Dumas presented an updated version of their Lincos pictographs (DDM2), the Arecibo Message, the Bilingual Image Glossary, and the same Public Part. The structure was as follows:.

DDM2 â DDM2 â DDM2 â AM â AM â AM â SIGNIFICANT â BIG â BIG â BM â ESM â PP,.

The destinations for this message included five more stars, with all transmissions occurring on the same day (July 6th, 2033). They included GJ 49, a G-type star located 32 light-years away in the constellation Cassiopeia, on July 6th, 2003. This was followed by Gliese 208, an M-type (red dwarf) star 37 light-years away in the constellation Orion; 55 Cancri, an M-type star 41 light-years away in Cancer; HD 10307, a binary star system with a G-type primary and an M-type companion 42.6 light-years away in Andromeda; and 47 Ursae Majoris, a G-type star located 45.3 light-years away in Ursa Major.

The Cosmic Calls were the most ambitious public SETI/METI effort mounted to date. While Team Encounter went bankrupt in the years that followed, their messages established a precedent that would be joined by several more METI efforts in the newly introduced millennium. Zaitsev would play a key role in several, and his work with his colleagues would culminate by 2008 in the creation of METI International. More on that soon!

Latest Update: Cancer Cells Are Turning Antioxidants Into Weapons Against the Immune System

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1070 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly discovered weakness in cancer cells could open the door to treatments that help the immune system overcome tumors that have resisted immunotherapy.
  • According to recent reports, cancer immunotherapy has helped some patients fight even advanced cancers, yet many tumors still find ways to escape the immune system.
  • The finding, published in the journal Science, points to a potential new target for cancer treatment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly discovered weakness in cancer cells could open the door to treatments that help the immune system overcome tumors that have resisted immunotherapy.

According to recent reports, cancer immunotherapy has helped some patients fight even advanced cancers, yet many tumors still find ways to escape the immune system. Researchers have now uncovered one possible reason why. Cancer cells can release a protein that removes chemical signals needed by the very immune cells trying to destroy them.

The finding, published in the journal Science, points to a potential new target for cancer treatment. It also challenges a familiar assumption about antioxidants, which are generally associated with protecting cells from damage.

At the center of the discovery are reactive oxygen species (ROS), often called free radicals. These molecules have long been linked to aging, DNA damage, and cancer. In small amounts, however, they serve another purpose. Cancer-fighting immune cells called T cells rely on ROS to activate and attack tumors.

Sources indicate that researchers found that some cancers exploit this dependency by releasing an antioxidant enzyme called peroxiredoxin-1 (PRDX1). The protein removes ROS from the surrounding environment, depriving T cells of signals they need to function.

Industry observers note that “One of the surprising findings is that antioxidants aren’t always beneficial in the context of cancer,” remarked Robert L. Eil, M.D., a physician-scientist who co-led the research. “While reactive oxygen species sound threatening, T cells actually need them to perform their tumor-fighting job. What we found is that tumors can exploit the T cell’s dependency by removing the reactive oxygen species the immune system depends on.”.

Eil is an associate professor of surgery in the Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU) School of Medicine and a member of the OHSU Knight Cancer Institute. The study was conducted alongside investigators at the University of Cambridge.

Sources indicate that the researchers uncovered the mechanism by examining tumor interstitial fluid, the liquid surrounding cells within tumors. They found high levels of PRDX1, creating an antioxidant-rich environment that could interfere with the immune response.

To determine whether the protein was directly helping cancer survive, the team used CRISPR gene-editing technology to prevent cancer cells from producing PRDX1. Without the enzyme, immune activity increased and tumor growth declined across multiple experimental models.

In one melanoma model, the immune system rejected tumors lacking PRDX1 without additional treatment. In other models, removing the protein made previously resistant tumors respond to immune checkpoint blockade, a type of immunotherapy that helps T cells recognize and attack cancer.

In a recent development, the researchers also looked for evidence of the same process in humans. They analyzed published data from human cancer cell lines, studied gene activity across thousands of tumors, and measured PRDX1 in fluid collected from patient tumors. All three approaches provided evidence that human cancers release PRDX1 into their surroundings, where it can suppress T cell activity.

Recent findings suggest that “We tend to think of reactive oxygen species purely as damaging byproducts of metabolism. But we are increasingly understanding that ROS have key functions within cells, and T cells require them to activate,” mentioned Alexander J. Wesolowski, Ph.D., the study’s first author and a researcher in the Department of Pathology at the University of Cambridge. “Our study develops this picture, revealing that tumors can exploit this very dependency to evade elimination.”.

Sources indicate that the team also found that cancer cells increased PRDX1 production during a process called immunoediting. As tumors evolve under pressure from the immune system, they can develop characteristics that help them survive. Producing more of this antioxidant protein appears to be one way they may strengthen their defenses.

The researchers describe the mechanism as a previously unrecognized “redox checkpoint,” referring to the way tumors manipulate ROS levels to suppress immune activity.

Understanding this process could be particularly useful for improving immunotherapy, which remains ineffective for many patients despite its success against certain cancers.

“The immune system has already shown us that it can eradicate advanced cancers in some patients,” Eil stated. “The challenge is that current immunotherapies don’t work for most people, and even when they do, complete responses remain relatively uncommon. The more we understand how tumors suppress T cells, the more opportunities we have to design therapies that reverse that suppression.”.

Recent findings suggest that possible treatments could include drugs that neutralize antioxidants released by tumors, therapies that block PRDX1 activity, or engineered immune cells capable of functioning in antioxidant-rich environments. These approaches remain possibilities for future research rather than established treatments.

Sources indicate that “What’s exciting is that we’ve identified a target nobody was really looking for before,” Eil said. “This doesn’t put a drug in patients’ hands tomorrow, but it gives us an entirely newly introduced pathway to pursue. Discovering new targets is how future treatments begin.”.

Eil and his collaborators proposal to continue investigating how tumors weaken immune responses and whether those defenses can be overcome with next-generation immunotherapies, including engineered T cell treatments.

Industry observers note that “This is one more victory against ignorance in understanding why cancers are so difficult to treat,” Eil remarked. “Every time we uncover a new way tumors suppress the immune system, we gain another opportunity to fight back. That’s how better treatments are built.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Universe as we know it is comprised of three "things": baryonic matter (planets, stars, galaxies, us), dark matter (still unexplained) and dark energy (really, really still unexplained). Of the three, dark energy remains the most challenging. It's "something" that's driving the acceleration of the expanding Universe but that's all we know about it. We can't see it, or even put a description to it, other than "it's mysterious".

It has been revealed that this cosmic component accounts for about 70 percent of the known Universe's energy budget. Physicists have spent a lot of time trying to explain it, often invoking some hitherto-unknown fields, or exotic physical particles, or some kind of "cosmological constant" that is the same everywhere in space and time. Despite these and other attempts at explaining dark energy, physicists still don't know exactly what it is. However, there's hope that an explanation will come in our lifetimes. A team of scientists at Canada's University of British Columbia and the University of Sheffield (in England) have come up with a possible model that provides an explanation. They think dark matter may be a product of the same physics that governs the strength of the atomic nucleus. If that's true, then they could use the standard model of particle physics to understand this mysterious thing that is pushing the Universe apart.

Dark energy has many descriptions, which reflects our incomplete understanding of it. It could be a negative pressure that pushes space outward, although thereâs no proof of that. It could be vacuum energy, which is an idea that thereâs a background of energy that permeates all of the Universe. Itâs also been called âquintessenceâ, which is a sort of imaginary âfluidâ that fills space. Or it could be a combo of dark matter and dark energy, both yet unexplained. The wildest idea is that dark energy could be a wrinkle in the fabric of space-time, or even something leaking from another universe. All those explanations are fairly wild, and oftentimes in science, the simplest is the best explanation. Thatâs where the work in Canada and England is coming in handy, if particle physics can provide insight.

According to lead scientist Ariel Zhitnitsky of UBC, using particle physics means we don't need exotic explanations for dark energy. âOur theoretical framework suggests no new particles may be required at all,â said Zhitnitsky, who developed the theoretical ideas explained by the team. âThe characteristic energy scale predicted from the QCD vacuum and gravity comes out close to the observed dark-energy scale today without having to introduce an ad hoc new field nor new parameter.â.

What Zhitnitsky and others are talking about is a theory called quantum chromodynamics (QCD). It focuses on the strong nuclear force that holds quarks inside the protons and neutrons that make up atoms. QCD describes the actions of the strong force. Those actions could be affecting space, and in particular what it contains.

Recent findings suggest that A NASA illustration of the strong force at work in an atomic nucleus. Credit: NASA.

Sources indicate that space is never empty. Rather, itâs filled with subatomic fields and something called quantum energy. That's energy that exists in individual packets called âquantaâ. This creates a âquantum vacuumâ with properties that can affect space over large distances. Now, add in the fact that the Universe is expanding, and that has implications that need further explanation. The team, led by scientist Dong Ha Lee, proposed the following: as the Universe expands, the subatomic structure in the quantum vacuum responds differently as time goes by. That response generates a small energy shift that is just enough to drive the acceleration of universal expansion. The team points out that you donât need fresh particles or other exotic things for this: the current particles are just fine, Lee suggested. âThe idea that the quantum vacuum as described by QCD could have the right properties to account for the accelerated expansion of the universe is very intriguing,â said Lee.

It has been revealed that so, if this idea holds up, it means that dark energy could have a connection to the strong nuclear force. Scientists could create models to test this using at the moment available physics models. The big test would be to compare it to cosmological data, according to Lee. âOur analysis demonstrates that such a model can reproduce the evolving dark energy behaviour suggested by current observations. This motivates further theoretical work to better understand how the QCD vacuum responds to cosmic expansion and to develop predictions that can be tested with future observations.â.

It has been revealed that when tested against real astronomical data including light from distant supernovae and leftover radiation from the early Universe, the team found that their model matched observations just as well as standard cosmological models. In addition, it offers a possible way to explain what is causing dark energy. The next step for the team is to keep refining their model and calculations in order to build as robust a model as possible. By that time, observations and data from the next generations of telescopes, such as the Nancy Grace Roman telescope, could prove very useful in testing ideas about the true nature of dark energy and its effects on the expanding Universe over time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It was a hot, dry day in the Kalahari Desert, and Mathilde Martin was running after a meerkat.

Industry observers note that the animal wore a GPS tracker around its neck and bolted between shelters, like an action hero running for cover, indicates Martin, a biologist at the University of Zurich. She and her colleagues had captured the meerkat earlier that morning, driven it 1.5 kilometers from its pack and then released it into the desert. They were trying to find out how well individual meerkats could find their way back home.

According to recent reports, the answer was quite well, the researchers reported November 19 in the Journal of Experimental Biology. The results suggest that meerkats can navigate expertly on their own, perhaps relying on mental maps charted early in life. “They all seem to be very, very good,” Martin states. It’s a surprise finding for a species known for its group cooperation.

Meerkats (Suricata suricatta), which live in southern Africa, form tight-knit family groups of up to 50 members. These social animals cooperate in many aspects of life, including by babysitting each other’s pups and watching for predators while traveling along foraging paths. Martin and her colleagues thought meerkats might also rely on one another for navigating. Some pack members, perhaps those who’ve had more opportunity to explore solo, might have spatial knowledge of their territory and lead the rest, she says. But that’s not what the team discovered.

In a recent development, in separate catch and release experiments with 20 individual meerkats, 18 made a beeline back home, back to their group or back to the site where they were captured. (The other two may have been too stressed to get moving, Martin indicates.).

Recent findings suggest that neither age nor individual experience, which researchers had been tracking, seemed to factor into the meerkats’ homing skills. Nearly all of them knew where to go, Martin claims. She thinks these crackerjack navigators relied on visual cues to orient themselves. They’d pop up on their hind legs and scan the landscape before scampering off in a direct line to their target.

It’s likely that scent played a role, too, though distant scent marks may have faded by the time the meerkats were released. The researchers dropped the animals off in territory they hadn’t visited for at least 30 days. “Otherwise,” she says, “it would have been a bit too easy for them to find their way back,” she says.

Upcoming Discovery Could Transform How We Treat Chronic Back Pain

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Restoring a protein that declines in aging spinal discs reduced DNA damage in human cells in the lab, revealing a potential fresh target for back pain treatments.
  • Sources indicate that for people living with persistent back pain, everyday activities such as walking, bending, or even sitting comfortably can become difficult.
  • Spinal discs are cushion-like structures between vertebrae that allow the spine to move.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Restoring a protein that declines in aging spinal discs reduced DNA damage in human cells in the lab, revealing a potential fresh target for back pain treatments.

Sources indicate that for people living with persistent back pain, everyday activities such as walking, bending, or even sitting comfortably can become difficult. New research from the University of Utah points toward a possible way to address one of the underlying causes of age-related back pain by protecting the cells that keep spinal discs healthy.

Spinal discs are cushion-like structures between vertebrae that allow the spine to move. In a study published in Aging Cell, researchers found that older and damaged discs contained lower levels of a protein called BLST, which is encoded by the ZNF865 gene. The study is the first to characterize the function of both the gene and its protein.

Industry observers note that to understand whether declining BLST levels contribute to disc deterioration, the researchers used CRISPR, a gene-editing tool that can be used to regulate the activity of specific genes. Restoring BLST production in human disc cells reduced signs of cellular aging and DNA damage, while decreasing its activity in mouse and rat models led to disc degeneration and pain-related behaviors. The findings suggest that BLST helps maintain healthy spinal discs by protecting cells from damage and dysfunction as they age.

Sources indicate that “This paper directly shows a novel understanding that DNA damage is a driver of back pain, and that we can regulate BLST therapeutically with CRISPR,” remarked Robby D. Bowles, the study’s lead researcher and an associate professor of biomedical engineering. “Back pain is the number three leading cause of disability as measured by disability-adjusted life years, only behind cardiac disease and drug use disorders.”.

Although increasing BLST activity could eventually offer a way to prevent or treat age-related back pain, additional preclinical studies and, ultimately, clinical trials are needed to determine whether targeting the protein with CRISPR is safe and effective in people.

The research brought together Bowles and members of his laboratory in the John and Marcia Price College of Engineering, specialists in orthopedics and arthritis at the Spencer Fox Eccles School of Medicine, and researchers at Huntsman Cancer Institute at the University of Utah.

Because DNA damage is involved in numerous diseases, the discovery could have applications well beyond spinal health.

“It has been the highlight of my career to work on a protein that was unknown and be the first to identify its function,” Bowles noted. “While this work focuses on its application to back pain, the mechanisms identified have the potential to be applied to treat cancer, neurodegeneration, and any disease in which DNA damage is involved.”.

Further research is needed to establish whether the protective mechanisms observed in spinal disc cells also play a role in age-related cancers.

Recent findings suggest that “The fact that a single gene can restore normal cell function and reverse aging-related effects is incredible,” stated Jason Gertz, a professor in the Department of Oncological Sciences at the University of Utah and co-leader of the Genomics, Epigenetics, and Metabolism Program at Huntsman Cancer Institute. “BLST is widely expressed across tissues and could be a promising target for cancer treatment and prevention, since boosting BLST activity should improve the repair of DNA damage and the overall health of aging cells.”.

It has been revealed that reference: “ZNF865 (BLST) a Novel Regulator of DNA Damage and Cell Senescence in Back Pain” by Christian Lewis, Hunter Levis, Jonah Holbrook, Jacob T. Polaski, Timothy D. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Comets are time capsules of the origins of the solar system, containing materials that have existed for billions of years. While comets primarily orbit in the farthest reaches of the solar system, specifically the Kuiper Belt or Oort Cloud, some make their way closer to the Sun. When this happens, the increased heat cause cometary icy material to evaporate, producing a spectacular tail while also revealing the rocky material underneath, known as a cometâs nucleus. But how well can astronomers use telescopic observations to study the composition and temperatures of a cometary nucleus?

Recent findings suggest that now, a team of researchers from Japan might be one step closer to scientists better understanding comets, specifically a cometâs nucleus. Through findings recently published in The Astronomical Journal, the researchers presented new analyses regarding the shape and temperature of a comateâs nucleus, providing researchers with key observations that could be used to understand both the formation and evolution of comets and the solar system.

For the study, the researchers analyzed archival data on Comet 2P/Encke originally obtained from the Cooled Mid-Infrared Camera and Spectrometer (COMICS) on the Subaru Telescope in November 2003. During this time, Comet 2P/Encke traveled as close as 0.26 astronomical units (AU) from Earth, or about 37 million kilometers (26 million miles), enabling several ground-based telescopes, including the Subaru Telescope, to conduct mid-infrared observations of Comet 2P/Encke. This distance from Earth also put Comet 2P/Encke about 1.09 AU from the Sun, or about 163 million kilometers (101 million miles). Unfortunately, COMICS was retired from Subaru in 2020, leaving Subaru without a mid-infrared instrument, thus limiting its studies to archival data.

Recent findings suggest that the primary goal of the study was to ascertain the composition of Comet 2P/Enckeâs nucleus while isolating its signal from the surrounding ice, gas, and dust that envelopes the comet and becomes larger and denser as the increased Sunâs heat evaporates it. In the end, the researchers found the nucleus of Comet 2P/Encke measured about 7 kilometers by 3 kilometers (4.3 miles by 1.9 miles) while its surface temperature is estimated to be about 328 Kelvin (55 degrees Celsius/131 degrees Fahrenheit).

It has been revealed that "Our study of Comet Encke showed that mid-infrared observations can directly capture thermal emission from the nucleus itself," said Dr. Takafumi Ootsubo, who is assistant professor in the Department of Basic Sciences at the School of Medicine at the University of Occupational and Environmental Health in Japan, and lead author of the study. Despite COMICS retiring in 2020, Dr. Ootsubo is actively working to restart the program. "By restarting COMICS, we hope to study the shapes, temperatures, and surface materials of many more cometary nuclei in detail and get closer to revealing their true faces.".

Recent findings suggest that as noted, comets originate from the far reaches of the solar system, specifically the Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud, with Comet 2P/Encke originating from the former. However, some comets periodically migrate inward and become whatâs known as a Jupiter-family comet, which is what happened to Comet 2P/Encke. This means Comet 2P/Enckeâs orbit has been both captured and reshaped by Jupiterâs massive gravity, resulting in its orbit becoming significantly shorter than traditional comets at only 3.3 years. This is in stark contrast to traditional comets, which can take anywhere from decades to millions of years to travel from the outer solar system to the inner solar system and potentially be observed from Earth.

Industry observers note that while its orbit is only 3.3 years, this doesnât mean it encounters Earth every 3.3 years. Instead, Comet 2P/Enckeâs orbit is constantly reshaping, meaning it has only had a limited few encounters with Earth in the last few decades. Along with the November 2003 encounter, Comet 2P/Encke came within only about 0.19 AU (28.5 million kilometers/17.7 million miles) from Earth in July 1997 and is slated to come within 0.62 AU (93 million kilometers/58 million miles) from Earth in February 2027.

Sources indicate that what new insights into Comet Encke and other comets in our solar system will researchers make in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that A leafy branch was out of reach for two gorillas at the Ramat Gan Safari, and an electric barrier around the trunk blocked a direct climb.
  • Sources indicate that the most extensively documented event came to light in September 2024, when keepers noticed the pair peacefully eating bark and leaves from a large branch that had previously been beyond their reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two zoo gorillas repeatedly teamed up for food despite rarely spending time together, showing that a shared effort does not always end with a shared meal.

It has been revealed that A leafy branch was out of reach for two gorillas at the Ramat Gan Safari, and an electric barrier around the trunk blocked a direct climb. The female western lowland gorillas, half-sisters Amelia and Lisha, formed a “living ladder,” with Lisha providing a steady back for Amelia to stand on.

Sources indicate that the most extensively documented event came to light in September 2024, when keepers noticed the pair peacefully eating bark and leaves from a large branch that had previously been beyond their reach. Staff reviewed security camera footage to find out how they had obtained it.

The recording indicated Amelia walking over and climbing onto a rock beneath a Peltophorum dubium tree. Lisha joined her and stood firmly on all fours on the rock. Amelia then climbed onto Lisha’s back, stood upright, and reached up to grasp and break off a branch approximately 4.5 meters, or 15 feet, above the ground. The rock, Lisha’s stable posture, and Amelia’s reach together made the branch accessible.

Researchers documented three events involving the same pair in 2021, 2024, and 2025, with each gorilla performing the same role every time. Neither had been trained to perform the maneuver. The team describes their behavior as a rare example of spontaneous cooperation between adult gorillas, with a clear division of roles.

Recent findings suggest that published in Primates, the study was led by Michael Levitzky and Prof. Israel Hershkovitz of the Department of Anatomy and Anthropology at the Gray Faculty of Medical and Health Sciences and the Dan David Center for Human Evolution and Biohistory Research at Tel Aviv University.

Yehonatan Samocha, Head of the Primate Section at the Ramat Gan Safari (Zoological Center Tel Aviv-Ramat Gan), said, “At the Ramat Gan Safari we have observed and studied animal behaviors for years, closely following their relationships, social bonds, and fascinating capabilities. Particularly among great apes, including gorillas, we repeatedly encounter behaviors that demonstrate high intelligence, learning ability, problem-solving, complex communication, and cooperation.

Sources indicate that “This is why we are so thrilled, though not necessarily surprised, by the cooperation between Amelia and Lisha. We are familiar with their abilities and understand how intelligent and curious they are, and how capable they are of learning from one another and working together. Sometimes, our surprise tells us more about our expectations of animals than their actual abilities. The study’s great importance lies in providing scientific documentation and analysis for observations and behaviors we encounter in our daily work, allowing us to enhance our knowledge of gorillas, their social world, and their cognitive abilities.”.

In a recent development, in the June 2025 footage, Lisha positioned herself with her back toward Amelia, who was not observed using force. Levitzky, who initiated and led the study, explained how the recording helped the researchers interpret Lisha’s participation.

In a recent development, “When I first watched the footage, it was clear to me that this was something extraordinary. What I find fascinating is that Leisha did more than simply serve as a ‘step’ for Amelia. She appeared to participate actively and willingly in solving the problem, approaching on her own initiative and positioning herself in exactly the right place, without Amelia physically guiding her. This is the difference between using another individual as a tool and true cooperation, in which both individuals work together toward the same goal.

“For years, gorillas were considered less cognitively sophisticated than other great apes. As more observations like these accumulate, we will be able to deepen and refine our understanding of their social and cognitive abilities. Future studies involving systematic documentation and audio recordings could help us decipher how they coordinate with one another, and perhaps also teach us something about the roots of cooperation in our own species.”.

The sisters generally spend little time together, sleep in separate night quarters, and rarely groom one another. Their teamwork also had different outcomes at feeding time. Although keepers reported peaceful sharing after the 2024 event, Amelia alone ate the vegetation in the observed 2025 sequence, showing that cooperating to obtain food did not necessarily lead to sharing it.

Sources indicate that hershkovitz remarked, “Our observations reveal how two gorillas can join forces and assume complementary roles to solve a problem that neither can solve on her own. It is particularly intriguing that this cooperation recurs even though the two do not usually display much closeness, and even when the food is not shared between them afterward. These observations are vital for understanding human evolution because they offer an explanation, albeit a partial one, for how we survived on the savanna – through social support and a high level of cooperation that can occur even without language or preplanning. Although the number of observations is small, they offer a window into gorillas’ ability to learn from experience, coordinate their actions, and draw on one another and their surroundings to achieve a shared goal.”.

The study involved only two gorillas and three documented events. The available footage could not establish whether they communicated through vocalizations or subtle gestures, or whether they planned their actions in advance.

According to recent reports, reference: “Cooperation in adult female western lowland gorillas: complex problem-solving through learned spatial affordances and mutual agency” by Michael Levitzky, and Israel Hershkovitz, 24 October 2026, Primates. DOI: 10.1007/s10329-026-01297-6.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Star formation is a galaxy's foundational process. Astronomers study how star-forming gas moves around in a galaxy, where it's compressed, and in which parts of a galaxy stars form. In a barred spiral galaxy like the Milky Way, star formation is mostly concentrated in the spiral arms. In the central bar, star formation is more sluggish.

Industry observers note that recent research shows that though the central bar contains many stars, star formation there is mostly concentrated in the bar ends. Shear forces, streaming motions, and overpowering shocks that make the gas in the bars turbulent all combine to to inhibit star formation.

Recent findings suggest that the Milky Way is a typical barred spiral galaxy, and astronomers have studied it intently to understand where star formation is concentrated. There's ongoing scientific debate about what happens in a barred spiral galaxy's central bar. Observations of other spiral barred galaxies show that star formation suppression there isn't necessarily universal. Part of the difficulty in understanding our own galaxy is observing the region. Since we're embedded in the galaxy, it's difficult to observe the bar. In many ways, astronomers have an easier time observing other galaxies.

Researchers from Australia and Sweden have found an unusual structure in the Milky Way's center that appears to set it apart from many other barred spiral galaxies. It's a vast collection of rotating stars in the central bar that's generating powerful and large shock fronts in the gas. These shock fronts are triggering star formation in the structure, which goes against the idea that stars can't form there.

Recent findings suggest that the results are in fresh research titled "The nature of the Norma arm as a bar-driven star-forming shock front," and it's published in Nature Astronomy. The lead author is Dr. Hilary Davis from the University of Sydneyâs School of Physics and Sydney Institute for Astronomy. The research is casting doubt on the existence of one of the Milky Way's spiral arms, the Norma arm.

Recent findings suggest that this illustration reveals the Milky Way's major and minor spiral arms, as well as its central bar. The Norma arm is close to the galaxy's center. Image Credit: NASA.

Sources indicate that "The Milky Way is commonly depicted as having four main spiral arms, including the Normaâouter arm, and a central stellar bar whose properties remain debated," the authors write. In past work, researchers have used astrophysical masers, which are coherent microwave emissions from young massive stars, to trace part of the Norma arm that extends from the central bar. So those results suggest that the masers reside along the Norma spiral arm.

But the Milky Way's bar is tricky to study. âThe Galactic bar cannot be easily observed because of a combination of our position in the Galaxy and dust obscuring our view,â Dr Davis said. âAs a result, the barâs properties have been highly debated.â.

This latest research, based on observations and massive astrophysical simulations suggests that what those masers really trace is the shock front or dust lane in its bar. Since stars form along shock fronts where gas is compressed, star formation is at the heart of this work. "This implies that the bar dust lane is star-forming, shedding new light on our understanding of star formation processes in the Milky Way," the authors explain.

It has been revealed that this graphic demonstrates modelling of the Milky Way with the Norma arm overlapping the bar shock front in the Milky Way. It's based on observations of masers from young stars. Previous research suggested those masers and young stars were in the Norma arm, but this work shows they're tracing star formation along a shock front in the Milky Way's central bar. Image Credit: Hillary Davis/University of Sydney.

According to recent reports, âAt its heart, star formation is a process we understand from everyday physics. Forces set matter in motion. In this case gas is compressed, and that compression can create the conditions for new stars to be born on a massive scale,â lead author Davis said.

Industry observers note that modern telescopes give us clear views of other galaxies on a regular basis. Observations of other spiral galaxies show that star formation is abundant in their spiral arms, where gas is compressed by density waves.

Recent findings suggest that âIn most similar galaxies, star formation very commonly occurs along spiral arms. Whatâs extraordinary is seeing this happen in a different region of our Galaxy, where shocks are usually so strong that star formation is often suppressed,â mentioned Davis.

In a recent development, the researchers used large-scale astrophysical models run on powerful computers to try to understand the masers and what they meant for star formation, and what part of the Milky Way's structure they traced. They found that the masers indicated star formation along a shock front in the bar, not in the Norma arm. Observational challenges made it seem like those masers were in the Norma arm.

âWe believe that the Milky Wayâs bar has star formation occurring along its shock front, which is uncommon for most bars in nearby galaxies,â Dr Davis stated.

Sources indicate that this figure from the research shows how what appears to be a spiral arm with star formation is actually the shock front from the central bar where stars are forming. "The red scatter points with black borders are the Norma masers," the authors write, but they actually line up with the shock front and may not be a spiral bar at all. Hence, the association of Norma masers with the Galactic bar shock front suggests that SF is occurring along the Galactic bar dust lane," the authors explain.

The result is that part of the Norma arm may have lost its status as a spiral arm.

According to recent reports, âWe found that masers previously associated with the Norma arm closely align with the shock front predicted by our simulations,â Dr Davis said. âThis suggests that at least part of the so-called Norma arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a region of star formation along the leading edge of the Galactic bar.".

These results show that stars can more readily form in the central bar, something that seemed prohibitive. âThis raises questions about the Galaxyâs spiral structure, and the bar region of the Milky Way, which needs further investigation,â she stated.

Astronomers have studied the Milky Way's central bar and argued about its nature for decades. According to recent reports, in plain language, they're saying that the bar's full, end-to-end length is about 28,000 light years, its width is about 15,000 light years, and it's tilted about 20 degrees from our line of sight. It also takes about 154 million years to complete one rotation.

For comparison, prior estimates of the bar's length range from 3,000 to 16,000 light years, and its width has been estimated between 8,000 and 16,000 light years. Measurements of its time to complete one rotation range from 102 to 246 million years. So these results are inside existing ranges.

Sources indicate that the wide ranges for its size and rotation speed illustrate how difficult studying the bar is. A fast-growing heart is good for the Grinch. People are another story

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Seuss tale, How the Grinch Stole Christmas, the Grinch starts out with a heart “two sizes too small.” He’s a mean one, disguising himself as Santa Claus and stealing all the Whos’ toys, food and decorations.
  • In a recent development, “They say that the Grinch’s small heart grew three sizes that day,” giving him “the strength of 10 Grinches plus two,” indicates the narrator of the 1966 movie version.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In the classic Dr. Seuss tale, How the Grinch Stole Christmas, the Grinch starts out with a heart “two sizes too small.” He’s a mean one, disguising himself as Santa Claus and stealing all the Whos’ toys, food and decorations. Poised to throw it all off a mountain, the grumpy loner has a change of heart as joyous song rises from Whoville.

In a recent development, “They say that the Grinch’s small heart grew three sizes that day,” giving him “the strength of 10 Grinches plus two,” indicates the narrator of the 1966 movie version. With a beatific smile, he pulls the stolen goods back from the brink and returns everything.

Would a too-small heart make you grumpy like the Grinch? And what would happen if your heart went from too small to really big in an instant? The answer depends on what causes the heart to shrink or swell, experts say. And whether or not you are a snake.

Heart size is generally pegged to body size, says Michelle Kittleson, a cardiologist at Cedars Sinai Smidt Heart Institute in Los Angeles. Bigger people tend to have bigger hearts. But some people, she says, have hearts that are naturally bigger or smaller than average for their bodies. It’s not clear why. However, she says, “there are negative consequences of having a too-small heart.”.

In one 2025 study, researchers looked at medical records from more than 360,000 people in Australia. Those with smaller-than-average hearts had a higher risk of dying within five years than people with average or larger hearts, the team reported in JACC: Advances.

Smaller hearts may not pump blood as well as larger ones, making it harder for people to exercise. And if the Grinch didn’t exercise enough, maybe “then that made him really tired, and that made him grumpy,” Kittleson indicates. “Or maybe he did the research, and he found out that his life expectancy was shortened because of it, and that made him even grumpier.”.

But would rapidly increasing his heart’s size be good for the Grinch?

As the Grinch slides downhill toward Whoville, pulled by a sled piled high with presents he’d stolen and now was returning, he physically undergoes a change. What started as a heart two sizes too small swelled three sizes, both curing his grumpiness and giving him super strength. Or so the classic tale goes. A person going through such a dramatic change may not fare as well.

There are many ways a heart can grow, claims Leslie Leinwand, a molecular biologist and geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder. With vigorous exercise, “your heart gets bigger in good ways,” Leinwand says. That can be true for athletes who do lots of cardio, such as swimmers and marathon runners.

Recent findings suggest that “Their heart gets bigger and thicker,” Kittleson says. “But it’s a good thing in them because it helps them pump more blood per minute than someone with a normal-size heart.” Pregnancy also makes the whole organ expand to boost blood to the developing fetus. If people stop exercising, or give birth, their hearts will shrink back to normal size within months.

Recent findings suggest that some diseases, though, can enlarge hearts in deadly ways. “If you’ve got untreated high blood pressure,” Leinwand says, “you can get a huge heart, and it’s not good for you.”.

Recent findings suggest that stress, bad heart valves and some genetic diseases can also result in bigger, but weaker, hearts. In those cases, the heart muscle grows in order to pump more blood. At the same time, the inside of the left ventricle — the heart chamber that pumps oxygenated blood to the body — can shrink. That makes it harder for the heart to push blood out. This kind of growth takes time, Kittleson indicates.

There is one rare condition in which the heart can inflate suddenly. Called takotsubo or stress cardiomyopathy — or in some cases, broken-heart syndrome — it is brought on by extreme stress. That can include positive things like winning the lottery or entering a surprise party or negative stress such as break-up or losing a job.

A surge of epinephrine, or adrenaline, from stress can make the left ventricle bulge into the shape of a pot used to catch octopuses. (Takotsubo is Japanese for “octopus pot.”) That causes immediate heart failure as the heart chamber gets too significant to pump blood.

According to recent reports, so instead of becoming super strong, the Grinch “would have keeled over and collapsed,” Kittleson claims. (People can survive with prompt medical care and their hearts can return to normal size in a few months.).

Given the Grinch survived his rapid growth, there’s another possible scenario: Maybe his heart is more like a snake’s.

Pythons’ hearts can balloon by up to 25 percent in a day after the snakes eat a large meal — sometimes as substantial as an adult deer. And the bigger a python’s meal, the more its heart grows. Larger hearts pump blood with more force, Leinwand and her colleagues reported in 2024 in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The researchers don’t know if this makes the snakes stronger overall.

Recent findings suggest that once a meal is digested, the heart shrinks again. Snakes can go through many shrink-and-grow cycles with no ill effect. Leinwand hopes that studying these snakes will lead to treatments that make human hearts healthier.

But becoming kinder, like the Grinch? Maybe not.

Notes Leinwand, “our snakes, when they eat a lot, they get rather aggressive.”.

America’s Data Centers Have a Hidden Death Toll, MIT Researchers Warn

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1006 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An MIT analysis estimates that powering America’s data centers contributed to hundreds of premature deaths in a single year, with rural populations facing greater risks than city dwellers.
  • As artificial intelligence drives the rapid construction of data centers across the United States, concerns about their environmental impact are taking on a new dimension.
  • Researchers at MIT estimate that air pollution associated with data center electricity consumption contributed to approximately 650 premature deaths in the United States in 2023 alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An MIT analysis estimates that powering America’s data centers contributed to hundreds of premature deaths in a single year, with rural populations facing greater risks than city dwellers.

As artificial intelligence drives the rapid construction of data centers across the United States, concerns about their environmental impact are taking on a new dimension. The electricity needed to keep these facilities running around the clock can increase air pollution in communities far from where the data centers themselves are built, potentially putting the health of people who live nowhere near them at risk.

Researchers at MIT estimate that air pollution associated with data center electricity consumption contributed to approximately 650 premature deaths in the United States in 2023 alone. Iowa, Nevada, South Dakota, and Kansas had the highest estimated rates of premature deaths per capita, even though much of the electricity demand was concentrated in northern Virginia and Texas. Rates in Virginia and Texas were only about half those in most Midwestern states.

It has been revealed that “When people think about the negative impacts of data centers, they usually focus on the neighbors. But our study indicates that the air quality impacts of data centers are very widespread across a large region. Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data center near you, think again,” claims Noelle Selin, senior author of the study, a professor in the MIT Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS) and the Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences (EAPS), and director of the Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy.

Industry observers note that lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that data centers’ electricity needs accounted for about 4 percent of total U.S. energy demand in 2023 and approximately 4.4 percent of the nation’s overall emissions. Those proportions have likely grown as more facilities have been built.

According to recent reports, determining who bears the health consequences of that growing demand is complicated by the interconnected nature of the nation’s power grid. A data center in Virginia, for example, may increase electricity production at power plants in the Ohio Valley, where a greater proportion of older coal and natural gas plants produce higher levels of emissions.

“Different regions have different mixes of power. If you turn on a major new demand source, by plugging a data center into the grid, you might have to fire up your really dirty power plant to meet that new demand,” Selin indicates.

The pollution can then travel into neighboring states, where local atmospheric conditions can make matters worse. In agricultural regions such as Iowa and Nebraska, ammonia released from fertilizer promotes the formation of fine particulate matter (PM2.5), microscopic airborne particles that can cause heart attacks, strokes, and lung disease.

The estimated health consequences also extend to Kansas, South Dakota, Missouri, and Arkansas. Overall, the researchers found that rural populations face a significantly higher estimated mortality risk from data center electricity demand than urban populations.

Recent findings suggest that to understand how these risks are distributed, the team developed a model that tracks electricity production and transmission between regions on an hourly basis. While many previous studies relied on average power grid emissions, the researchers assumed that data centers operated around the clock and identified which individual generators would respond to their additional electricity needs.

“Generators that respond to additional electricity demand are often natural gas plants, although the response varies by place and hour,” indicates Yuang (Albert) Chen, an MIT graduate student and co-author of the study.

Sources indicate that “It was a challenge to gather all the data,” Chen says. “There are more than 10,000 generators in the U.S. grid, and we needed to make sure the data provided for each generator is valid and validated across other data sources.”.

Industry observers note that the researchers calculated emissions of nitrogen oxides and sulfur dioxide from individual generators. Both pollutants contribute to the formation of fine particulate matter, while nitrogen oxides also help produce ground-level ozone, commonly associated with smog.

Using a separate atmospheric model, the team simulated how these pollutants formed and traveled across regions. They then drew on epidemiological research linking air pollution to premature death to estimate the resulting health impacts.

Recent findings suggest that of the approximately 650 premature deaths estimated for 2023, 513 were attributed to fine particulate matter and 137 to smog. Together, they represented about 5.3 percent of all estimated electricity-related premature deaths nationwide.

“While it is not surprising that any additional source of air pollution will result in mortalities, with data centers, when and where these deaths are occurring are different than you might expect,” Selin notes.

As companies continue to expand their computing infrastructure, the findings suggest that decisions about where to build data centers and how to power them need to account for public health well beyond the immediate surroundings.

“When people are thinking about data center siting and operations, it is important to consider more than just things like land and energy prices. They should also take air quality considerations into the equation,” Chen notes. “This is a good baseline to think about where we should build data centers and how we should supply those data centers with electricity.”.

According to recent reports, the researchers hope to investigate the air quality consequences of a growing industry trend in which data centers incorporate their own on-site power plants. They could also examine whether adjusting when these facilities consume electricity could reduce their impact on air quality.

Reference: “Spatially distributed air quality and health impacts of data center electricity demand in the United States” by Yuang Chen, Shen Wang, Juan Ramon L Senga, Andrew Scott White, Anthony YH Wong, Lyssa M Freese, Michelle L Bell and Noelle E Selin, 19 November 2026, Environmental Research Letters. DOI: 10.1088/1748-9326/aebbd4.

This research was funded, in part, by the MIT Energy Initiative Society of Energy Scholars and the MIT Martin Family Society of Fellows for Sustainability.
