In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Recent findings suggest that sebnem Ece Eksi did a double take. Proteins typically studied in the brain were turning up in prostate cancer cells from high-risk patients. These proteins, called neuronal adhesion molecules, play a key role in the circuitry associated with memory.

The finding, made during her Ph.D. days at the University of Illinois Chicago, raised so many questions to which Eksi is still seeking answers. Now at the Oregon Health & Science University in Portland, Eksi has made it her lab’s goal to find out how nervous systems communicate with cancer. What were once two separate fields might be connected more closely than previously thought.

“What we’re learning is that tumors are actively communicating with the nervous system,” Eksi says. “In a way, it makes sense to me that a growing tumor in our bodies, in an organ, would be immediately sensed and detected by the nervous system.”.

Recent findings suggest that eksi now aims to test an AI image-based recognition algorithm to identify nerve fibers in human patients. This is exciting, she says, because these nerves aren’t normally visible in patient tumors. But through biopsies, she hopes to map out and observe how the nervous system — which impacts sleep, cognition and pain — changes as cancer progresses. The implications are significant, she says. Could experts use the nervous system to detect cancer early? Can they improve patients’ quality of life?

It has been revealed that “This field of cancer neuroscience can change all different stages of cancer diagnosis and treatments,” Eksi notes. “It’s growing so rapidly, the field itself.”.

Emergency repairs at Etruscan tombs in Italy uncovered stone thrones and a jar that looters had missed

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Archaeologists in Cerveteri, Italy, uncovered Etruscan tombs with stone thrones, red-painted walls and a decorated jar overlooked by looters.
  • Emergency work at the Monte Abatone necropolis in Cerveteri, the Etruscan city of Caere, has turned up stone thrones, walls painted red, and a nearly intact decorated jar.
  • Industry observers note that the work was carried out by Italy’s heritage authority for the province of Viterbo and southern Etruria, the Soprintendenza Archeologia, Belle Arti e Paesaggio.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Archaeologists in Cerveteri, Italy, uncovered Etruscan tombs with stone thrones, red-painted walls and a decorated jar overlooked by looters.

Emergency work at the Monte Abatone necropolis in Cerveteri, the Etruscan city of Caere, has turned up stone thrones, walls painted red, and a nearly intact decorated jar.

Industry observers note that the work was carried out by Italy’s heritage authority for the province of Viterbo and southern Etruria, the Soprintendenza Archeologia, Belle Arti e Paesaggio. Some of the tombs had collapsed or become unstable.

Clandestine diggers had entered these tombs before the archaeologists arrived. They left the jar behind.

The collapses and instability meant the tombs had to be investigated, documented and secured. The team cleared the entrances and, as a precaution, removed the fill that had built up inside.

It has been revealed that the chambers were dug into tuff, a soft volcanic rock. Excavators have also found places on the hill where blocks of tuff were quarried in several stages.

During a 2019 excavation, a team including the University of Bonn documented a Monte Abatone tomb whose ceiling had partly fallen in along a crack.

It has been revealed that the researchers linked such cracks to movements of the tuff layer over a less stable layer of clay. The Soprintendenza has not remarked what caused the latest collapses, or when they occurred.

One of the chambers still keeps much of its original vaulted ceiling.

In another Etruscan chamber tomb, the funerary furniture was carved directly out of the tuff, including thrones.

A third chamber has extensive red painted decoration on its walls.

Industry observers note that similar furnishings are known from earlier work at Monte Abatone. In 2019, years before the emergency repairs, excavators recorded kline-type death beds, shaped like couches, and narrower benches lining the walls of another chamber.

Cerveteri’s larger Banditaccia necropolis and the Monterozzi necropolis at Tarquinia together form a UNESCO World Heritage property. At Banditaccia, thousands of tombs are laid out in a city-like plan, with streets and small squares.

The most complete find is an olla stamnoide, a jar shaped like a stamnos. It is almost intact. Its surface carries incised figures of animals, with some details picked out in red paint.

Industry observers note that the jar will be cleaned and restored, then put on public display. No date or venue for the display has been confirmed.

The earlier clandestine digging compromised the original context of the burials. Some materials survived it and were recovered.

Looters have missed objects at Monte Abatone before. In the 2019 excavation, Tomb 642 demonstrated signs of their digging, yet it still held a large pithos, a bucchero drinking set, Ionian bowls and Corinthian ointment jars.

In a recent development, monte Abatone lies immediately south of the ancient city. It flourished in the seventh and sixth centuries BCE, according to a 2022 report on Monte Abatone.

Sources indicate that in the 1950s and 1960s, surveys and excavations explored 641 tombs there. That work was carried out on behalf of the heritage authority in response to heavy looting.

Burial types at the site include simple trench graves, chamber tombs and tombs under burial mounds, among them the Campana Tumulus.

That great mound dates to the middle of the Orientalizing period and had not been surveyed since the first half of the 19th century.

Older finds show that burials there continued from the late eighth century BCE into the Hellenistic period and the early Roman Empire.

Researchers also examined the area west and north of the Campana Tumulus. It held tombs of the sixth to third centuries BCE, excavated in the past and partly backfilled, and funerary terraces facing the city.

Recent findings suggest that A research project on Monte Abatone began in the early 1990s. After a upcoming project was set up in 2017, a group of Italian and German universities ran excavation campaigns at the site from 2018 to 2021.

Ground-penetrating radar was used across an area of about 7.4 acres (3 hectares) east of the Campana Tumulus. An earlier geophysical test had revealed a densely packed cluster of tombs.

Sources indicate that A 2021 trial excavation opened about 13,500 square feet (1,250 square meters) south of the great tumulus. It exposed tombs with small mounds, up to about 36 feet (11 meters) across, set in two roughly parallel rows and all facing northwest.

Excavations on the south side also uncovered what the team describes as a “possible ‘family’ cluster of tombs,” used from the early Orientalizing period into the Archaic period.

“This suggests the existence of a planning by some form of ‘urban’ authority,” the authors of the 2022 report wrote about the rows of mounds.

Laser scanners recorded the site in fine detail, producing a combined model of about 4.3 billion points, roughly 1.2 billion of them for the Campana Tumulus alone. A drone survey added a photogrammetric model of the plateau.

The information was obtained from the Soprintendenza for the province of Viterbo and southern Etruria.

#111697. Wild baboons seem to blueprint breakfast around a favorite fruit

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1388 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Wild baboons seem to blueprint breakfast around a favorite fruit

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1388 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wild baboons stopped visiting their favorite fruit trees after a fire destroyed the crop, suggesting flexible food planning.
  • Wild Guinea baboons in West Africa travel to the same area each year to feed on a favored fruit.
  • Industry observers note that the fire reached the area just as the fruit was beginning to ripen on the trees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wild baboons stopped visiting their favorite fruit trees after a fire destroyed the crop, suggesting flexible food planning.

Wild Guinea baboons in West Africa travel to the same area each year to feed on a favored fruit. In 2019, this annual pattern was disrupted by a fire that swept through the feeding grounds.

Industry observers note that the fire reached the area just as the fruit was beginning to ripen on the trees. Only a single visit to the fruit trees was recorded during February of that year.

The baboons resumed their usual visits the following year, when ripe Natal oranges were available again.

These observations suggest that the animals do more than simply recall where and when food can be found. Their foraging looks also appear to be revised when a familiar food source is lost.

The study was led by Lisa Ohrndorf of the German Primate Center in Göttingen, Germany.

“The year of the fire gave us a unique opportunity: We were able to observe how the animals react when a normally reliable food source suddenly becomes unavailable during their usual season,” said Ohrndorf.

It has been revealed that her co-authors were Roger Mundry, Dietmar Zinner and Julia Fischer. All three are affiliated with the center and with the University of Göttingen.

The baboons inhabit Niokolo-Koba National Park in southeastern Senegal, where several groups have been followed by researchers since 2007.

Earlier work carried out at the same center had shown that these baboons share meat with close companions.

According to recent reports, A clear preference for the Natal orange is shown by the animals during the dry season. The fruit is roughly the size of a common orange and is protected by a hard outer shell.

Inside the shell the seeds are embedded in a layer of soft pulp that is eaten by the baboons.

Natal oranges ripen between January and March and reach their greatest abundance in February. Data from recent years indicate that nearly a fifth of February feeding time was devoted to this fruit.

Industry observers note that very few other plants in the park are known to produce fleshy fruit during the dry season. The long journey to the Natal orange trees is therefore likely to be well rewarded.

Most of the Natal orange trees are found in the northern parts of the home ranges of the baboons.

These trees cannot be seen from the riverside forest in which the animals usually spend the night.

Sources indicate that in 2023 a series of evenly spaced survey routes was walked by the researchers through the area. A total of 5,847 Natal orange trees was counted along these routes.

The densest stand found in this survey was then used as the target area for the analysis of baboon movements.

Fires are a regular feature of the park and are recorded in every dry season. They normally burn between mid-December and early January and mainly consume the tall grass left after the rains.

The fires of 2019 were unusual because they arrived much later than in most years.

Satellite records indicate that most of the target area burned within a few days at the end of January. By that point the Natal oranges had already begun to ripen.

Sources indicate that nearly all of the ripe fruit was destroyed by the heat of the fire. The trees themselves suffered little lasting damage and plant growth in the following rainy season was close to normal.

Nine years of observation records for seven baboon groups were examined by the team. Each group contained an average of 29 animals.

Industry observers note that the baboons were observed on 22 days in February 2019 but entered the target area on only one of them. In other years between eight and 29 visits were recorded in February with an average of about 16.

During the fire year the baboons were seen feeding on the fruit of fan palms. The fruit of a shrubby tree growing in other parts of their range was also eaten.

The baboons visited the area four times in March 2019, at the low end of the range of four to 22 visits recorded in other years.

The baboons may have returned in March to feed on fruit from taller trees, where it hangs higher and is less exposed to the heat of a fire.

By 2020 the Natal oranges had recovered and the usual pattern of visits to the area had resumed.

The researchers also analyzed 2,922 GPS tracks that had been collected over a period of nine years.

Of those tracks, 530 showed a group entering the area where the fruit trees grow.

Sources indicate that when Natal oranges were in season the baboons were found to follow more direct routes to the trees. Their average travel speed on these trips was also about 14% higher than at other times of year.

Recent findings suggest that the distance involved in these trips was considerable. From the known sleeping sites the trees lay roughly 1.4 miles (2.2 kilometers) away in a straight line.

Baboons are generally slow to leave their sleeping trees in the morning. More than an hour commonly passes between sunrise and their departure.

On trips to the feeding area, the baboons left their sleeping sites about 40 minutes earlier when the fruit was in season.

Cold weather normally delays departure because the animals tend to sun themselves before setting off.

Sources indicate that mornings in the fruit season were in fact colder on average. Since the baboons still left earlier, warmer temperatures cannot account for the change.

In studies of animal learning a distinction is drawn between habitual behavior and behavior driven by an expected reward. A habit may persist for some time after the associated reward is no longer available.

Industry observers note that the direct and rapid trips to the trees could in principle have reflected nothing more than a fixed yearly routine. The response of the baboons to the fire argues against that interpretation.

According to recent reports, if the visits had been governed by habit alone the empty trees would probably have continued to be visited. The baboons instead shifted their foraging to food sources located in other parts of their range.

The results suggest that the value of a journey is assessed by these baboons before the journey is undertaken.

It has been revealed that comparable behavior has been described in several other primates. Chacma baboons have been observed leaving their sleeping sites early in order to reach fig trees. Female chimpanzees leave their nests earlier when a preferred fruit is located far away.

According to recent reports, memory for food locations is not restricted to primates. Small birds such as chickadees are able to recall where large numbers of their food stores were hidden.

Responses to fire are also known to vary widely among animals. Some deer return to burned ground within days while certain lizards detect smoke and move away before the flames arrive.

It has been revealed that the late fire occurred only once during the study period. Visit numbers could therefore be compared across years but full statistical testing of the fire year was not possible.

GPS positions were recorded at 30-minute intervals during follows that usually ended around 1 p.m. Some movement was missed as a result and the actual routes were probably longer and less direct.

It has been revealed that the means by which the baboons navigate through their home range also remains unclear. Repeated use of the same trails and roads and stream crossings points to a reliance on learned routes.

A further open question concerns the way in which the baboons recognize that the Natal oranges are ready to eat.

Recent findings suggest that day length and temperature or the appearance of other seasonal foods may serve as cues for the animals. These possibilities were not tested in the present study.

The study offers a closer look at the way wild baboons make decisions about where to search for food.

Knowledge of where food grows is clearly useful but knowing when to stop searching may be equally important.

The full study was published in the journal Animal Cognition.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Yian Yin seeks to understand the dynamics of science itself. The computational social scientist is particularly interested in how innovations happen and how they may be accelerated.

“I want to understand what the secret sources or recipes of success are,” states Yin, of Cornell University.

He applied machine learning techniques to accepted and rejected research proposals to understand how scientists learn from failures. What he found was that scientists fail, and they fail often. Some switched gears after some rejections, but others who continued their research and incorporated feedback found success at a faster rate. Those who changed ideas or scrapped original proposals did not leverage a lot from their experience.

“A group that’s not only failing better and better,” Yin says, “is also failing faster and increasingly faster towards their eventual success.”.

More recently, Yin has been investigating how generative AI is changing scientific publishing. Journals are receiving more AI-assisted submissions than ever before, which is leading the peer-review process to falter. More seemingly well-written papers that lack substance are getting through, he found. Coming up with large-scale solutions requires looking at the issue in a measurable way, Yin says.

“Considering both the technological and social side of scientific ecosystems would be something that’s really beneficial for the ongoing public debate and discussion about how we accelerate science in the age of artificial intelligence,” Yin says.

Latest Update: Stomach problems in autistic children raise new questions about gut bacteria

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1257 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A study found that autistic children with more severe digestive symptoms tended to have more difficulty picking up on social cues.
  • Children with autism often have stomach problems.
  • Little evidence for that explanation was found in a new study.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A study found that autistic children with more severe digestive symptoms tended to have more difficulty picking up on social cues.

Children with autism often have stomach problems. What causes them, however, is still up for debate. Some scientists believe the lining of the gut becomes damaged or inflamed.

Little evidence for that explanation was found in a new study.

Autistic children with more severe digestive symptoms tended to have more difficulty picking up on social cues, according to parent questionnaires.

The researchers also found links between certain gut bacteria and digestive symptoms.

Recent findings suggest that the study was led by J. Marc Rhoads. He is professor and chief of the Division of Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Nutrition at McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston.

Many children with autism are unable to explain where they feel pain. In such cases a change in behavior may be the first sign of a problem.

“Families may notice increased irritability, repetitive behaviors, or self-injurious behaviors when a child is experiencing gastrointestinal challenges such as gas, constipation, or diarrhea,” Rhoads remarked.

“For children who are nonverbal, these behaviors may be one of the few ways they can communicate discomfort.”.

About one in 31 American eight-year-olds had been identified with autism in 2022. This estimate was published by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Significant digestive problems have been reported in 31% to 84% of people with autism in earlier studies.

The researchers examined 72 children with autism who were between four and 16 years of age. All of the children had been enrolled in a probiotic trial. Their data were collected between 2016 and 2023.

It has been revealed that boys made up about 78% of the group and roughly a quarter of the children did not speak. Children with known digestive, liver or kidney diseases were excluded from the study. Those who had recently taken antibiotics or probiotics were also left out.

Several symptoms were assessed by the team. These included constipation, gas, stomach pain, unusually smelly stools and waking up at night.

According to recent reports, A score of seven or more on a 17-point scale was taken to indicate significant digestive problems. About 63% of the children were placed in this group.

Parents were also asked to complete a questionnaire about the social behavior of their children. Higher scores on this questionnaire reflected more pronounced autism traits.

Higher scores were generally seen in children with worse stomach problems. The connection was not particularly strong but it reached statistical significance.

The clearest difference was observed in social awareness. This area covers abilities such as noticing the facial expressions, feelings or actions of another person.

Sources indicate that children with significant digestive problems scored about 7.5 points higher in this area. Their scores were compared with those of children who had milder symptoms.

The cells that line the intestines are packed closely together. The spaces between them are sealed by specialized proteins.

Substances from inside the gut may pass into the bloodstream if these seals are weakened. Inflammation could then be triggered in the body. This process is commonly described as a leaky gut.

Blood samples were tested for two proteins associated with these seals. Another blood protein linked to intestinal inflammation was measured as well. Stool samples were also analyzed for calprotectin, a protein routinely used by doctors to detect gut inflammation.

In a recent development, most of the results fell within the normal range. Elevated calprotectin was detected in only two children and neither of them had significant digestive symptoms.

“Biomarkers of intestinal inflammation and gut permeability remained within normal ranges and were not associated with gastrointestinal symptom severity or autism symptom severity,” Rhoads mentioned.

Children with worse stomach problems therefore did not show more signs of inflammation or a leaky gut on these tests.

In a recent development, mixed results have been produced by earlier research. High calprotectin levels were found in up to a third of autistic children in some studies. No significant difference was found in a more recent review.

The bacterial findings proved to be more revealing than the blood tests.

Industry observers note that additional stool samples were obtained from Texas Children’s Microbiome Center. This allowed the analysis to be expanded to 135 children. The group included children with autism, their siblings and unrelated children without autism.

According to recent reports, fewer types of gut bacteria were present in children with autism than in their siblings. A similar difference was seen when they were compared with unrelated children. However, this second result may have arisen by chance.

Sources indicate that the bacterial communities of children with autism also resembled one another more closely. Greater variety was observed among the other children.

In a recent development, two groups of bacteria were more abundant in autistic children with significant digestive problems. One of these groups is known as Ruminococcus.

Children with higher levels of these bacteria reported more gas and stronger-smelling stools. Night waking was also more frequent in these children. Their overall digestive symptom scores were higher as well.

Recent findings suggest that ruminococcus feeds on the mucus that protects the intestinal wall. Higher levels of this bacterium in one-year-olds were linked to greater social difficulties at age three in an earlier study.

Industry observers note that another bacterial group called Sarcina was associated with gas, stomach pain, diarrhea and night waking. The researchers noted that Sarcina had not been linked to autism in previous studies.

The study captured a snapshot of digestive symptoms, gut bacteria and behavior.

The children were examined at a single point in time. It was therefore not possible to tell which change came first.

Gut bacteria may cause stomach problems, or digestive problems may alter the bacterial population.

Diet could also play a part in this relationship. Many children with autism prefer a limited range of foods. The bacteria living in the intestines are strongly influenced by what a person eats.

According to recent reports, the study also had a few other limitations. Blood was not collected from healthy children for ethical reasons. Results were compared with established normal ranges instead.

Industry observers note that children with known digestive diseases were excluded by the team. Some of the analyses did not account for other factors that might have influenced the findings.

Children could be followed over several years in future studies. Such work may show whether changes in gut bacteria occur before digestive or behavioral changes.

Rhoads believes that everyday habits deserve more attention.

“This study highlights the importance of supporting a healthy gut microbiome in children with autism,” Rhoads stated.

“A varied diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains, along with healthy toileting habits, may help improve both gastrointestinal health and behavior.”.

“Our team has also found promising results with probiotic treatment.”.

According to recent reports, the results of the probiotic trial have not yet been published. Scientists are still working to determine which probiotic supplements are helpful and under what conditions.

The most useful lesson for parents may concern the recognition of discomfort rather than bacteria.

A child may suddenly become irritable, sleep poorly or show more repetitive behaviors. Such changes may be caused by something as ordinary as constipation or stomach pain.

Many children are unable to put this discomfort into words. Behavior may be one of the ways in which they ask for help.

The study is published in the journal Pediatric Research.

#111693. Plants can grow elaborate leaves, so why are most of them so simple?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1567 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Plants can grow elaborate leaves, so why are most of them so simple?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1567 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A study suggests that the way leaves grow helps explain why most flowering plants have simple leaves, even though complex shapes have evolved many times.
  • Recent findings suggest that the leaves of a maple tree, a rose bush and a magnolia bear very little resemblance to one another.
  • Complex leaf shapes have arisen many times during the evolution of flowering plants.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A study suggests that the way leaves grow helps explain why most flowering plants have simple leaves, even though complex shapes have evolved many times.

Recent findings suggest that the leaves of a maple tree, a rose bush and a magnolia bear very little resemblance to one another. Deep cuts are seen in some of them. Others are made up of several small leaflets or one unbroken blade.

Complex leaf shapes have arisen many times during the evolution of flowering plants. Simple leaves have nevertheless remained by far the most common form.

A fresh study suggests that the way leaves grow helps explain why leaves with a single blade and no deep cuts are so common.

Random changes were introduced by the researchers into a computer model that simulates a growing leaf.

No particular shape was favored in those runs but simple leaves were still produced far more often than other kinds.

The research was led by James Malone, a graduate student in the Department of Physics at the University of Oxford.

He was joined by Ard Louis, a professor of theoretical physics at Oxford. Researchers in Barcelona and at Stony Brook University in New York also took part.

“What we found is that you can largely explain which leaf shapes dominate in evolution simply by looking at how leaves develop and how mutations affect that process, without needing to invoke natural selection,” remarked Malone.

“The bias towards simplicity is built into the developmental system itself.”.

For the purposes of the study, every leaf was assigned to one of four broad groups based on its outline.

It has been revealed that an unlobed leaf consists of a single blade with no deep cuts along its edge. In a lobed leaf the blade is divided by cuts into distinct sections.

Industry observers note that those cuts extend much further toward the center in a dissected leaf. Separate leaflets attached to one shared stalk are what make up a compound leaf.

Industry observers note that large differences in leaf form can be found even among closely related plants. All four leaf types are represented among species of the geranium group Pelargonium.

Both lobed and unlobed leaves may even be produced on a single mulberry tree, as the authors pointed out.

Industry observers note that different leaf shapes do not necessarily require different genes. Much of the variety depends on the timing and location of gene activity inside a developing leaf.

Comparable genetic processes determine whether single leaves or leaves divided into three parts are grown by strawberry plants.

Sources indicate that for centuries, botanists have collected, pressed and dried plants for long-term storage. Such specimens are held in collections known as herbariums that now serve as a record of plant diversity.

In a recent development, the team looked at 8,911 digital images of specimens from the Naturalis Biodiversity Center in Leiden, the Netherlands. The shape of each leaf was identified by hand.

According to recent reports, the identified shapes were then placed onto five large family trees of flowering plants. One of these trees included 9,506 species and was based on information from 353 genes.

In 2012 an earlier study of 561 plants had reported that about 76% of them carried unlobed leaves. That share rose to between 86% and nearly 89% in the much larger trees used for the latest study.

It has been revealed that the frequency of leaf shape changes during evolution was then estimated from those labeled trees. Complex leaves were found to give way to unlobed ones far more readily than unlobed leaves became complex.

All five family trees revealed this pattern. No disagreement was seen among the trees on the direction of any clearly established shift.

It seems natural to assume that simple leaves give plants some kind of edge over complex ones.

Sources indicate that the shape of a leaf is known to influence the way heat and water are managed by the plant. Sunlight capture and protection from plant-eating animals may also be affected by it.

In a recent development, in one experiment with paper leaves, symmetrical unlobed shapes sank the fastest. Such behavior could allow the nutrients in fallen leaves to stay closer to the parent tree.

In a recent development, when earlier research was reviewed by the authors, the evidence for selection proved much stronger for leaf size. Far weaker support was found for selection on these four broad shapes.

According to recent reports, in many of those studies it was shown that shape changes how a leaf works. Far fewer showed that a given shape actually helps a plant survive and reproduce. Many also looked only at certain groups of plants.

“For many biological traits, such as the camera eye with its lens and retina, complexity clearly accumulates over time through natural selection,” Louis said.

“But leaf shape highlights the opposite pattern. Complexity evolves – and then evolution frequently abandons it.”.

A different explanation was therefore explored using a model built by Adam Runions and colleagues in 2017.

Leaf growth in this model is driven by the veins and edge along with chemical signals acting on that edge.

Before the main experiment began the model was compared with results that had been obtained in real plants.

Earlier work on thale cress and hairy bittercress had shown that compound leaves need two genes active together.

Lobes alone were formed in thale cress when only one of those two genes was switched on.

The model behaved in the same way once its two most comparable settings had been adjusted.

Twenty of the 25 tested combinations of those settings went on to produce simple unlobed leaves.

The main experiment was started from 48 virtual leaves that represented all four shapes between them.

According to recent reports, each setting in turn received a small random change and this went on for 320 steps. Five runs were made from every starting leaf and 76,800 virtual leaves came out of the experiment.

Rejection was limited to physically unrealistic leaves such as those in which veins filled too little of the blade.

No leaf was rewarded for its shape and yet about three-quarters of the virtual leaves were found to be unlobed.

Within the margins of error the model’s rates of change toward simple shapes matched those of the family trees.

The model’s settings can be imagined as a long list of instructions for growing one leaf.

Random edits to that list would mostly still end in a leaf with a simple outline.

A far more specific combination of settings is needed to produce a more elaborate leaf, as the researchers found.

The settings for unlobed leaves were grouped into only three separate regions within the model.

Lobed leaves by contrast were spread over 131 regions while dissected leaves occupied 96 and compound leaves 235.

Many of the small regions that gave complex leaves were located inside the much larger region that gave simple ones.

The arrangement can be compared to a mostly green map on which hundreds of tiny blue patches have been scattered.

A few random steps taken from a blue patch would often lead a walker onto green ground.

It has been revealed that someone who started out in the green area might travel a long way before reaching any blue at all. Leaf development appears to work in a comparable way according to the study’s results.

Complex leaves are easily turned into simple ones by random genetic change while the opposite outcome is less likely.

Switches from one complex shape to another such as from lobed to compound were handled less well by the model.

The real family trees were also more likely to disagree with one another about these particular changes.

The authors suggested that natural selection may have had a larger influence on those shifts. It is also possible that some of the finer details of complex leaf growth are not captured by the model.

Closed net-like vein patterns cannot be recreated by it and the parallel veins common in grasses are also absent.

Much of what is known about leaf growth has been learned from a handful of laboratory plants.

Every group of flowering plants may therefore not be represented equally well by a single model.

It has been revealed that the small teeth found along the edges of some leaves were not included in the analysis. Hand classification of thousands of herbarium images also put a limit on the amount of usable data.

Whether similar patterns exist elsewhere in nature is the question the researchers hope to answer next.

Tree and root shapes will be examined next along with tooth complexity and the fins of African cichlid fish.

“By continuing this approach – combining large-scale analysis of evolutionary trees with computer simulations – we will gain a much greater understanding of how the complexity of a trait evolves over time across different kingdoms of life,” stated Louis.

Folded RNA molecules and grouped proteins had already shown a similar preference for simple forms in earlier work.

Evolution can certainly produce complicated structures but greater complexity is not always the direction it takes.

One reason simple leaves may be so common is that plants have more ways to grow them.

The full study was published in the journal eLife.

#111692. Industry News: Lightning could strike the ground more than twice as often by the end of the century

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (894 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Lightning could strike the ground more than twice as often by the end of the century

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If greenhouse gas emissions stay high, lightning strikes that reach the ground could rise 76% to 140% worldwide by 2100, with even larger increases in Alaska.
  • Lightning strikes that reach the ground could become 76% to 140% more frequent worldwide by the end of this century, compared with 1995 to 2014, if greenhouse gas emissions stay high.
  • The numbers are far above previous estimates, and they surprised the researchers who produced them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If greenhouse gas emissions stay high, lightning strikes that reach the ground could rise 76% to 140% worldwide by 2100, with even larger increases in Alaska.

Lightning strikes that reach the ground could become 76% to 140% more frequent worldwide by the end of this century, compared with 1995 to 2014, if greenhouse gas emissions stay high.

The numbers are far above previous estimates, and they surprised the researchers who produced them.

Recent findings suggest that during that baseline period, most of Alaska averaged fewer than one strike per square kilometer per year. By the end of the century, the statewide increase could reach 594%.

The study was led by Andreas Krause, an Earth system scientist at the Technical University of Munich.

Lightning has been genuinely hard to forecast, because its two essential ingredients pull in opposite directions under a warming climate.

It starts with heat. Air near the ground warms, becomes buoyant and rises, a process called convection.

It has been revealed that that rising air stirs up the much colder atmosphere above it. In the turbulence, tiny ice crystals in the frigid mid-level clouds collide and swap electric charge.

The lighter crystals get carried upward while the heavier ones sink, separating positive from negative and building an electric field between them. When the field grows strong enough, the air breaks down and a bolt fires.

Warmer air near the ground can fuel stronger updrafts, increasing the chances that ice particles collide and build up an electric charge.

We can already see the pattern: lightning peaks in the early afternoon, the hottest part of the day, and the tropics get far more of it than the high latitudes.

Warmer air aloft could mean fewer ice crystals, making it harder for storms to build up the electric charge that produces lightning.

It has been revealed that “There is actually quite a large uncertainty about how lightning will respond to climate change,” Krause said. “It’s not quite clear which of these is more notable.”.

Rather than build the physics from scratch, the team trained a machine learning model on a single year of observations from 2019.

The researchers paired actual lightning records with the weather conditions that produced them: temperature, rainfall, humidity, air pressure, wind speed, and incoming solar radiation.

Then they ran it backwards. Applied to the climate of 1901 to 1920 and again to 1995 to 2014, the model demonstrated cloud-to-ground lightning rising 11% over the 20th century. That works out to roughly 12% more lightning per degree Celsius of warming.

The forward projection is where it gets uncomfortable. Under a high-emissions scenario, that sensitivity nearly triples, to about 30% more lightning per degree.

Compared with the 1995 to 2014 baseline, ground strikes would become 76% to 140% more common by 2100, depending on which climate model you feed in.

In a recent development, for comparison, the highest previous estimates put the figure between 8% and 17% per degree. The gap comes mostly from a different mathematical approach and from this study’s use of a newer, more reliable global lightning dataset.

Recent findings suggest that “I was quite surprised that the projections were so high,” Krause noted. “I expected smaller changes.”.

The projections apply specifically to cloud-to-ground lightning, the bolts that actually touch down.

Most lightning never reaches the surface, staying within or between clouds, and it does little harm there.

What comes down is another matter. Cloud-to-ground strikes ignite wildfires, damage wind turbines, power lines and offshore oil rigs, and kill several thousand people and hundreds of millions of trees worldwide every year.

Sources indicate that the increases won’t be evenly spread. In absolute terms, the biggest rises come where lightning is already thickest: the Amazon, Southeast Asia, and Oceania.

The Amazon projection carries the largest caveat, and the researchers are upfront about it.

Their model learned from the Amazon as it exists today, and that forest may look very different by 2100. Some studies actually predict less tropical lightning in the future, not more.

The biggest proportional changes happen at high latitudes, where lightning is currently rare enough that any increase looks dramatic.

Many of those regions could see strike density more than double. Alaska is the extreme case, somewhere between 116% and 594% above its baseline.

Whether more lightning translates into more danger is a separate question, and it depends on timing.

Krause pointed out that the risk to people may hinge on whether the extra bolts arrive during the early stages of storms.

That’s when someone outdoors is most likely to be caught off guard, before the sky has made its intentions obvious.

Sources indicate that the study didn’t examine how forests would cope. In general, Krause said, conifers show more visible damage from a direct strike than broadleaved trees.

According to recent reports, within the tropics, some studies suggest that forests already accustomed to frequent lightning handle it better. That resilience is something he wants to look at next.

According to recent reports, “Trees basically evolved to adapt to the local lightning frequency,” Krause said. “But are there any species that are particularly tolerant of lightning strikes and more likely to survive them? There’s not much information out there.”.

The study is published in the journal Earth’s Future.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a South China Sea trial, researchers turned liquid CO₂ into an ice-like solid that was still visible on the seabed 40 days later.
  • Nearly 1,700 meters below the South China Sea, researchers have turned liquid carbon dioxide into an ice-like solid.
  • It has been revealed that china National Offshore Oil Corporation and Huairou Laboratory carried out the experiment in November 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a South China Sea trial, researchers turned liquid CO₂ into an ice-like solid that was still visible on the seabed 40 days later.

Nearly 1,700 meters below the South China Sea, researchers have turned liquid carbon dioxide into an ice-like solid. A mound remained visible 40 days later, offering an early test of a possible new carbon storage method.

It has been revealed that china National Offshore Oil Corporation and Huairou Laboratory carried out the experiment in November 2025. Shouwei Zhou and Junlong Zhu describe it as the first exploratory sea trial of deep-water CO₂ hydrate solidification and storage.

It has been revealed that the team injected 70 tons of liquid CO₂ across two wells in the Qiongdongnan Sea Area. They wanted to see whether the deep ocean’s natural cold and pressure could help hold the carbon in solid form.

Capturing carbon dioxide is only part of the job. Keeping it out of the atmosphere requires somewhere to put it, with confidence that it will stay there.

Conventional geological storage involves injecting CO₂ underground, including into formations containing salty water. Before injection begins, engineers must assess the rock, possible escape routes, and the layers expected to seal the reservoir.

According to recent reports, the upcoming approach seeks to reduce that dependence on geological seals. Under suitable conditions, CO₂ combines with water to form a hydrate, a solid whose water molecules enclose the gas.

In a recent development, it looks like ice but is neither ordinary frozen water nor dry ice. The researchers’ aim is to form this material beneath the sea and let the surrounding conditions keep it stable.

The deep ocean supplies two conditions that would otherwise have to be created: low temperatures and high pressure.

Those conditions favor hydrate formation. Rather than simply pumping CO₂ into a space where it remains mobile, the team wants it to accumulate as a solid.

Industry observers note that the idea draws on work with natural gas hydrates, which contain methane. Extracting gas from those deposits means overcoming the conditions that keep them solid.

For carbon storage, the researchers want the opposite result. A material that stays solid and remains in place could be useful precisely because it is difficult to release.

They identify loose muddy silt and weakly cemented sand-and-mud layers as promising settings for injection and hydrate accumulation.

Industry observers note that the operation used the “SS Amazonia” deep-water platform. Beneath it lay 1,696.5 meters of water, with the target reservoir reported at 119 meters below the seabed.

Liquid CO₂ was injected through two wells, LS18-1-C1 and LS18-1-C2. The trial brought together drilling, injection control and underwater monitoring equipment.

During the observed release, the liquid passed through tubing and a nozzle containing several openings. The nozzle dispersed it into small droplets, helping it make contact with seawater.

It has been revealed that white hydrate composite particles formed around the drill column. The account calls the cloud of newly formed material “ice mist”.

That was the immediate result. The follow-up inspection would show what could still be seen after several weeks in the deep sea.

Forty days later, images from a remotely operated vehicle revealed an accumulated hydrate body on the bottom. Its visible height ranged from 2 to 30 centimeters above the seabed.

The researchers describe it as an artificial CO₂ hydrate “iceberg”. The name is striking, although the formation was a low mound rather than a floating mass.

Recent findings suggest that finding solid material after 40 days takes the demonstration beyond an instant of successful chemistry. It demonstrates that an accumulation remained visible well after injection.

It has been revealed that but the images do not tell us how much of the injected CO₂ was retained in that mound or elsewhere. Nor can a 40-day observation establish whether the carbon will remain contained over much longer periods.

Those are questions for further measurements, rather than conclusions the photographs can supply.

Sensors near the operation measured seawater pH and CO₂ concentrations. The team reported pH holding near 7.4, without unusual spikes in carbon dioxide.

It has been revealed that the readings suggest the monitored water experienced little disturbance during the trial. Equipment mounted on the underwater vehicle helped track conditions during injection and release.

Industry observers note that that is useful evidence from a first experiment. Still, the absence of a detected change nearby is narrower than proof that the technique has no environmental impact.

In a recent development, A larger operation would need monitoring over a wider area and a longer period. Researchers would also need to establish how the stored material behaves and whether surrounding marine life is affected.

It has been revealed that the researchers see potential savings in a method that needs fewer specific geological features. If suitable sites are widespread, finding storage locations could become easier.

They also propose reducing some of the evaluation and infrastructure demands associated with conventional storage.

For now, those are expected advantages rather than commercial results demonstrated by the trial.

Industry observers note that the work establishes a preliminary engineering system, including drilling in soft sediments, controlled injection and several kinds of underwater observation. It gives the team something concrete to build on.

The remaining questions concern the carbon itself: how much becomes hydrate, how much stays contained, and how conditions change with larger injections.

Costs will also have to include getting captured CO₂ to the offshore site.

The seabed mound is a promising start. Turning it into dependable carbon storage will require showing that the material can hold its carbon long after the cameras leave.

The study is published in the journal ENGINEERINGenergy.

#111689. Mindfulness training can backfire at work, and personality may explain why

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1197 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Mindfulness training can backfire at work, and personality may explain why

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1197 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mindfulness training may increase negative feelings and rude behavior among employees who already tend to distrust and manipulate others.
  • Many companies offer mindfulness training in the hope that it will help employees manage stress, get along better and treat each other with kindness.
  • In a month-long experiment, some workers who practiced mindfulness reported more anger, disgust, and contempt toward coworkers than people with similar personalities in the other groups.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mindfulness training may increase negative feelings and rude behavior among employees who already tend to distrust and manipulate others.

Many companies offer mindfulness training in the hope that it will help employees manage stress, get along better and treat each other with kindness. But it doesn’t seem to work that way for everyone.

In a month-long experiment, some workers who practiced mindfulness reported more anger, disgust, and contempt toward coworkers than people with similar personalities in the other groups.

Workers who felt more of this hostility also reported more rudeness at work.

The pattern emerged among employees who scored high on a personality trait called Machiavellianism.

Industry observers note that people who score high on this trait tend to distrust others and manipulate them for personal gain. Psychologists group it with two other personality traits under the name dark triad.

Previous research has linked mindfulness to greater empathy and helping coworkers. So why did these employees respond so differently?

The study was led by Adam Kay, an assistant professor in the School of Management at the University of South Florida‘s Muma College of Business.

“Mindfulness training makes us more aware of our thoughts and feelings, but that doesn’t necessarily make us better people,” Kay said.

Kay carried out the experiment at a large North American healthcare organization with 12 hospitals, 90 community health sites and 33 other workplaces.

Six hundred employees volunteered, roughly two-thirds of whom were healthcare professionals. Kay randomly divided them into three groups.

The first group followed a 30-day online mindfulness program. It involved five minutes of daily instruction, along with emails and text messages reminding employees to take five mindful breaths, five times a day.

The idea was simple. Notice the colors around you, listen to nearby sounds or feel your feet touching the floor. Then focus on your breathing and notice your feelings without judging them.

According to recent reports, the second group followed a similar breathing exercise without being asked to focus on the present moment. The third group received training later.

Industry observers note that after some employees dropped out and others failed attention checks, 473 remained in the study. Before the experiment, they had completed a personality survey containing statements such as “It’s not wise to tell your secrets.”.

Three weeks into the experiment, Kay asked employees how often they had felt anger, disgust and contempt toward their coworkers over the previous two weeks.

For people who scored low on Machiavellianism, it barely mattered which group they belonged to.

Things were different for those with high scores. Employees who practiced mindfulness reported stronger negative feelings than people with similar personalities in the other two groups. The difference was moderate.

Interestingly, people in both training groups felt more mindful afterward. Yet the same rise in negative feelings did not occur among those who simply practiced breathing.

Paying closer attention to their inner experiences may have made the difference.

After the program ended, employees answered another survey. This time, Kay wanted to know how they had treated their colleagues during the training.

One statement on the survey read, “I ignored or excluded a colleague from professional camaraderie.”.

Industry observers note that psychologists call these small acts of disrespect workplace incivility. They’re often subtle enough that it’s hard to tell whether someone intended to be hurtful.

It has been revealed that the more anger, disgust and contempt employees felt, the more rude behavior they reported. This helped explain the link between mindfulness and incivility among workers with Machiavellian traits.

Industry observers note that “Workplace incivility isn’t always obvious,” Kay stated. “It usually involves subtle acts of disrespect that are easy to dismiss or deny – but that doesn’t make it harmless.”.

More obvious forms of mistreatment, such as embarrassing someone in front of other coworkers, did not follow the same pattern.

“That workplace incivility can be so damaging yet so difficult to pin on perpetrators may be precisely why it appeals to Machiavellians, who tend to be calculating and reputation-conscious,” Kay said.

According to recent reports, imagine working alongside someone you secretly dislike. Most days, you’re too busy answering emails, attending meetings or finishing your work to give those feelings much thought.

Now you spend part of every day paying attention to your thoughts and emotions. You may begin to notice just how much you dislike that person.

Recent findings suggest that kay suspects something similar happened during the experiment. Mindfulness may not have created those negative feelings. Instead, it may have made existing ones harder to ignore.

The paper even opens with a reference to philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche’s famous observation about staring into an abyss that stares back at you.

It has been revealed that kay considered several other possibilities. Employees were not spending more time dwelling on angry thoughts, hiding their emotions or viewing their colleagues as less than human.

A bad mood didn’t explain the findings either. Neither did the other two dark triad traits, narcissism and psychopathy.

Sources indicate that this isn’t the first time researchers have discovered unexpected effects of mindfulness. Earlier research found that it can reduce people’s motivation to repair damaged relationships.

It has been revealed that machiavellianism is a personality trait that exists to varying degrees in the general population. Companies could encounter similar problems in almost any workplace.

Kay isn’t suggesting that employers abandon mindfulness training or start testing their staff for certain personality traits. Doing so could raise serious concerns about privacy, fairness and stigma.

Recent findings suggest that instead, companies could pay closer attention to how employees treat one another after completing a program. Lower stress and better productivity aren’t the only outcomes worth measuring.

Programs that teach compassion and ethical behavior alongside mindfulness might help. However, the people who could benefit most from such lessons may also be the least interested in taking them.

There’s an vital limitation to this research. Everything Kay learned about the employees’ feelings and behavior came from the employees themselves.

It has been revealed that perhaps mindfulness simply made some workers more willing to admit that they had been rude. Although Kay protected their anonymity, he cannot completely dismiss that possibility.

He considers it less likely because the pattern appeared only among workers with high Machiavellian scores who practiced mindfulness, and only for subtle acts of disrespect.

The experiment also took place at a single healthcare organization and used a commercial mindfulness program that hasn’t been independently tested.

Hospitals have strict rules about professional behavior, which may discourage more obvious forms of hostility.

Recent findings suggest that future studies could ask coworkers whether they noticed changes in behavior. Researchers could also observe employees directly or test different mindfulness programs.

In a recent development, “Mindfulness training can bring our darker feelings into sharper focus,” Kay remarked. “And sometimes, it’s our coworkers who pay the price.”.

It has been revealed that learning to recognize our feelings and learning to treat others better are two different things. Mindfulness may help with the first without necessarily improving the second.

The study is published in the Journal of Business Ethics.

Habits like nail biting may be clues to hidden mental health struggles in teens

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1391 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • About one in eight students surveyed in England reported significant distress over nail biting, skin picking, or hair pulling.
  • In a recent development, nail biting and skin picking are widely regarded as nothing more serious than bad habits.
  • Recent findings suggest that the survey was answered by 5,437 students.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

About one in eight students surveyed in England reported significant distress over nail biting, skin picking, or hair pulling.

In a recent development, nail biting and skin picking are widely regarded as nothing more serious than bad habits. In a survey of students in England, most teens who reported these behaviors stated they caused little or no distress.

Recent findings suggest that the survey was answered by 5,437 students. More than half of them reported sometimes picking, pulling, or biting at their hair, skin, or nails.

The behavior was described as difficult to control, although little or no distress was reported by most of these students.

Sources indicate that about one in eight students gave a different answer. These students stated the behavior upset them quite a lot or a great deal. This distress was closely associated with anxiety, depression, and bullying.

Sources indicate that the study was led by Clare Mackay, a professor in the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Oxford. The behaviors are familiar to her from her own life.

Researchers have a name for them: body-focused repetitive behaviors, or BFRBs.

“BFRBs aren’t simply bad habits. They’re often signs that a young person is struggling,” Mackay noted.

According to recent reports, because the students were surveyed only once, the answers can indicate which problems occur together. The order in which those problems appeared cannot be established from the data.

The questions formed part of the 2025 OxWell Student Survey, which reached 32,102 students in England.

A total of 49 secondary schools and colleges took part, and most were state schools in Oxfordshire and Merseyside.

Industry observers note that the survey was usually completed online during a lesson. An optional set of questions was then offered, and some students continued to it.

Within that group, the questions about picking, pulling, and biting were answered by 5,437 students aged 11 to 18.

It has been revealed that three questions were written for the survey by Mackay’s team. Before being sent to schools, the questions were tried by 26 people with personal experience of the behaviors. Those people also commented on the questions.

Recent findings suggest that in the first question, students were asked about picking, pulling, or biting at hair, skin, or nails. Only behavior that feels difficult to control was covered by this question.

Sources indicate that in the second question, students were asked how much the behavior upset them. Four possible answers were offered, ranging from not at all to a great deal.

The third question asked whether the behavior interfered with home life, friendships, leisure activities, or classroom learning.

Industry observers note that overall, at least one such behavior was reported by 58.5% of the students. Nail biting was the most common at 43.6%. It was followed by skin picking at 31.3% and by hair pulling at 14.5%.

For most of these students, the behavior was not experienced as a source of distress.

It has been revealed that among students who reported a behavior, 35.2% noted it didn’t upset them at all. Another 42.6% said it upset them only a little. One of the two highest distress ratings was chosen by the other 22.2%.

It has been revealed that the researchers then focused on that smaller group. It was made up of 691 students, or 12.7% of everyone surveyed. The highest rating was chosen by 182 of them.

According to recent reports, the lowest levels of distress were reported by students who only bit their nails. One of the two highest distress ratings was chosen by 11% of them.

Recent findings suggest that the share was 29% among students who picked their skin. Among students who pulled their hair, a share of 37% was recorded.

Recent findings suggest that hair pulling and skin picking are listed as disorders in psychiatry’s diagnostic manuals. No separate category has been given to nail biting.

Considerable overlap between the behaviors was also observed.

Recent findings suggest that at least one other behavior was reported by 84% of the students who pulled their hair. Among students who picked their skin, the corresponding figure was 76%.

The authors suggested that the behaviors may share one underlying process. On this account, they may not be separate conditions.

Interference with daily life was also reported more often for hair pulling than for nail biting.

Depending on the area of life, interference was reported by 5% to 13% of students who only bit their nails. For students who pulled their hair, the range was 18% to 39%.

At least one behavior was reported by 45.6% of boys and 64.6% of girls.

Sources indicate that A third group consisted of 272 students who identified as trans or gender diverse, or who were unsure. Within that group, a share of 84.2% was recorded.

In a recent development, distress was also lowest among boys. Distressing behaviors were reported by 5.6% of boys and 16.4% of girls. In the trans, gender-diverse, or unsure group, the figure was 25%.

In a recent development, the team then accounted for anxiety, depression, bullying, and age. The gaps between boys and the other two groups remained.

According to recent reports, in studies of adults seen in clinics, about four women have been reported for every man with these conditions. A much smaller gap between girls and boys was observed among the students.

According to Mackay’s team, these behaviors had not previously been reported in trans and gender-diverse adolescents.

A standard 25-question checklist of anxiety and depression symptoms was also completed by the students.

Distressing behaviors were reported by 6.3% of students whose scores fell in the normal range. The share was 19.4% in the borderline range. In the highest range, which is labeled clinical by the checklist, it was 34.2%.

Distressing behaviors were also more common among students who reported bullying.

Among students who reported no recent bullying, 9.6% had distressing behaviors. A share of 27.1% was recorded among students bullied about once a week or more.

The team then analyzed these factors together. Anxiety and depression symptoms revealed the strongest link to distressing behaviors. Gender and frequent bullying also remained linked.

Sources indicate that distressing behaviors were reported about twice as often by students who noted they had autism, ADHD, or both. The comparison was made with students who reported neither condition.

Once anxiety, depression, gender, and bullying had been accounted for, that difference was no longer statistically significant.

It has been revealed that the authors wrote that picking, pulling, and biting may work as a way of managing difficult feelings. The behaviors can then become a source of shame.

Young people may stay silent about the behaviors because of shame and stigma, said Polly Waite. For the same reasons, help may not be requested.

Waite is a co-author from Oxford’s Department of Experimental Psychology.

That question cannot be answered by the survey. Since each student answered only once, it cannot be shown whether anxiety leads to picking and pulling.

It is also possible that anxiety is increased by the behaviors.

Earlier work suggests that the relationship may run in both directions.

According to recent reports, the students also may not represent English teenagers as a whole. Participation in the optional questions was a matter of choice.

Compared with the full survey, this group included more girls and gender-diverse students. Higher anxiety and depression scores were recorded in it as well.

As a result, students with emotional difficulties may have been over-counted.

The three questions are fresh and have not yet been formally tested. It also cannot be determined from them which students would meet the criteria for a diagnosis.

Mackay’s team wrote that these behaviors are rarely asked about in schools and clinics. A single screening question was therefore suggested by the authors.

Recent findings suggest that it asks whether picking, pulling, or biting upsets a young person. It also asks whether the behavior stops them from doing things they want to do.

The next question is whether distress tied to these behaviors would be eased by reducing anxiety, depression, or bullying.

The authors wrote that this could be tested in future studies, especially among girls and gender-diverse young people.

The full study was published in the journal BMJ Mental Health.

Ancient hunters in Australia had more on the menu than archaeologists expected

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ancient bones from two sites in northwestern Australia suggest that a varied diet gave hunters more options as rainfall and prey availability changed.
  • Ancient hunters in northwestern Australia ate a wide range of animals, and their leftovers suggest they could be choosy.
  • A study spanning roughly 50,000 years found that dietary variety could reflect plentiful food and skilled hunting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ancient bones from two sites in northwestern Australia suggest that a varied diet gave hunters more options as rainfall and prey availability changed.

Ancient hunters in northwestern Australia ate a wide range of animals, and their leftovers suggest they could be choosy.

A study spanning roughly 50,000 years found that dietary variety could reflect plentiful food and skilled hunting.

According to recent reports, the research was led by Tiina Manne from the University of Queensland. Her team examined ancient animal remains from Riwi rockshelter and Boodie Cave on Barrow Island.

It has been revealed that A widely used archaeological model predicts that hunters first concentrate on prey offering the greatest returns. They add less rewarding animals when preferred foods become harder to obtain.

The newly introduced research challenges that reading of dietary diversity. At both Australian sites, people ate many kinds of animals from early in the occupation records.

“First Nations peoples in Australia were much more sophisticated and strategic in the animals they chose to hunt,” Manne said.

“Flexibility, not fixation on a few species of prey, was the smartest way to live in an unpredictable climate.”.

It has been revealed that riwi stands on Gooniyandi traditional lands near the Great Sandy Desert. People began using the rockshelter about 45,000 years ago.

According to recent reports, its deposits contain remains of wallabies, echidnas, possums, flying foxes, lizards, and snakes. Small wallabies, lizards, and snakes dominate the earliest part of the analyzed sequence.

Boodie Cave’s first occupation dates to between about 51,100 and 46,200 years ago. Barrow Island was then part of the mainland, with its surroundings changing as sea levels fell and rose.

It has been revealed that the team identified 1,167 specimens from Riwi and 2,083 from Boodie Cave by animal group or body size. The varied diets persisted across substantial environmental changes.

Burned bones and impact marks at Riwi helped link the remains to human food preparation. Some fractures also occurred while the bones were fresh.

“In a land of unpredictable rainfall, a variety of foods signal ‘plenty’, and flexibility was the best strategy,” Manne explained.

Recent findings suggest that some of the most revealing findings were bones still joined together, known as articulated remains. Their condition suggested that people had discarded body parts with little nutritional value.

“On Barrow Island, which was then connected to the mainland, the diet included wallabies, turtles and reef fish, and articulated bones suggest only the most nutritious parts were eaten and the rest were discarded,” Manne remarked.

“This isn’t the behavior of people short of food – they could afford to be choosy, so a broad diet reflected choice, not scarcity.”.

The paper dates these articulated remains to around 7,200–6,800 years ago, long after the earliest occupation. Around this time, rising seas were cutting Barrow Island off from the mainland.

The researchers documented 24 groups of joined bones, including fish spines and parts of turtle limbs.

They interpret these discarded portions as evidence that people could select the more rewarding parts of their catches.

It has been revealed that an animal’s value depended on more than its size. Weather affected both its condition and the effort needed to catch it.

“When water and vegetation were plentiful, large kangaroos were spread thin across the landscape, but in arid conditions they became easier to ambush as they stayed near waterholes,” Manne said.

“Small animals like bandicoots were also a good option when it got dry, because they stayed fat by switching to eating insects.”.

“Hunters who kept their options open could shift between prey as conditions changed.”.

At Riwi, large kangaroo remains became prominent after about 34,000 years ago, as conditions grew drier. The authors suggest hunting them became less risky when water drew the animals into more predictable locations.

Industry observers note that fat mattered, too. Opened leg bones at both sites point to the extraction of marrow, while smaller insect-eating animals could retain valuable fat during drought.

Many Australian animals hide in burrows, vegetation, or rock crevices during the day. Finding them requires knowing which traces to follow.

The paper draws on First Nations ecological knowledge, including signs such as fresh tracks, disturbed soil, and scratches on bark. These can reveal prey that a hunter cannot see directly.

“A tremendous amount of ecological knowledge is passed on in oral histories, including subtle signs of not only how to find prey, but the best prey depending on the season and circumstances,” Manne said.

Where hidden animals were abundant and diverse, investigating those signs could reward hunters with many different foods. A smaller animal could be a dependable catch even when a larger one promised more meat.

The authors argue that archaeological diets need to be understood through local animal behavior, food availability, and hunting costs.

A fixed ranking of desirable prey can miss how those factors change with rainfall.

Industry observers note that animal remains also reveal only part of a meal. Plant foods, documented at other northern Australian sites, would have supplied key carbohydrates alongside meat and fat.

“Importantly, our work suggests archaeologists around the world should re-consider how they have interpreted diet choice and diversity,” Manne concluded.

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the Natural Academy of Sciences.

Virtual reality can make you feel sick even when the scene around you stays still
