💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a five-minute VR experiment, watching a single moving ball increased nausea, eye discomfort, and disorientation as the eyes aimed and focused at different distances.
  • Volunteers spent five minutes in a virtual reality headset watching a speckled ball glide toward them and away against a black background.
  • The ball was designed to put two jobs the eyes normally do together at odds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a five-minute VR experiment, watching a single moving ball increased nausea, eye discomfort, and disorientation as the eyes aimed and focused at different distances.

Volunteers spent five minutes in a virtual reality headset watching a speckled ball glide toward them and away against a black background. Afterward, they reported more nausea, eye discomfort, and disorientation than before.

The ball was designed to put two jobs the eyes normally do together at odds.

As it appeared to move closer, the volunteers’ eyes turned inward to follow it, but the headset kept the image in focus at a fixed distance.

A cap of 64 electrodes recorded their brain activity shifting while it happened.

The research was conducted by Mattie Johnson, a computer science doctoral student at the University of Maryland.

Amitabh Varshney, a computer science professor and dean at the university, led the study, and Sujal Bista of the University of Maryland Institute for Health Computing was a co-author.

The team worked with the Food and Drug Administration and Sony on the study.

Sources indicate that the team is careful about what the electrode readings mean. The scene used for comparison differed from the test scene in more than one way, and the authors can’t fully rule out eye and facial muscle activity.

So the paper calls the brain changes candidate correlates, not a signature of this kind of sickness.

Look at a real object and your eyes do two things at once: they turn inward to aim at it, and their lenses adjust to bring it into focus.

In a recent development, the two distances agree. A headset breaks the agreement. Its screens sit at one fixed focal distance while the 3D picture asks the eyes to aim nearer or farther.

According to recent reports, the Meta Quest 2 used here has its focal plane about 4.3 feet (1.3 meters) in front of the eyes. The team measured that with a camera and a test pattern.

Within about half a diopter of that distance the mismatch is mild. Outside it, discomfort builds.

So the team demonstrated volunteers a black-and-white speckled ball on a black background. It glided from 11 inches (0.275 meters) out to 4.7 feet (1.425 meters) and back, one round trip every 3.9 seconds.

The ball grew as it receded and shrank as it approached, so it always looked the same size.

The researchers designed the scene to reduce the feeling that viewers themselves were moving while still making their eyes aim nearer and farther.

Forty people, 65% of them men and nearly all between 18 and 30, took part.

It has been revealed that the researchers analyzed brain recordings from 38 people and complete questionnaires from 38 people. Each analysis excluded a different pair of participants.

Each person sat through five minutes with eyes closed, five minutes looking at a headset’s static home screen, and then five minutes of the moving ball.

Recent findings suggest that before and after the ball, they filled out a 1993 simulator sickness questionnaire, the SSQ. It scores nausea, eye-related symptoms, and disorientation.

All three scores rose, and the total score rose by what statisticians call a large effect. Men and women both reported more symptoms, though men’s disorientation scores didn’t rise by a reliable amount.

Most participants described themselves as not at all or only slightly prone to this kind of sickness.

The electrode cap sampled the scalp 250 times a second. Software stripped out blinks and muscle noise as best it could.

The team compared 50 seconds of brain activity near the end of the home-screen baseline with 50 seconds near the end of the moving-ball scene.

In clusters of activity toward the front of the head, power in the fast beta and gamma brain waves fell. In clusters toward the back, power in the slower theta waves fell.

“In the frontal lobe, we found a statistically significant decrease in high brain wave frequencies during cybersickness, and in the occipital lobe we saw a statistically significant decrease in low brain wave frequencies,” Johnson said.

“These changes in what we call EEG clusters could be useful predictors of a cybersickness experience.”.

The pattern is not the one Varshney’s group found in 2022 for the motion kind of virtual reality sickness, where slower waves grew stronger over the center of the head.

The studies found different patterns, but the researchers still don’t know whether the latest pattern reflects sickness, differences between the scenes, or both.

In a recent development, the baseline scene and the ball differed in brightness, content, and layout. Volunteers were told where to look during the ball but not during the baseline.

It has been revealed that some of the drop in slow waves at the back of the head may simply be visual processing of a different picture. The front of the head is also where eye movements leak into recordings most.

The team didn’t record whether participants wore glasses or contacts, and nearly everyone was under 30.

According to recent reports, the authors also wrote that the headset’s three fixed lens-spacing settings fit a larger share of women than men poorly. That could add to symptoms in ways the study can’t separate.

Whether the brain changes track the sickness itself, the change of scenery, or both is the question the authors leave open.

Settling it would need a baseline scene matched to the test scene, which the authors recommend. It would also need eye tracking to remove the eyes’ own electrical traces, which Johnson’s team prepares to add.

The goal beyond that is a headset that detects the pattern and adjusts the scene.

“Ultimately we want to inform technology to mitigate symptoms in real time, improving user comfort and productivity over extended periods of immersion,” Johnson stated.

Bista put it as a shift in who gets asked.

“The SSQ still has its uses, but now we have the tools to go from asking participants how they’re feeling to asking the brain and body what’s really going on,” he noted.

The full study was published in the journal Virtual Reality.

Breaking: In 1950, Michigan beat Ohio State in the Snow Bowl without a first down, and the blizzard behind it dumped up to 62 inches of snow

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1183 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Snow Bowl storm, later called the Great Appalachian Storm, contributed to at least 160 deaths and is the worst Ohio Valley snowstorm NOAA has analyzed.
  • It has been revealed that on the Saturday after Thanksgiving in 1950, Ohio State and Michigan played their annual game in Columbus in a blizzard.
  • Recent findings suggest that michigan won 9-3.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Snow Bowl storm, later called the Great Appalachian Storm, contributed to at least 160 deaths and is the worst Ohio Valley snowstorm NOAA has analyzed.

It has been revealed that on the Saturday after Thanksgiving in 1950, Ohio State and Michigan played their annual game in Columbus in a blizzard. At noon, the temperature at the city’s airport, a few miles from Ohio Stadium, was 10°F, and visibility was half a mile.

Recent findings suggest that michigan won 9-3. It did so without a single first down and without completing a pass, according to the National Weather Service. The game became known as the Snow Bowl, and some call it the Blizzard Bowl.

The storm that buried the field was much bigger than one football game. Over the following days, it dropped as much as 62 inches of snow in West Virginia, sent temperatures down to 3°F in Atlanta, and pushed hurricane-force gusts into the Northeast.

It ranks as the worst Ohio Valley snowstorm analyzed by scientists at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

The game’s place in history has little to do with the quality of the football, the weather service’s office in Wilmington, Ohio, indicates.

It is remembered for “the weather, as the game was played in a significant blizzard unlike any that either school had played in before, or since.”.

It has been revealed that neither team could move the ball, so they kept punting it away. Michigan punted 24 times, and its total offense for the whole game was 27 yards. Ohio State punted 21 times, and four of those punts were blocked by the Wolverines.

Industry observers note that all of the scoring came from blocked kicks. Ohio State blocked a punt that led to a field goal. Two of Michigan’s blocks led to a safety and a touchdown.

“It speaks to the severity of the storm, the remarkable conditions, and just how debilitating extreme weather can be,” the Wilmington office wrote.

The weather service has analyzed the afternoon’s hourly observations at Port Columbus Airport. The temperature climbed only from 10°F at noon to 16°F at 4 p.m.

Sustained winds blew at 17 to 22 mph, with gusts of more than 35 mph, so wind chills stayed between -8°F and -1°F. Visibility dropped as low as a quarter of a mile in snow and blowing snow.

It has been revealed that two days earlier, the weather had been very different. On Thursday evening, November 23, which was Thanksgiving Day, it was 39°F in Columbus at 8 p.m.

It has been revealed that an arctic cold front then moved through, and by midnight it was 20°F. By 7 a.m. on Friday, the temperature had fallen to 8°F.

On the day of the game, 7.5 inches of snow fell on Columbus. The weather service indicates that is still the city’s record for a single November day.

Recent findings suggest that from Thursday night to the following Tuesday, the city got 14.9 inches. Its November 1950 total of 15.2 inches remains the snowiest November on record there.

The cold front that arrived on Thanksgiving night was the precursor to the Great Appalachian Storm of 1950.

According to the weather service office in Jackson, Kentucky, the arctic air behind it sent temperatures to all-time November lows across the Upper Midwest and the Ohio Valley.

Chicago dropped to -2°F on November 24, tying its lowest November reading, and the next day Louisville hit -1°F and Lexington -3°F, both records for the month.

On November 25, low pressure formed over the Carolinas, the Jackson office notes. It moved northwest into Ohio by the middle of the next day, spreading heavy snow as it went, then spun over Lake Erie before it weakened and left for Canada on November 29 and 30.

Sources indicate that the snow piled up from western Pennsylvania deep into West Virginia. Several places received more than 50 inches, and Coburn Creek, West Virginia, reported the largest total, 62 inches, according to NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI). Pittsburgh got about 30 inches.

The cold reached far into the South. Temperatures fell to 22°F in Pensacola, Florida, 5°F in Birmingham, Alabama, 3°F in Atlanta and 1°F in Asheville, North Carolina, NCEI claims, and the record cold damaged crops in Georgia and South Carolina.

According to recent reports, the storm drew arctic air in on one side and warm Atlantic air in on the other. While Pittsburgh was buried under snow at single-digit temperatures, Buffalo, New York, about 200 miles to the north, had temperatures in the 40s and no snow at all, the Jackson office claims.

Sources indicate that in the Northeast, the problem was wind. Fresh York City recorded a gust of 94 mph, and Newark, New Jersey, 108 mph. Bear Mountain, just north of New York City, had a 140 mph gust, and Mount Washington in New Hampshire reached 160 mph.

The winds caused extensive tree damage and power outages, and coastal flooding that broke through dikes at LaGuardia Airport and flooded its runways.

Fierce winds are still a feature of big East Coast storms, as earth.com saw when blizzard winds battered the coast in a more recent storm.

In a recent development, heavy rain on the warm side of the storm brought near-record flooding to eastern Pennsylvania. Then, in the first week of December, unusually warm weather melted the snow quickly. The Ohio River rose to 28.5 feet in Pittsburgh and 56 feet in Cincinnati, 4 feet above flood stage in both cities.

Recent findings suggest that the storm contributed to at least 160 deaths, NCEI says. Insurance companies paid out more for its damage than for any earlier storm or hurricane, according to the Jackson office. They call it the costliest storm on record up to that time. NCEI describes it as one of the costliest storms on record.

NCEI rates major snowstorms with its Regional Snowfall Index, which combines how much snow fell, how large an area it covered and how many people lived there.

The 1950 storm scored 34.7 in the Ohio Valley, the highest of the 232 storms analyzed there. The second-worst, in March 1993, scored 24.6. In that region, more than 6.1 million people lived where at least 18 inches of snow fell.

In the Northeast, it ranks ninth of 230 storms, just behind the storms of February 2003, February 2010 and January 2016.

In a recent development, scientists are still studying how storms like this work. NASA-backed scientists have flown research planes straight into snowstorms to learn how their heaviest bands of snow form.

Recent findings suggest that the information was obtained from the National Weather Service’s pages Snow Bowl – November 25, 1950 (Wilmington, Ohio) and The Great Appalachian Storm of 1950 (Jackson, Kentucky), from NOAA NCEI’s article The Great Appalachian Storm in Historical Context, and the Michigan vs. Ohio State team game records of the University of Michigan’s Bentley Historical Library and the Ohio State University Archives.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

According to recent reports, in an increasingly fire-prone western North America, Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, looks at fire with a holistic eye. She considers her work with landscapes recovering from catastrophic wildfire to be “deliberately unfocused,” spanning soil microbial ecology, restoration ecology, invasion biology and historical biology.

In a recent development, grenz analyzes historical ecological records, like how Indigenous people have shaped and cared for ecosystems over time, to paint a comprehensive picture. “I’m interested in how those histories leave ecological legacies and hints of the stewardship of the past,” says Grenz, who leads the Indigenous Ecology Lab at the University of British Columbia in Canada. “What changed on the land that made it more vulnerable?”.

Grenz spends time with many kinds of specialists, such as archaeologists, anthropologists and Indigenous elders who provide oral histories.

Moving forward, her lab will examine ecology below ground, including soil, microbial communities and root networks. The goal is to understand the role of underground ecology in critical topics like carbon sequestration, climate change, biodiversity and sustainable management.

Recent findings suggest that “My motivation is in our interior Salish Territories in the southern interior of British Columbia, where my ancestors rest and where my people are,” Grenz notes. “The responsibility I feel to them and to our Tmícw, which means our lands, [is] to not take us back to the past, but to show that we have the deep knowledge to help us move forward.”.

#111681. Would we know if lab-grown brain tissue became conscious?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (856 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Would we know if lab-grown brain tissue became conscious?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (856 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists propose testing whether lab-grown brain tissue can learn a pattern and detect when it changes, a possible clue in the search for signs of consciousness.
  • Scientists can grow small clusters of human brain cells in a dish.
  • Sources indicate that two neuroscientists have now proposed a way to check what such tissue, called a brain organoid, can do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists propose testing whether lab-grown brain tissue can learn a pattern and detect when it changes, a possible clue in the search for signs of consciousness.

Scientists can grow small clusters of human brain cells in a dish. One set of joined clusters has reacted to capsaicin, the compound found in chili peppers, but a reaction like that doesn’t show the tissue feels anything.

Sources indicate that two neuroscientists have now proposed a way to check what such tissue, called a brain organoid, can do. Their plan borrows tests already used on infants, sleeping people, and patients who can’t respond.

According to recent reports, the tests ask whether an organoid can learn a pattern and notice when the pattern is broken. The proposal reports no results, and the authors wrote that it is highly unlikely today’s organoids are conscious.

Lucia Melloni of Ruhr University Bochum in Germany and Stanislas Dehaene of the Collège de France in Paris wrote the proposal. Both belong to a brain and consciousness research program at CIFAR, a Canadian research organization.

“I don’t believe that brain organoids currently possess consciousness,” Melloni said.

“But given the pace with which the technology is advancing, they may do so in future. That’s why we need to start thinking about how we can find out.”.

Recent findings suggest that organoids are grown from human stem cells. The cells organize themselves into tiny tissues that copy some features of the early developing brain.

Researchers can also fuse several organoids into what they call an assembloid. The one that reacted to capsaicin joined four organoids to rebuild a basic pain pathway.

“A reaction, however, is not proof that the tissue feels anything,” Melloni noted.

In a recent development, other teams have wired brain cells into machines, including one hooked to a simplified version of the video game Pong. Melloni and Dehaene wrote that those setups are too complex to show what the living tissue itself worked out.

In a 2024 study they cited, a gel that responds to electricity produced similar results in place of the cells.

The central test comes from research on how people process sequences.

Recent findings suggest that A person hears ba-ba-ba-ba-bu again and again. The brain reacts to the bu because it differs from the four sounds before it.

After many repeats, the person learns the whole pattern. If the sequence then comes as ba-ba-ba-ba-ba, the brain reacts again, this time because the expected bu is missing.

The second reaction is the harder one. It depends on a memory of the whole sequence, built up over many repeats.

An organoid has no ears, so researchers would use electrical pulses or light in place of sounds.

They would stimulate two or more separate groups of cells in sequence and record how the tissue’s activity changes.

The question would be whether the same sequence produces a different response depending on what came before it.

Monkeys can learn patterns like this one too. That has let researchers study the brain activity behind the reactions in animals that have no language.

Industry observers note that in people, the first kind of reaction survives sleep and anesthesia. The second seems to require a person to be awake and paying attention.

It has been revealed that doctors have also tried the test on patients who can’t communicate. In those patients, 80% of the ones whose brains indicated the second reaction later regained consciousness.

According to recent reports, the test missed many others. Only 35% of the patients who recovered had shown the reaction.

Melloni and Dehaene wrote that no single test would be enough. Their confidence would rise if an organoid passed this test along with several other known signs of consciousness.

The authors wrote that a failed test is perhaps the more likely outcome. A failure would lower confidence that an organoid is conscious.

In a recent development, dehaene has a financial interest in this kind of testing. He is a co-inventor on a patent for methods to monitor consciousness and an associate at a company that uses those methods in clinics.

In a recent development, the authors wrote that there is no evidence current organoids hold any rich picture of the outside world or of themselves. The tissues are tiny, and they are cut off from a body and from surroundings.

Organoids can be kept alive for months to years, though, and they keep changing as they age. The authors proposed running the same tests on an organoid again and again as it matures.

Human babies show the second kind of reaction at 3 months of age, and it may be present before birth, after 35 weeks of pregnancy.

Repeated testing would show when each ability appears in an organoid.

The authors also wrote that if several signs ever pointed the same way, the ethical treatment of these tissues should change with the evidence.

Melloni and other researchers have called for an international board to oversee organoid research.

The full study was published in the journal Neuron.

  • Sources indicate that blue light has become the villain of bedtime.
  • Yet the same light, delivered for half an hour after waking, made a group of office workers sleep longer and better that night.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Office workers given morning blue light for 30 minutes slept about 11 minutes longer that night and brought more energy to work the next day.

Sources indicate that blue light has become the villain of bedtime. Phones get dimmed at night and glasses that block it sell as sleep aids.

Yet the same light, delivered for half an hour after waking, made a group of office workers sleep longer and better that night. The gain carried into the next day’s work.

The effect was modest, about 11 minutes more sleep a night and a small lift in how well people said they slept.

It has been revealed that participants who reported sleeping better also reported more alertness and less mental fatigue the next day. Greater alertness was linked to more engagement at work.

Kathleen Keeler, who studies management and human resources at Ohio State University’s Fisher College of Business, led the study.

Christopher Barnes of the University of Washington’s business school and Brian Gunia of Johns Hopkins University’s Carey Business School were among her co-authors.

The glasses came from a manufacturer called Ayo, which donated half the pairs used.

Industry observers note that barnes said the mechanism is not a morning jolt from the blue light itself. “It’s that the blue light helps them sleep better later that night, which helps them the following day,” he noted.

The body runs on a roughly 24-hour cycle that decides when a person feels sleepy and when they feel awake.

Light is the strongest signal that keeps that internal clock on time, and blue light, in particular, is what the clock responds to most.

Blue light at night pushes the clock later and holds back melatonin, the hormone that brings sleep on.

In a recent development, that is the part everyone has heard. The same light in the morning pulls the clock earlier, which, in principle, should make sleep come sooner and run smoother that night.

Industry observers note that workplace researchers had tested the night half of that idea with blue-blocking glasses and found better sleep and better work. Workplace studies had not tested the morning half.

The team invited 200 full-time employees at a large Midwestern university, all working roughly nine to five, and 182 finished the study.

Industry observers note that nearly three in four were women, and the typical participant was in their early forties. They had been with the university for about a decade on average.

Industry observers note that for 10 workdays, each wore glasses that shine blue-turquoise light toward the eyes for 30 minutes right after waking, between 5 and 10 a.m. On average they started just before 7 a.m.

For one of the two weeks the blue glasses ran at full power. For the other they ran at 1%, a glow so faint that in earlier tests people couldn’t tell the two settings apart.

Which week came first was decided at random, so every person served as their own comparison.

Participants filled in a survey each morning about the night’s sleep and their energy, and another each afternoon about their work, from engagement to helping coworkers to slacking off.

The team collected 1,259 daily surveys and registered its predictions in advance.

Each participant kept the glasses and a year of the companion app afterward.

According to recent reports, after a full-power morning, people reported sleeping about 11 minutes longer that night, and rated the night’s sleep about 3.5% higher. Neither number is large. The team then traced the effect through the next day.

Longer and better sleep predicted more alertness the next day, and better sleep predicted less of the feeling that one’s mental energy is running low.

Sources indicate that alertness, in turn, predicted stronger work engagement and more helping behavior. Less depletion predicted better task performance and fewer behaviors like taking an overlong break.

Each link in that chain was small, and the team noted so.

“This is a pretty small, cheap, easy intervention, and we’re getting meaningful movement on work outcomes that matter,” Barnes said.

The morning blue light didn’t increase alertness that same day.

Alertness that same day was no higher, which is why the authors read the whole effect as running through sleep.

The benefit also built across the week rather than appearing in full on day one.

According to recent reports, two groups gained more than the rest. People who arrived with existing sleep problems saw a bigger improvement in sleep quality.

Younger employees saw a bigger gain in sleep length, with effects on engagement and helping that the older workers did not show.

The authors tied the age gap to the eye’s declining sensitivity to light with age, and called both findings exploratory.

It has been revealed that barnes had a cheaper suggestion. “The best thing you could do in the morning is get outside,” he remarked.

Every measure here was self-reported, including how well people noted they performed, so the findings wait on a replication with objective records.

Everyone studied worked daytime hours at one university, and most were women. The authors stated shift workers, who often miss morning light altogether, might gain more, but no one in this study worked nights.

The measure of workplace misbehavior was also short and noisy, which the authors said may have hidden a larger effect rather than created a false one.

What the glasses add on top of a sunny walk is the open question, since the study compared bright glasses with dim ones, not glasses with daylight.

The authors said the next test belongs with people whose schedules fight their body clocks.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Applied Psychology.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hubble’s portrait of NGC 4394 shows how a bar of stars fits into a spiral galaxy and offers a rare perspective on the structure of our own Milky Way.

Today’s Image of the Day features a nearly face-on view of the spiral galaxy NGC 4394.

It has been revealed that A pale gold bar stretches across the galaxy’s bright core, while thin lanes of dust curve around the center. Farther out, two spiral arms sweep into the dark.

That angle makes the bar easy to spot and gives us something we can only imagine for our own Milky Way: a view down onto the disk, with the center and the spiral arms visible in the same frame.

The European Space Agency released this Hubble Space Telescope image on November 24.

Industry observers note that the galaxy lies about 55 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices. Its light was already on its way here long before humans appeared on Earth.

Industry observers note that on a clear, dark night, the Milky Way looks like a hazy band across the sky. That band is part of our galaxy’s disk seen from within.

When we look along the disk, stars at many different distances crowd into the same field of view, and dust obscures much of the light coming from the center.

Astronomers have used infrared telescopes such as Spitzer to look through some of that dust and trace the distribution of stars.

Industry observers note that those observations helped establish that our galaxy has a central bar. A face-on view of NGC 4394 makes it easier to picture how such a feature fits into a spiral galaxy.

The angle also makes it easier to follow the dust. In Hubble’s image, narrow dark filaments arc around the core and wind through the disk.

They stand out where they block light from the stars behind them. Farther along the arms, blue and pink knots punctuate the softer glow of the surrounding stars.

A bar may look like a solid feature in a still image, but the stars that make it up are moving around the galaxy.

Recent findings suggest that one way a bar can form is when nearly circular stellar orbits become stretched. If enough of those elongated orbits line up, the combined light from the stars takes on the shape of a bar.

In a recent development, A passing galaxy can disturb a disk through gravity and help set that process in motion. A disk can also become unstable through gravitational interactions among its own stars.

Either way, a feature that spans a large part of the galaxy can emerge from changes in the paths of individual stars.

Recent findings suggest that once a bar forms, its gravity can help channel gas inward. That matters because gas supplies the raw material for upcoming stars.

A bar can therefore influence where a galaxy builds its next generation of stars, even though the bright feature we see in the image is mostly the light of stars already there.

Hubble first captured NGC 4394 while studying a different galaxy. One instrument was trained on nearby Messier 85 and its star clusters, while another recorded an adjacent patch of sky containing NGC 4394.

Hubble’s team released that earlier image about a decade ago.

The latest portrait combines those observations with data from a program studying 40 galaxies. NGC 4394 belongs to the Virgo Cluster, a gathering of more than 1,000 galaxies.

The researchers want to understand how star formation winds down in crowded environments and whether it follows a different course in galaxies with fewer neighbors.

Sources indicate that star clusters give researchers a way to look backward. By comparing how brightly a cluster shines at different wavelengths, astronomers can estimate its age.

It has been revealed that A young cluster marks a place where stars formed relatively recently. Older clusters preserve evidence of earlier activity.

Taken together, their ages and locations can help researchers reconstruct where star formation persisted and where it faded.

That gives the specks along the spiral arms a second role in the image. The bar is the feature you can pick out at a glance, and it offers an immediate point of comparison with the Milky Way.

Sources indicate that the star clusters are harder to spot. Each one carries a piece of the galaxy’s history, and Hubble can pick them out even though their light has crossed 55 million years of space to reach us.

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Industry observers note that dor Minzer remembers sitting in an undergraduate computation class at Tel Aviv University. He was intrigued by his professor and soon found himself pulled into a fresh world: the mystifying intersection of math and computation, first laid out by Alan Turing during World War II. Working with the professor, Minzer became deeply interested in the limitations of what computers can and can’t do.

Industry observers note that “My part is actually to prove not only do I not know how to do it, but I can prove that it’s impossible,” Minzer notes. “You have to really be curious.”.

Minzer’s hard work has paid off. In 2018, he proved a theoretical computer science problem called the 2-to-2 games conjecture. It asks whether computers can efficiently distinguish games where almost all rules can be satisfied from those where almost none can be satisfied, when the rules have a strict structure.

In September, Minzer and his two graduate students at MIT posted a 95-page milestone paper on the unique games conjecture, which builds off the 2-to-2 conjecture. The paper wasn’t quite ready, but they published to get ahead of a press release from OpenAI, describing its proof for the same problem, slated for only days later. It’s a situation that many mathematicians have found themselves in this year as AI companies flood the field with findings at lightning speed.

Minzer says it’s critical to remember that math, and all the research and contemplation behind it, is very human. “It’s a human activity,” he says. “Research is sort of a living organism, a living body.”.

Sources indicate that minzer teaches his own students now. Some days, he talks to his class and gets the sense that nobody is paying attention. But other days, he gets a few students that participate. They have ideas, they’re excited, and they remind him of his own days as a graduate student.

“I feel like now I feel like I’m passing the torch,” he says. “Before you have a Ph.D. adviser, you’re like a upcoming person in a dark room. There are infinite places to go. Your Ph.D. adviser is the person that holds your hand and says, ‘Okay, let’s walk here.’”.

Latest Update: Forest birds get more warning about predators when many other bird species live nearby

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1394 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • More bird species meant more alarm calls when a model hawk flew past, and recordings of more species drew bigger crowds of mobbing birds.
  • Industry observers note that when an owl demonstrates up in a forest during daylight hours, the small birds that see it make lots of noise.
  • A newly introduced study of forest birds in eastern China found more of these interspecies callings in places with greater bird species diversity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More bird species meant more alarm calls when a model hawk flew past, and recordings of more species drew bigger crowds of mobbing birds.

Industry observers note that when an owl demonstrates up in a forest during daylight hours, the small birds that see it make lots of noise. They gather around the owl and chirp out their calls. Almost immediately, birds of other species hear the calls and come to join the outcry.

A newly introduced study of forest birds in eastern China found more of these interspecies callings in places with greater bird species diversity. Joining forces allowed them to make more calls per minute, alerting everyone within earshot of the owl’s presence.

The result suggests that birds in forests that have fewer species may get less predator warnings, leaving them more vulnerable.

Two doctoral students, Agnishikhe Kumar and Jiahao Wu, are the study’s first authors. Both are at Xi’an Jiaotong-Liverpool University in Suzhou, China, and the University of Liverpool.

Kumar and Wu worked with Eben Goodale, the study’s senior author, and with colleagues at Zhejiang University and other institutions in China, France, and the United States. All of the fieldwork took place in forest reserves in China.

Over more than two years, the team worked in ten nature reserves spread along about 1,025 miles (1,650 kilometers) of eastern China, from tropical Hainan to temperate Shaanxi.

In a recent development, birds make two different kinds of calls about predators. Alarm calls go out when a predator is moving and attacking, and they often send the birds in a flock scattering into thick vegetation.

It has been revealed that mobbing calls are for a predator that isn’t moving, like an owl in daylight. These calls draw other birds toward the caller, and the crowd harasses the predator and can drive it away.

To set off alarm calls, the researchers used a slingshot to fire an 8-inch (20-centimeter) plastic hawk into the air beside mixed flocks of several species.

For mobbing, they put out a painted foam model of a collared owlet, a small owl that can attack birds, and played recordings of its calls.

Each time, they recorded how many species called, how many calls came per minute, and how quickly the first call came. They also measured the range of pitch the calls covered.

In an interview with Earth.com, Goodale credited his two students with the fieldwork. “Yeah, this was a ton of work,” he noted. By his count, the total was 1,277 experiments.

Before each owl test, the team counted the bird species at the site. Where they counted more species, more kinds of birds joined the mobbing and more individual birds took part.

The birds at those sites also called at a higher rate, and their calls covered a wider range of pitch.

In a recent development, pitch range matters because birds respond most to calls of other species that sound like their own. A broader mix of calls should reach more kinds of listeners.

On 41 islands in Thousand Island Lake, a reservoir in Zhejiang Province, the team saw a similar pattern. The number of bird species on those islands goes up with the size of the island.

Industry observers note that alarm calls were far rarer than mobbing calls. The plastic hawk set them off in 79 of 150 flocks.

The flocks that called gave a median of four alarm calls a minute, compared with a median of 52 calls a minute in the owl tests. One highly social species, Huet’s fulvetta, made 60.2% of all the alarm calls.

A bird that calls while a hawk is near may put itself at risk. Goodale told Earth.com the team thought the pattern might not hold for alarm calls, reasoning that “after one species calls, everyone else should eavesdrop on that and remain quiet.”.

Instead, in flocks with more species, more kinds of birds gave alarm calls. The calls came at a higher rate and covered a wider range of pitch.

Sources indicate that “We think it may be because the initial information may not be reliable,” Goodale said. Other species may need to keep calling, he added, to stress the threat and make sure the warning reaches their own kind.

In Sri Lanka, the authors wrote, the first bird to call in a flock is usually a babbler. That babbler often calls at any large or fast-moving bird, so the later calls of other species help mark a real attack.

The team found no significant link between a flock’s species count and how promptly the first alarm call came.

In a recent development, the hawk and owl tests showed how much calling went on. To learn whether birds of other species made use of it, the team ran an experiment at seven sites on the largest island in the lake.

Through two speakers, the researchers played the mobbing calls of one, two, four, or eight local species and recorded which birds responded. A recording of crickets, played to check that birds weren’t simply reacting to noise, drew no response.

Recent findings suggest that across 406 trials, recordings with more species drew more kinds of birds and more individuals. The birds that came made more calls, across a wider range of pitch. The increase leveled off as the number of species in the recording went up.

According to recent reports, birds of species that weren’t in the recording were also more likely to call within the first minute when the recording held more species. When the team counted all responding birds together, the first-minute pattern was too weak to rule out chance.

In a recent development, huet’s fulvetta leads the mixed flocks in the region and often starts the mobbing. Goodale mentioned the team expected it to play an outsized role in spreading information.

The experiment revealed little sign of that. The team compared recordings of four species with and without each of the eight birds, across five measures.

In only four of those 40 comparisons was the response stronger when a particular species was included, and the four involved four different species.

Recent findings suggest that all eight species drew relatively similar responses, Goodale mentioned. “It seems birds are responding to the small acoustic differences between species and registering a higher response when they hear more species,” he added.

To test that idea, the team had built each recording two ways. In one version, every recording had 104 calls per minute, however many species were in it. In the other, each species called at its usual rate, so more species meant more calls.

In a recent development, birds responded more to recordings with more species even when the number of calls stayed the same. The researchers took that as evidence that the variety of calls matters.

On most of the five measures, adding species had a stronger effect when the number of calls rose too. So the amount of calling appears to matter as well.

Goodale said the finding also applies in reverse. In areas with fewer animals because of habitat loss, hunting, or other causes, the animals that remain could be less informed.

It has been revealed that or they could come to rely more on collecting information themselves. When the information is about predators, he stated, that could come at great cost.

The authors compared their finding to earlier studies that tied species diversity to pollination, seed dispersal, and pest control, and wrote that it helps justify conservation.

The experiments recorded how birds called and gathered, so they can’t show whether birds in places with more species are caught by predators less often.

It has been revealed that only mobbing calls were tested with recordings, and only on a single island. Earlier experiments elsewhere, which mostly compared one species with two, found weak effects on communication or no difference in response.

The larger scale of this study partly explains its stronger result, the authors wrote.

Industry observers note that the same idea could apply to other information, such as where to find food or habitat, and to other animals. The researchers suggested that experiments with the chemical signals of insects and other invertebrates may be particularly useful.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Biology.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 23: Double star Kurhah in Cepheus.

Full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. A Super Moon occurs when the Moon reaches Full phase close to perigee, its closest point to Earth, making our satellite appear larger and brighter than average. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon.

Sources indicate that A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars. This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope (just note that you may want a Moon filter if available, as our satellite is so big and bright). The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

The 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed rapidly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. The latter two may be difficult to catch from the Midwest without optical aid, as sunrise is fast approaching. If you are using binoculars or a telescope in this region, make sure to put them away several minutes ahead of sunrise from your location. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

COP31 ended without a major climate agreement after countries clashed over fossil fuels, emissions cuts and climate funding.

Recent findings suggest that the final draft of the main agreement at this year’s UN climate summit had one glaring omission. Nowhere in the document did the words fossil fuels appear.

Several countries rejected it for that reason.

COP31 ended on Sunday, November 22, in Antalya, Türkiye. The talks lasted two weeks and then ran two more days. That made it the longest UN climate summit on record.

Governments still did not agree on the main text.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres called the outcome “deeply disappointing.”.

“There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science,” Guterres said in a statement.

Murat Kurum, Türkiye’s environment minister, was the president of COP31. He had little good news at the end of the summit.

Industry observers note that “I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted,” Kurum noted.

It has been revealed that australia led the negotiations. For several days it worked with Türkiye on upcoming versions of the agreement. Both countries tried to find language that everyone could accept.

Some countries wanted a firm commitment to use less coal, oil and gas. Countries that sell fossil fuels abroad worried about what that would mean for their economies.

The proposed text mentioned the world is heading for more than 2.7°F (1.5°C) of warming.

Under the Paris Agreement, governments agreed to hold warming well below 2°C above preindustrial levels and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.

Industry observers note that the text also asked for more technology to remove carbon dioxide from the air. It said nothing about burning less fossil fuel in the first place.

In a recent development, the European Union would not accept an agreement that avoided the subject. The bloc described the omission as “unconscionable.”.

Panama had sent a letter to the summit presidency with its priorities. Its delegation noted governments had a responsibility “not to negotiate the minimum threshold, but to act.”.

In the Marshall Islands, where much of the land lies just above sea level, the stakes are particularly high.

Accepting the deal, the country’s delegation noted, would mean betraying its own people. It rejected what it called “false solutions” and pushed for a faster, adequately funded shift away from fossil fuels.

Speaking for the African Group, Ghana raised concerns about climate funding and financial assistance for countries suffering climate damage.

There was also the question of how to support workers and communities as fossil fuel industries decline.

That glitch got “a single generic sentence,” according to Ghana.

Nevertheless, the African Group chose not to block the deal, acknowledging that the text reflected the views of many countries.

Industry observers note that saudi Arabia saw things differently. Speaking for the League of Arab States, it defended keeping carbon capture and storage in the agreement.

This technology traps carbon dioxide and stores it before it reaches the atmosphere.

Was this simply greenwashing? Saudi Arabia argued otherwise, pointing to scientific assessments that give carbon capture a role in limiting global warming.

Sources indicate that pakistan urged countries to keep talking. Its delegation said climate action needs “bridges, not barriers.”.

Part of the frustration at COP31 goes back three years.

At the 2023 climate summit in Dubai, governments agreed to transition away from fossil fuels. Guterres noted countries now need to speed up that transition and pay for it.

“We can’t put out the fire while pouring fuel on it,” he stated.

Guterres also blamed powerful fossil fuel interests for holding back climate action while they keep making profits.

Industry observers note that he wants deeper emissions cuts before 2030. He also wants more money for vulnerable countries to cope with climate change.

Sources indicate that not everything fell apart in Antalya. Governments agreed on several smaller decisions.

Simon Stiell, the head of UN Climate Change, pointed to progress on the just transition.

Picture a town where hundreds of families depend on a coal mine. When the mine closes, those families need help. A just transition means supporting workers and communities through changes like that.

Recent findings suggest that governments will continue their work on the matter for three more years. They will also set up a mechanism in stages. Plans for it were first agreed at last year’s summit in Belém, and formal adoption is expected at COP32.

Countries that make up about half of the world economy backed a goal of 35% electrification by 2035.

In practice, that means more cars, heating systems and factory machines running on electricity instead of burning fuel.

The International Energy Agency estimates the pledge could raise the global electrification rate from 23% to more than 33% by 2035.

Stiell stated progress like this could help bring about positive tipping points in climate action.

According to recent reports, tropical rainforests got some good news too. Pledges to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility, which helps protect these forests, reached $8.3 billion.

Recent findings suggest that stiell talked openly about what went wrong in Antalya in his closing remarks. “The world cannot afford a repeat of this moment,” he noted.

He also spoke about how governments make decisions at these summits.

“This process belongs to 194 Parties. Consensus works best from the ground up,” Stiell mentioned.

Next year, Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, will host the climate talks. Countries will pick up where they left off in Türkiye.

There is still no agreement on how swiftly the world should move away from coal, oil and gas. For poorer nations, another problem remains: who will pay for the transition?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

Industry observers note that the next Full Moon will be the December Cold Moon, which occurs at 8:28 p.m. EST on Wednesday, Dec. 23, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

The waning gibbous Moon is the brightest object here; next brightest is Jupiter, located to the Moon’s upper right and glowing at magnitude –2.2. The gas giant stands nearly side by side with Mars (to Jupiter’s left); the Red Planet is fainter but still a respectable magnitude 0.4. And shining between Mars and the Moon is 1st-magnitude Regulus, often drawn as both the heart of Leo and the base of the Sickle asterism’s handle. The curving backward question mark of stars that forms the Sickle’s blade and the Lion’s head in profile lies above the grouping in the sky before dawn.

The phases of the Moon are: Upcoming Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

RELATED: 20 things to see on the Moon.

It has been revealed that there are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

According to recent reports, blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

It has been revealed that black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four New Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

What is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

Industry observers note that how does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and Fresh Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

In 1935, crews dangled from cliffs to build a Grand Canyon phone line, now the Park Service wants to its copper wire

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hanging wires in the inner canyon put helicopter and emergency operations and wildlife at risk.
  • Sources indicate that in the 1934-35 season, Civilian Conservation Corps crews built a telephone line down into the Grand Canyon and up the other side, according to a National Park Service history page.
  • The line connected the North and South rims in 1935.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hanging wires in the inner canyon put helicopter and emergency operations and wildlife at risk. The Park Service says removing some would be an adverse effect on a listed historic line.

Sources indicate that in the 1934-35 season, Civilian Conservation Corps crews built a telephone line down into the Grand Canyon and up the other side, according to a National Park Service history page. Workers often had to dangle from ropes on the cliffs to set poles into the rock.

The line connected the North and South rims in 1935. It gave the two rims instantaneous communication, though it could handle only one call at a time, according to the park.

Industry observers note that more than 90 years later, the Park Service has proposed removing sections of the line’s wire. Its original copper wire, now hanging or lying in places across the inner canyon, has become a hazard for helicopter and emergency operations and for wildlife.

The Trans-Canyon Telephone Line runs through the inner canyon, generally following the Bright Angel and North Kaibab trails, with a spur toward the South Kaibab Trail.

It was strung from tree to rock, the park says, and it was frequently out of commission. While the park’s history page says the CCC built the line, the agency’s newest notice describes it as “reconstructed by Civilian Conservation Corps crews in 1935.”.

According to recent reports, the Civilian Conservation Corps was created in 1933, when President Franklin Delano Roosevelt signed the law that set it up. The program gave poor, unemployed young men work on conservation projects across the country’s public lands.

At the Grand Canyon, its crews built trails, walls and shelters, and they helped the park put in roads, campgrounds and telephone lines. The program ended in 1942.

Today the line is listed in the National Register of Historic Places for its importance to the park’s communications, engineering and administrative history.

But according to the Park Service, suspended, hanging and fallen telephone wires have created risks to helicopter and emergency operations in the inner canyon. They can also pose entanglement hazards for wildlife.

Under the proposal, the park would remove sections of the historic wire where necessary to eliminate those hazards. On the wire it keeps, it would add visibility markers where appropriate.

The historic poles, cross-arms, insulators and other hardware would stay in place, unless one of them presents a safety hazard of its own.

Sources indicate that the plan is still a proposal, not finished work. The park took public comments for 15 days, from October 28 until midnight on November 11, 2026, and that comment period has now closed.

The Park Service acknowledges a cost to the historic line. Because the original copper wire is an crucial historic feature of the line, removing portions of it and adding markers “would alter characteristics that contribute to the property’s historical significance,” the agency said.

Under the National Historic Preservation Act, it added, “those changes are considered an adverse effect.”.

To deal with that, the park worked with Arizona’s State Historic Preservation Officer on a draft Memorandum of Agreement.

According to the Park Service, the agreement would let the park address known safety hazards while documenting and preserving the history and significance of the telephone line.

The telephone line is one of many pieces of the Grand Canyon that date to that era. Hikers on the Bright Angel Trail still use resthouses built by the CCC, and Bright Angel Campground sits on the site of the corps’ camp at Phantom Ranch, the park states.

Elsewhere in the park, the South Rim hotels reopened 81 days after a deadly flood, which echoed a disaster in 1966.

Sources indicate that the canyon’s rocks hold a far older record. Geologists have found fossils of unexpected creatures in the Grand Canyon’s Bright Angel Formation.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service news release Grand Canyon National Park Seeks Public Comment on Trans-Canyon Telephone Line (October 28, 2026) and the Grand Canyon National Park history pages Building the National Park and Civilian Conservation Corps.

  • Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

Industry observers note that in 1985, the W.M. Keck Foundation donated $70 million for the University of California and Caltech to construct a fresh observatory on Maunakea in Hawaii. The twin telescopes of the Keck Observatory would be larger than any previous telescope, and the first to use a segmented-mirror design. The goal was a facility that could see farther out into the universe, and with more detail, to study exoplanets, black holes, star and planet formation, and more.

Recent findings suggest that on Nov. 24, 1990, with only nine of the 36 segments of its mirror in place, Keck I turned skyward and achieved first light. The telescope’s image of NGC 1232 was an auspicious beginning of a long career for the Keck Observatory, furthered when Keck I was completed in 1992, and when Keck II was constructed and saw first light in October 1996. The twin telescopes would become the most scientifically productive optical and infrared telescopes in the world.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, damaged septic systems could expose waste on Rodanthe beaches, and drivers should avoid vulnerable parts of N.C. Highway 12 at high tide.

Sources indicate that people on North Carolina’s Outer Banks should stay out of the ocean, avoid driving on the beach and avoid vulnerable sections of N.C. Highway 12 at high tide on November 25 and 26, according to the National Park Service.

A coastal storm is forecast to bring strong, gusty winds and elevated water levels to Cape Hatteras National Seashore on those two days.

In the village of Rodanthe, threatened oceanfront structures “could partially or completely collapse,” the Park Service warned on November 24.

This is a warning, not a report of damage. But the seashore says the risk goes beyond the structures themselves.

Damaged septic systems could expose waste, the Park Service said, “creating serious hazards for people walking on the beach or wading nearby.”.

Recent findings suggest that most off-road vehicle routes on the beach will likely be impassable during the storm, according to the seashore, and hazardous surf will make swimming unsafe. Visitors should avoid beach driving and stay out of the water until conditions improve.

N.C. Highway 12, the main road along the islands, is also at risk. The Park Service notes travelers should avoid its vulnerable sections during high tides on November 25 and 26, and that hazardous weather may cause road closures.

It lists four areas where driving may be very difficult during the storm:.

On Ocracoke Island, a two-mile stretch of highway south of off-road vehicle ramp 59.

On southern Hatteras Island, the road between the villages of Hatteras and Frisco.

On central Hatteras Island, the area along the northern boundary of Buxton.

On northern Hatteras Island, the road between the Pea Island Visitor Center and the Basnight Bridge, as well as side streets in northern Rodanthe.

All of the seashore’s campgrounds remain open, the Park Service indicates, but minor flooding and strong wind gusts will make for unfavorable camping conditions.

It points travelers to the National Weather Service at weather.gov/mhx for forecasts and to the North Carolina Department of Transportation at drivenc.gov for road conditions.

The seashore has issued similar warnings in 2026.

In a recent development, on April 7, it urged visitors to use caution on east-facing beaches through April 11. The potential for multi-day, persistent northeast winds and breaking waves, it noted, could cause coastal erosion and “the partial or full collapse of one or more threatened oceanfront structures in Buxton and Rodanthe.”.

At that time, the entire beach in front of Buxton was closed because of hazards from threatened oceanfront structures “in or near the ocean,” according to the Park Service.

After a recent coastal storm, the seashore reported significant impacts in a September 28 enhancement. It noted Dare County had declared a state of emergency for Hatteras Island, and non-resident travel to the island was prohibited.

It has been revealed that the Avon Fishing Pier had an estimated 20-foot gap in its structure. The beach was closed from the northern boundary of Rodanthe to the pier in Rodanthe, and people were told to avoid the ocean because of possible poor water quality from damaged septic systems.

Private beach stairs and boardwalk decking, septic system parts, and wooden and metal debris from houses were littering the beach, the Park Service stated at the time.

Cape Hatteras National Seashore sits on barrier islands, and those islands are not fixed in place. One study predicts that barrier islands will retreat faster than they have in the past, and healthy dunes help protect the coasts behind them when storms hit.

It has been revealed that the Park Service’s advice for now is practical: use caution on the beach, avoid beach driving and stay out of the water during the storm, and check road conditions before driving N.C. Highway 12.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service news releases Cape Hatteras National Seashore Warns of Hazardous Conditions and Threatened Structures During Coastal Storm (November 24, 2026), Cape Hatteras National Seashore Reports Status Updates After Recent Coastal Storm (September 28, 2026) and Cape Hatteras National Seashore Urges Caution Near Threatened Oceanfront Structures in Buxton and Rodanthe (April 7, 2026).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Recent findings suggest that isabel Angelo spends her days searching the cosmos for exoplanets and signs of extraterrestrial intelligence. But Angelo’s head isn’t in the stars. It’s buried under mountains of 0s and 1s — data from space telescopes old and latest.

To piece together a fuller picture of what’s out there (alien megastructures around nearby stars, perhaps?), Angelo and her colleagues at the SETI Institute in Mountain View, Calif., are turning to machine learning models. These tools are analyzing the troves of telescope data for anomalies — things that look “weird” in space that we don’t know how to explain yet.

Most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust. “These are things that I would expect [the models] to find,” Angelo claims. “But the goal is to find something that’s not even in any of these categories.”.

In a recent development, in the meantime, Angelo keeps her whimsy and wonder for space alive by remembering historic moments, like the reveal of the first portrait of a black hole in 2019. The scientists “put all of these telescopes all over the Earth. They wait for the Earth to rotate. They do all this math to construct this one image,” Angelo claims. “I can’t believe how creative and innovative we have to be to learn about space. It’s such a specific and really fun challenge.”.

Latest Update: Why a NASA spacecraft bound for Jupiter is on its way back to Earth

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (781 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA’s Europa Clipper will fly past Earth on December 3 to gain speed and test its instruments before studying Jupiter’s icy moon Europa.
  • More than two years after leaving Earth, a spacecraft headed for Jupiter is about to pass within roughly 2,000 miles of home.
  • It has been revealed that it has already traveled as far as Mars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA’s Europa Clipper will fly past Earth on December 3 to gain speed and test its instruments before studying Jupiter’s icy moon Europa.

More than two years after leaving Earth, a spacecraft headed for Jupiter is about to pass within roughly 2,000 miles of home.

It has been revealed that it has already traveled as far as Mars. Now it needs a close encounter with the planet it launched from to gain enough speed for the next leg of its journey.

NASA’s Europa Clipper is scheduled to make its closest approach west of Africa at 3:14 p.m. EST on December 3.

While Earth’s gravity bends its flight path, all nine science instruments will collect data.

For the scientists who will eventually study Jupiter’s icy moon Europa, the pass offers a chance to check how their instruments measure a world they already know.

Industry observers note that even after a spacecraft leaves Earth, it continues to travel around the Sun. Its speed and direction determine the shape of that orbit and how far from the Sun it can reach.

A close pass by a planet can change both, saving propellant that the spacecraft would otherwise need to make a similar maneuver with its engines.

As Clipper approaches Earth, gravity pulls the spacecraft toward the planet and curves its path. Earth is moving around the Sun the whole time.

The approach is timed so that this encounter transfers a tiny share of Earth’s orbital energy to Clipper, sending the spacecraft away at a higher speed around the Sun.

The geometry can also work in the opposite direction. When Clipper passed about 550 miles above Mars in March 2025, that encounter slowed the spacecraft and reshaped its orbit.

It has been revealed that the upcoming path brought it back toward Earth for the December flyby. By the time Clipper reaches Jupiter in April 2030, it will have covered about 1.8 billion miles.

On its way past Earth, Clipper will measure a magnetic field that scientists have spent decades mapping.

Engineers can compare those measurements with existing data to check the spacecraft’s magnetometer and refine its calibration.

At Europa, the same instrument will help scientists look for an ocean they can’t see.

The search depends on how saltwater responds to a changing magnetic field.

Industry observers note that as Europa moves through Jupiter’s magnetic field, the field can drive electrical currents in a conductive ocean beneath the ice. Those currents would produce a magnetic signal of their own.

By measuring how that signal changes over repeated flybys, researchers hope to confirm the ocean is there and estimate its depth and salinity.

Clipper’s infrared camera will scan Earth every eight hours as the spacecraft approaches.

At Europa, it will map surface temperatures and look for areas that cool more slowly than their surroundings.

Those measurements can help scientists distinguish differences in the surface material and investigate whether any unusually warm spots point to activity below.

Comparing Clipper’s readings of Earth with observations from other spacecraft gives the team practice working with measurements taken from different vantage points.

Another gravity assist awaits Clipper at Jupiter. A close pass by Ganymede, the largest of Jupiter’s moons, will slow the spacecraft before it fires its engines to enter orbit around the planet.

From there, Clipper is set to make 49 flybys of Europa, some as low as 16 miles above the surface.

Each pass will take it over a different stretch of terrain, allowing scientists to piece together a picture of nearly the entire moon.

Europa’s surface is crossed by cracks and ridges. Some of the most revealing observations could come from looking at the same feature in several ways.

A camera can show where a ridge cuts across the ice, while temperature readings can reveal how quickly the surrounding ground cools.

Ice-penetrating radar can add a view beneath the surface, where echoes may reveal layers or pockets of liquid water.

Together with measurements of the moon’s composition, those observations could help scientists work out whether material moves between Europa’s surface and its ocean.

Recent findings suggest that that exchange matters because liquid water is only one ingredient of a habitable environment. Life also needs a source of energy and chemicals it can use.

It will take years for Clipper to make those observations at Europa. On December 3, the team will start with a closer and more familiar target.

As the spacecraft heads outward again, it will carry a fresh set of measurements from Earth that will help scientists interpret what they eventually find beneath another world’s ice.

#111664. Astronomers catch ‘galaxy-killing’ wind in the act

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1392 w)
