Astronomers catch ‘galaxy-killing’ wind in the act

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1392 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in the local universe, it is common to find galaxies that have stopped forming fresh stars.
  • Industry observers note that but ever since it first began surveying the cosmos, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has discovered more quiescent galaxies within the cosmos’ first 2 billion years than current models of galaxy formation and evolution predict.
  • According to recent reports, now, a team has found evidence that when galaxies collide — as they frequently did in the early universe — it can trigger a burst of star formation so intense that it generates winds capable of snuffing out the opportunity for any further stars to be born.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in the local universe, it is common to find galaxies that have stopped forming fresh stars. These so-called quiescent galaxies have lived for billions of years and over that time, gradually exhausted their star-forming gas. By contrast, galaxies that lie at much greater distances — and thus appear to us when they were young, in the early universe — should have plenty of gas and be readily forming stars.

Industry observers note that but ever since it first began surveying the cosmos, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has discovered more quiescent galaxies within the cosmos’ first 2 billion years than current models of galaxy formation and evolution predict. Astronomers don’t know why they have stopped forming stars so soon, but they have many theories. Some of them require dark energy to have had a stronger influence in the early universe than previously thought, and thus have profound impacts on our understanding of the universe and its evolution.

According to recent reports, now, a team has found evidence that when galaxies collide — as they frequently did in the early universe — it can trigger a burst of star formation so intense that it generates winds capable of snuffing out the opportunity for any further stars to be born. This could explain the high number of young but unexpectedly quiescent galaxies JWST has found without needing drastic changes to our understanding of dark energy and its influence over time.

In a recent development, in order to form stars, galaxies need reservoirs of gas that are dense and cold, lacking energy and prone to collapsing inward. One way to end a galaxy’s era of star formation — a process that astronomers call quenching — is to trigger strong winds that blast outward from the galaxy. These vast, high-speed flows of charged particles can blow away or heat this cold gas.

Such galactic winds can have two possible sources of energy. One is an actively accreting central supermassive black hole (called an active galactic nucleus, or AGN). The other is the energetic blasts generated by massive stars that form and then promptly die, ending their lives by exploding as supernovae. But astronomers have never caught such a wind in the act of draining its host of gas in the early universe, as it is difficult to get a detailed look inside a galaxy so far away.

Recent findings suggest that to better discern the inner workings of star-forming galaxies in the early universe, researchers carried out a joint survey combining observations taken with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) — a powerful radio observatory in Chile — and infrared data from JWST. They also turned to archival data from the Hubble Space Telescope. A team led by astrophysicist Rebecca Davies of Swinburne University of Technology in Australia spotted one particular galaxy, called CRISTAL-02, that shows what appears to be the first direct evidence of a wind powerful enough to halt star formation in a massive galaxy just 1.1 billion years after the Massive Bang. The discovery was published June 10 in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

According to recent reports, CRISTAL-02 is part of a larger sample of around two dozen star-forming galaxies at a similar distance (and therefore of a similar age). Observations showed a huge plume of cold gas extending outside the galaxy, almost as large as the galaxy it comes from. The plume is moving toward Earth at some 60 miles (100 kilometers) per second. Finding fast-moving gas so far from the galaxy is a sign the gas is being actively pushed out in a wind-driven process.

But to truly determine the nature of the plume, the team first had to rule out another possibility behind its formation: Because CRISTAL-02 also appears to be in the throes of merging with several other galaxies, the plume could be a tidal tail — gas stripped away by gravitational forces during the interaction, rather than a genuine wind. This was tricky to determine, Davies says, as no single measurement could settle the question of the gas’ origin; instead the team had to combine several different measurements to characterize the plume and confirm its cause.

In a recent development, first, Davies’ team measured how many upcoming stars the galaxy produces each year. Massive stars live much shorter lives than less massive ones, so looking at how many young, massive stars are in a galaxy indicates how quickly it is forming new stars to replace the ones that are dying. So, the team searched for signs of these young, massive stars in the galaxy’s spectrum and measured how bright those features appear.

The researchers also needed to determine how much gas the galaxy is losing. They did so by first using ALMA data to calculate the mass in the plume and then combining it with the gas’ velocity and distance from the galaxy’s center.

Sources indicate that the verdict: CRISTAL-02 is forming stars at roughly three times the rate of a typical galaxy its size at this distance, but is losing twice as much gas as the galaxy’s star-formation rate. “If this rapid blowout continues, the galaxy could be dead in less than 50 million years, explaining the origin of the mysterious massive dead galaxies in the early universe,” Davies said in a press release.

Industry observers note that finally, the team turned to identifying the cause of the plume. Was the gas being pushed out by energy coming from the galaxy’s central black hole, or was the galaxy’s burst of intense star formation — and the resulting supernova blasts — the culprit?

Models predict that the most powerful outflows from massive galaxies like these should be the result of accretion onto supermassive black holes, Davies indicates. But CRISTAL-02 demonstrates no sign of AGN activity in its center. On the other hand, based on the amount of massive young stars in the galaxy, Davies’ team calculated that the energy transferred to the surrounding gas as these stars die and explode as supernovae would be powerful enough to produce the observed plume.

According to recent reports, the speed of the gas backs this idea up. Supernova-driven outflows rarely exceed speeds of about 1,550 miles (2,500 km) per second, notes Christy Tremonti, an astronomer at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the study. Velocities higher than this usually point to an AGN as the energy source. CRISTAL-02’s outflow is moving around 400 miles (640 km) per second, comfortably within the range expected for a wind produced by a powerful starburst.

Recent findings suggest that davies notes that “the result is surprising,” going against the conventional wisdom that AGN are the cause of star-formation-ending winds. Tremonti notes that  “theoretical models love to use AGN feedback to shut off star formation in massive galaxies — almost every simulation does.” Yet CRISTAL-02’s star formation alone appears capable of triggering a wind that could exhaust its gas supply within tens of millions of years.

CRISTAL-02’s story may not be an isolated case, Davies indicates. Studies suggest that around 40% of massive star-forming galaxies in the early universe are merging, meaning many of them may be caught in similar growth spurts. If this commonly results in subsequent supernova-driven winds, it could help explain why so many early galaxies burned brightly and died young. “It may be the case that AGN are really key for keeping star formation off, but maybe they’re not the thing that shuts it down initially,” Tremonti says.

According to recent reports, the case isn’t entirely closed. Davies says her team cannot completely rule out the presence of an active supermassive black hole — either one too faint to detect, or one that may have flared briefly in the past and pushed gas away from the galaxy before subsequently fading from view. Tremonti agrees this is one of the hardest scenarios to eliminate. Future observations in the mid-infrared, which can peer through dust that might otherwise hide a buried black hole, could help close this gap.

As for CRISTAL-02, its fate is somewhat ironic: The explosive burst of star formation it is undergoing is also the underlying cause of its imminent death.

Shreejaya Karantha is a science writer based in India. Her work has appeared in Sky & Telescope, Phys.org, Live Science US, and The Hindu.

#111662. Phaethon’s fiery folly

Phaethon’s fiery folly

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (396 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even the best-laid aims can require a bit of luck to execute.
  • “I deliberately positioned myself near a local airport in the hope that an aircraft might cross the Sun during the eclipse,” he tells Astronomy.
  • In a recent development, the work wasn’t over: The image “required a somewhat more elaborate workflow” than the conventional stacking and sharpening of video frames.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even the best-laid aims can require a bit of luck to execute. During the solar eclipse of Aug. 12, 2026, in which parts of Iceland, Portugal, and Spain experienced totality, much of western Europe enjoyed a substantial partial eclipse. Astrophotographer Alexandre Tournay set up near Brussels to capture the Moon crossing the disk — as well as a transit of another kind.

“I deliberately positioned myself near a local airport in the hope that an aircraft might cross the Sun during the eclipse,” he tells Astronomy. “Against the odds, one did, passing across the partially eclipsed solar disk with its contrail trailing behind it.” Flight tracking data allowed him to pinpoint the flight: Cargolux 5933, a Boeing 747 freighter from Mexico City bound for Luxembourg.

In a recent development, the work wasn’t over: The image “required a somewhat more elaborate workflow” than the conventional stacking and sharpening of video frames. That process brings out the roiling details in the Sun’s chromosphere, but would oversharpen the edges of the airplane and Moon. So Tournay blended a 1,000-frame stack of the Sun with a single frame that preserved the silhouettes and froze their motion against the disk.

He named the resulting image “Phaethon’s Flight” after the boy in Greek mythology who journeyed east to prove that his father was Helios, the Sun god. Phaethon convinced Helios to let him drive his Sun-bearing chariot across the sky, but was unable to control the horses. He blazed an erratic path that brought climatic extremes to Earth — freezing cold and scorching heat — before Zeus intervened and struck him down dead.

Recent findings suggest that “There’s something fascinating about being able to photograph, with modern instruments, a celestial phenomenon that our ancestors could only understand and describe through mythology,” states Tournay. “And then, by pure chance, to have a flying machine cross the Sun at that exact moment, almost as though a modern-day chariot were dragging the eclipse behind it across the sky, made the story of Phaethon feel like a perfect fit. Seeing that plane cross the eclipsed Sun, I can almost hear the ancients screaming, ‘See?! I told you it was Phaethon!’ ”.

Mark Zastrow is Editor-in-Chief of Astronomy magazine. He holds masters degrees in astronomy and science journalism and has over a decade of experience covering science in the U.S. and in Asia.

  • Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.
  • Now, scientists have a new clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.

Now, scientists have a new clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.

Challenger Deep is found within the Mariana Trench, a crescent-shaped gouge in the seafloor east of the Philippines in the Pacific Ocean. The trench is the scene of a slo-mo tectonic collision called a subduction zone: The Pacific plate is diving beneath the Mariana plate, bending downward as it sinks into the mantle, forming a steep trench on the ocean floor.

All subduction zones are deep, but “it’s interesting why this is the deepest spot in the Earth’s ocean,” indicates geoscientist Robert Stern, an emeritus professor at the University of Texas at Dallas and a visiting researcher at the University of California, Los Angeles.

It has been revealed that he and colleagues employed a remotely operated robot called ROV Jason/Medea to descend to more than 6,000 meters and explore the Mariana Trench seafloor around the edges of Challenger Deep. The rocks turned out to contain pyroclastic deposits, evidence of an erstwhile explosive volcanic eruption. Those deposits included platelike blocks that could indicate eruption pulses, and lobe-shaped rocks where the volcanic flows ended and quickly cooled.

These are the deepest pyroclastic deposits found on Earth, the scientists report November 23 in Frontiers in Earth Science.

In a recent development, how explosive an eruption is at Earth’s surface depends on the chemical makeup of the magma. When the molten rock contains a high proportion of volatile gases, including water vapor, those gases suddenly expand when the magma reaches the surface, producing a violent explosion.

It has been revealed that such explosive volcanism shouldn’t be possible in the deep sea; the pressure is too high for any escaping gases to expand, Stern notes. Along with that mystery, the volcanic deposits were found unusually close to the trench, compared with what would be expected for a subduction zone.

Stern and his colleagues developed a hypothesis that incorporates these disparate pieces of evidence: The extreme depth of Challenger Deep, they say, may be at least partially due to an especially sharp bend in the Pacific Plate as it sinks into the mantle.

In a recent development, that tighter bend would explain why volcanism is happening closer to the subduction zone than usual. The classic subduction zone scenario is that the sinking plate heats up and melts partially as it descends; the magma rises through the overhanging plate and erupts, forming volcanic island arcs several hundred kilometers from the collision zone. Here, the volcanic deposits were just a hundred kilometers or so from the trench — which makes sense if the plate is dipping more steeply.

In a recent development, as for the pyroclastics, “we can’t answer if the eruptions were really explosive,” Stern notes. But at those pressures, any gases such as water vapor contained in the magma wouldn’t be able to explosively expand as they would at the surface.

Instead, the pyroclastic rocks might have formed through a fresh version of deep-sea eruption, one in which water emerging from the magma is initially in a supercritical fluid state. That would minimize any explosive expansion during the eruption and could also produce fragmented, dense deposits like those seen by Jason/Medea.

The discovery of deep-sea pyroclastics is “surprising and unprecedented,” notes William Chadwick, a geologist at Oregon State University in Newport. Challenger Deep may be the only place on Earth “with the ingredients to produce explosive volcanism in the super-deep ocean,” he says. “Imagining this happening is … pretty mind-boggling.”.

It has been revealed that A lot more work remains to be done to evaluate all of these newly introduced ideas, Stern states. “But a lot of things are now coming together.”.

November 24: A Super Beaver Moon occults the Pleiades.

Recent findings suggest that the distant ice giant Uranus reaches opposition tonight at 6 P.M. EST. Opposition is the best time to view a planet in our sky, and it’s visible roughly from dusk until dawn. Because Uranus is faint — magnitude 5.6 — you’ll want to give it a few hours after sunset to climb away from both light pollution and turbulent air near the horizon. Around 10 P.M. local time, you’ll find Uranus midway between the bright star Aldebaran and the Pleiades star cluster in Taurus the Bull, about 60° above the southeastern horizon. It has been revealed that although Uranus can be visible to the naked eye under clear, dark conditions, the bright waning Moon is nearby, so pull out binoculars or a telescope to view the far-off planet tonight. Once you land on its location, look for a “flat,” grayish-colored star. Uranus’ disk spans 4”, so you will likely be able to tell it is circular, rather than a pinpoint of light like any background stars.

  • Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

Born in Macon, France, on Nov. 25, 1783, Claude-Louis Mathieu showed an aptitude for mathematics from a young age. Despite his family’s poverty and his father’s wish for him to be a carpenter, Mathieu moved to Paris in 1801 to study for admission to the prestigious Ecole Polytechnique. He became a student at Ecole Polytechnique two years later and graduated from the school in 1805.

In a recent development, A varied career in astronomy followed, during which Mathieu served as secretary, assistant to the director, and later astronomer at the Paris Observatory, conducting research focused on calculating stars’ parallaxes and determining stellar distances. He also became a professor of astronomy at the College de France, a writer and editor, and a driving force behind the adoption of the metric system in France. Mathieu was elected president of the International Metre Commission in 1870 although he was in his late 80s, and continued to work in that position into his 90s.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A recent short sailing onboard Royal Caribbean’s Oasis of the Seas became a cruise to nowhere due to adverse weather conditions.
  • Departing from Fort Lauderdale on November 16, 2026, the vessel was initially scheduled to operate a four-night cruise to the Bahamas.
  • The sailing’s original itinerary included visits to Nassau, as well as Royal Caribbean’s private island destination of Perfect Day CocoCay.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A recent short sailing onboard Royal Caribbean’s Oasis of the Seas became a cruise to nowhere due to adverse weather conditions.

Departing from Fort Lauderdale on November 16, 2026, the vessel was initially scheduled to operate a four-night cruise to the Bahamas.

The sailing’s original itinerary included visits to Nassau, as well as Royal Caribbean’s private island destination of Perfect Day CocoCay.

The ship initially cancelled its visit to Nassau before being forced to skip the call to the private destination as well.

“Adverse weather conditions producing high winds and ocean swells impacted our operations at Perfect Day CocoCay, preventing us from safely welcoming guests ashore,” Royal Caribbean noted in a statement shared with guests onboard.

“As a result, we won’t be able to visit the port and will instead enjoy a relaxing day at sea,” the company continued.

Royal Caribbean added that any shore excursion booked through the manufacturer for the destination would be automatically cancelled and refunded to their original form of payment.

“We truly appreciate your understanding and flexibility regarding this unexpected change. To thank you for your continued loyalty and to help make up for the inconvenience we are pleased to offer a non-refundable onboard credit,” the organization continued.

The credit was based on passengers’ cabin category and occupancy, with inside and outside cabins receiving $50, while balcony cabins received $75 and suites received $150. Cabins with third, fourth or more guests received a $25 extra credit per additional person.

“We’re sorry for this last-minute change caused by the weather – your safety is our top priority,” Royal Caribbean added.

Having repositioned from New Jersey earlier this month, the Oasis of the Seas is presently offering a series of short cruises to the Bahamas from Fort Lauderdale.

The three- and four-night itineraries will be offered through April 2027 and are highlighted by regular visits to Perfect Day CocoCay.

‘Mitt & Ted’ recounts how a political odd couple changed U.S. health care

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Senator Ted Kennedy often visited the cancer ward at Boston Children’s Hospital, where his eldest son was battling osteosarcoma.
  • In a recent development, kennedy spent decades fighting for health care reform, representing his home state of Massachusetts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In 1973, U.S. Senator Ted Kennedy often visited the cancer ward at Boston Children’s Hospital, where his eldest son was battling osteosarcoma. Kennedy witnessed other parents on the ward make impossible decisions regarding their child’s care when insurance didn’t cover it. Their stories lit a fire within the senator that burned bright for the rest of his life.

In a recent development, kennedy spent decades fighting for health care reform, representing his home state of Massachusetts. He even teamed up with a former political rival from across the aisle: Mitt Romney. The story of this unexpected alliance is recounted in Mitt & Ted, the newest season of the GBH News podcast The Significant Dig. Over eight episodes, journalist and host Ian Coss explores how their work laid the foundation for the Affordable Care Act, one of the most significant and divisive health care reforms in U.S. history.

It has been revealed that we first meet Romney as a young upstart Republican challenger vying to flip Kennedy’s Senate seat in 1994. The race seemed close until a legendary debate. Romney had Kennedy on the defensive until the sitting senator pivoted to the concern near and dear to his heart: health care.

“Kennedy is the elder statesman, in command of the issue,” Coss says. “Romney is like an eager student trying to pass the test.” Using his deep knowledge, Kennedy buries the less experienced Romney. In the election, Kennedy then beat Romney by a landslide, even when many Democrats were ousted by Republican challengers that same year. But the loss may have motivated Romney to keep going.

According to recent reports, several years later, Romney unexpectedly became a champion of health care reform as the newly elected governor of Massachusetts. The state’s health care system was facing the potential loss of about a billion dollars in federal funding, threatening hospitals that served vulnerable populations. Romney’s administration created Romneycare, which was supported by three features: individual and employer mandates, affordable options for low-income people, and a health care exchange where people could compare looks from different providers.

With Senator Kennedy’s help, the groundbreaking law passed in 2006 and expanded health insurance coverage to 98 percent of Massachusetts’ population.

Romneycare gained national attention and kicked off years-long efforts to replicate it on the federal level. Finally, in 2010, President Obama signed the Affordable Care Act, or ACA. Modeled on Romneycare, the law (colloquially called Obamacare) adapted the reforms made in Massachusetts for all 50 states, a challenge since many states had larger shares of uninsured people than Massachusetts had even before Romneycare.

The Democrats in Congress also sought to include a government insurance proposal in the reform, similar to Medicaid but available to more people. Republicans were wary of the ACA generally, but a government-provided insurance option was a line they wouldn’t cross. The ACA eventually passed without the public option, but by then the political winds had shifted. If there ever was a chance to secure bipartisan support for the law, it was gone by the time Democrats were willing to compromise on the public option. And as soon as the ACA became law, Republicans started fighting it.

It has been revealed that the podcast traces an impressive number of political twists and turns on this health care reform journey. Though I got turned around a few times, I never fully lost the plot thanks to Coss’ well-placed reminders and takeaways.

Beyond the story of Romney and Kennedy, the podcast gives voice to many more people who made the ACA a reality: government workers who went from foes to allies who enlisted unlikely help from the conservative Heritage Foundation; longtime friends in the Massachusetts state legislature who were driven apart by the reform; a father who struggled to afford health care and how he advocated for reform with his church. I teared up more than once listening to the human stories behind these policy changes.

It has been revealed that overall, Mitt & Ted gave me newly introduced appreciation for why passing a reform is so difficult, despite how life-changing and life-saving access to health care can be. The series points to moments when stars aligned to make reform possible and suggests that more of those opportunities lie ahead.

“The work of American health care remains very much unfinished,” Coss notes. “When the perfect alignment of frustration and opportunity arrives again, that might be what determines whether our leaders actually work together.”.

  • As part of the expanded season, the MSC Musica will mark the brand’s return to Paranaguá, a port on the Southern Brazilian coast after a two-year absence, offering weeklong cruises to Rio de Janeiro, Búzios, Ilhabela and more.
  • Other highlights of the deployment include the debut of the MSC Virtuosa, which will become the largest vessel to operate in South America, and the return to the MSC Seaview.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MSC Cruises recently kicked off its 2026-27 season in South America, which will see five ships sailing from eight homeports in Brazil, Uruguay and Argentina.

As part of the expanded season, the MSC Musica will mark the brand’s return to Paranaguá, a port on the Southern Brazilian coast after a two-year absence, offering weeklong cruises to Rio de Janeiro, Búzios, Ilhabela and more.

Other highlights of the deployment include the debut of the MSC Virtuosa, which will become the largest vessel to operate in South America, and the return to the MSC Seaview.

The MSC Divina and the MSC Splendida will also sail in the region, offering three- to nine-night itineraries from Santos, Rio de Janeiro, Itajaí, Balneário Camboriú, Buenos Aires, Salvador and Maceió.

Speaking during a ceremony onboard the MSC Divina, Adrian Ursilli, MSC’s country manager in Brazil, stated that the firm’s expansion reflects a broader recognition of the industry’s economic impact and its overall importance, not only within the industry, but also various levels of government.

“Authorities increasingly view the activity as an notable economic driver and job generator for the country, alongside its role in cultural exchange and well-being,” he added, noting that the addition of new cruise terminals and destinations has also contributed to the development of the Brazilian market.

However, Ursilli stressed that port expansion must go hand in hand with structural reforms and objective solutions to keep South America attractive for global fleet deployment and solve other bottlenecks that still affect the industry, as well as other sectors of the economy.

Mentioning an upcoming tax reform, he stated that clarity and a path forward are needed to reduce the cost burden and make the country more competitive to attract further investment, since South America is competing for deployment with other markets, such as the Caribbean, Europe and Asia.

In a recent development, “Right now, Brazil needs to be more competitive in terms of operational costs, port infrastructure, and legal certainty. These items make up our agenda of discussions with federal, state, and municipal governments so we can truly open the horizon for more sustainable future development.”.

The company confirmed further growth for South America in 2027-28, with the larger MSC Meraviglia replacing the MSC Seaview for itineraries to Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay.

#111654. The notion of ‘positive masculinity’ is dividing the male studies field

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Sciencenews ↗ Open Full Page

The notion of ‘positive masculinity’ is dividing the male studies field

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1900 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Industry observers note that ryon McDermott set out seven years ago to create a upcoming scale measuring masculinity.
  • Recent findings suggest that for almost half a century, the many social science scales that measure gender or masculinity have consistently shown that rigid fealty to Western masculine norms — such as prioritizing work, power-seeking and status — link with poor mental and physical health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Industry observers note that ryon McDermott set out seven years ago to create a upcoming scale measuring masculinity. McDermott, along with other researchers studying male psyches, was tired of the field’s long-standing assertion that the manlier the man, the worse his outcomes. It was high time to measure masculinity in a positive light.

Recent findings suggest that for almost half a century, the many social science scales that measure gender or masculinity have consistently shown that rigid fealty to Western masculine norms — such as prioritizing work, power-seeking and status — link with poor mental and physical health. Endorsement of such norms also correlates with misogynistic beliefs and violent behaviors, including sexual violence, studies have shown.

But giving men a talking-to about their many defects rarely lands well. Nor does that negative focus help men thrive. But what approach would help? “We don’t really have a definition of men’s health. If we don’t know what we are going towards, how can we even do this [research]?” says Matt Englar-Carlson, a counseling expert at California State University, Fullerton.

What traits, the researchers wondered, define a healthy man? And could a healthy reframing of manhood improve men’s outcomes, such as by getting them to the doctor or lowering their high rates of social isolation, depression and even death by suicide?

Sources indicate that those questions would cleave the field, though as fights go, this one has been downright nice. McDermott, a psychologist of masculinity at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, would ultimately question positive masculinity’s very existence. Meanwhile, his friends and collaborators at Movember — a nonprofit research organization based in Richmond, Australia that encourages mustache-growing in November to spark conversations around men’s health concerns — are poised for a 2027 launch of the Healthy Manhood Index. That scale uses a positive framing and is designed to gauge men’s strengths, while illuminating areas for improvement.

The first gender measurement scale emerged almost a century ago. It positioned femininity and masculinity at opposite poles, with researchers assuming that the most gender-conforming men and women were the healthiest.

It has been revealed that that thinking has since unraveled. As women began smashing gender barriers, by doing everything from donning pants to entering the workforce, penalties for women acting more masculine largely disappeared.

Inspired by the feminist movement, researchers began studying the masculine psyche. Yet they largely framed masculinity as a barrier to health. The Male Role Norms Inventory, one of the most popular masculinity scales in use today, exemplifies that focus. Individuals rank statements like: “A man must stand on his own two feet and never depend on other people to help him do things.”.

The higher the score on that and more than 60 similar statements appearing in popular masculinity scales used over the past 50 or so years, the worse men’s outcomes, McDermott and his colleagues at Movember reported in July in Men and Masculinities. “Manlier” men often struggle with depression and substance use and engage in sexual aggression. They also tend to avoid asking for help or taking precautionary health measures, such as wearing a mask during the COVID-19 pandemic.

But almost 80 percent of the statements used frame masculinity as a problem to be solved, the team found. That deficit lens biases the findings, argues coauthor and social psychologist Peter Fisher of the Movember Institute of Men’s Health, the organization’s research arm. “If the only tools you have available to you are looking for deficits, you will find deficits,” says Fisher, who is based in Santa Monica, Calif.

That negative framing has also seeped into public discourse, so much so that some people now intuitively link “masculinity” with the word “toxic.”.

In a recent development, yet those most macho of men are the outliers, the small percentage who score highest on masculinity scales, Englar-Carlson claims. He suspects that what really matters for health is flexibility around when to behave in certain ways. Stoicism, a typically masculine-coded trait, can be calming in emergencies but scary when a man experiences a mental health crisis and refuses help.

Englar-Carlson and psychologist Mark Kiselica, of Penn State University, Harrisburg, developed the Positive Psychology Positive Masculinity, or PPPM, paradigm in 2010. Public health experts, therapists and others should focus on men’s strengths not deficits, they argued.

The ideas in PPPM are what McDermott began trying to turn into a masculinity scale a few years later. But his efforts sent him into a tailspin.

He and his colleagues began by identifying positive traits that people linked more with men than women. The team generated a list of 79 possible positive male attributes based on findings from focus groups and studies of positive masculinity and positive psychology, such as “having a good sense of humor,” “serving country or community” and “having passion for one’s work.” More than 1,000 individuals then rated those attributes on a scale from 1 for “strongly disagree” to 7 for “strongly agree” along three dimensions: positive, typically expected of men and typically expected of women.

Roughly 40 percent of the attributes, particularly those pertaining to protective behaviors and assertiveness, were seen as both positive and expected more of men than of women, McDermott and his colleagues reported in 2019 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

According to recent reports, but the study also showed that both men and women scored above the midpoint on almost all the allegedly male attributes. That could mean the supposedly gendered attributes had little to do with gender. And for many measures, such as patience and having good hygiene, women scored higher than men. Could that mean that the study’s list was rebranding attributes from feminism as masculine? The idea didn’t sit well with McDermott.

Then, the team’s research took a dark turn. The researchers had respondents fill out both their upcoming masculinity survey and a scale measuring sexist beliefs. That revealed that the more strongly respondents endorsed masculine ideals, the more likely they were to endorse sexist beliefs, the team’s unpublished work reveals. Think about a statement like, “A good man should be strong,” McDermott says. For many people, that translates to “a good woman should be weak.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I’ve looked at this across three different samples [of people], and I find the same results each time,” McDermott says. “Whenever you define masculinity, you are inherently defining it against femininity.”.

Most attributes are neither male nor female, but human, McDermott has come to believe. And gendering those universal traits merely reinforces sexist stereotypes. The work has left him gutted. “I really thought that there was such thing as positive masculinity,” he indicates. “But now I believe that it can never truly be positive.”.

According to recent reports, fisher is well aware of McDermott’s journey. “He’s been trying to create a positive masculinity scale, or isolate the positive characteristics of masculinity, for a while,” Fisher says. “And he’s been struggling.”.

Perhaps McDermott has set too high a bar, Fisher notes. Rather than trying to identify and measure masculinity through beliefs, he says, why not focus on men’s actions?

In a recent development, so for the past several years, Fisher and colleagues have been doing just that. They have organized numerous focus groups and tested survey statements with some 12,000 individuals across six countries. Besides addressing the lack of age and cultural diversity used to create most masculinity scales presently in use, Fisher and his team hope that their scale will provide men with a blueprint for what constitutes healthy behavior.

Below are qualities Movember Institute of Men’s Health researchers are evaluating to develop a new masculinity scale. The items are preliminary and may not appear in the final version. The rows show counterproductive behaviors that result from pressures facing men, healthy responses and possible wording for survey statements the men would then rate.

Movember Institute of Men’s Health.

All the statements in the Healthy Manhood Index start with “I” plus a verb, such as “I do,” “I talk” or “I check in,” Fisher notes. For instance, men often feel pressure to restrict their emotions, so the healthy response would be for men to open up emotionally. The index might have men rate a statement like: “I share difficult things I’m going through with people I trust.” Crucially, the higher the score on the index, the healthier the man.

Fisher’s goal is to move men toward healthy behaviors without alienating them. “We just want to meet men where they are,” he indicates.

A debate that could easily become acrimonious has remained almost cloyingly friendly. McDermott refers to Fisher as “brilliant.” Fisher credits McDermott for “letting the data change his mind.”.

Researchers in the field recognize that they share the same goals, states psychological researcher Michael Addis of Clark University in Worcester, Mass. They want men to be healthier and to treat others, including women and seemingly less masculine men, with respect. “The question is how do we do that? We either sell them on a latest masculinity, or we say ‘…. masculinity is always going to be in some ways a box,’” he says.

Though discussions around how to frame masculinity can feel wonky, the stakes are real, Addis and psychiatrist and behavioral scientist Ethan Hoffmann of Stanford University wrote in 2024 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

Industry observers note that consider suicide. Men who strongly endorsed masculine norms were less likely than others to seek help for depression and more likely to die by suicide, researchers reported in 2025 in Psychiatry International.

Theoretically, public health campaigns aimed at men can help. But what form should they take? A positive masculinity campaign may recast a statement like, “real men never ask for help” to “real men know when it’s time to ask for help,” Addis and Hoffman write. But a campaign that rejects gender labels may roll out statements like: “Real men aren’t real: It’s a fiction that could cost you your life.”.

Industry observers note that such postgender messaging may feel too abstract for the average guy, Fisher indicates. Convincing a 65-year-old man to stay on top of his prostate cancer appointments is hard enough without trying to shift his worldview.

McDermott counters that positive masculinity “makes the sex role stuff continue,” enshrining the idea that gender roles and hierarchies constitute a necessary organizing principle for societies.

Reconciliation may be possible, Addis indicates. Policy makers and public health experts could first rope men in with a more positive masculine approach. Then over time, they could help men question and relinquish gender norms. “I call it dancing with the devil,” or temporarily adopting the gendered approach as a means to a desired end, he says.

Industry observers note that however the debate unfurls, researchers are writing their own script on how to fight like real men — or real people. “There’s a lot of men in the psychology of men [field] who have worked really hard to not let our egos get in the way of good work,” Addis says. “It’s sort of like practice what you preach.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The fact of the matter is that it doesn’t take a lot of work to find a good pair of headphones these days. After decades of competition and high-tech design, the market is saturated with dozens of high-quality options at every shape, size, and price point. Whether you’re looking for a basic set of earbuds for less than $100, or would prefer to drop $300 to $500 on a pair of wireless ANC headphones with high-tech bells and whistles like support for lossless audio files, or even want to spend top-dollar on a pair of wired, audiophile-grade cans to plug into an immaculately constructed hi-fi system, you won’t be short on choices.

Over the past five years or so, there haven’t been many game-changing innovations in the audio space, but that has led to a flattening of the field that’s great if you’re looking for a bargain. Features that would have once been considered high-end, like active noise cancellation, have trickled down into budget products, and audio quality has been steadily improving among budget- and mid-tier headphones. There are benefits to buying a high-end pair, for sure, but there are more bargains than ever before.

Obviously there are hundreds, if not thousands, of headphones out there—more than even I can test. I’ve put in a lot of time, though, going over the best, the most interesting, and the most talked about headphones, to find the ones that stand out from the pack. Because even when there are a lot of good options out there, we all would rather bring home the best.

I’ve been professionally testing tech products and audio gear, especially headphones and earbuds, since 2011. When I evaluate headphones, I spend weeks and, in some cases, months using each product as my daily driver, assessing its sound, battery life, and ergonomics. I pair the headsets with phones and laptops and frequently switch between devices.

Sources indicate that my test routine included streaming an eclectic selection of tracks from Apple Music and Qobuz to evaluate each headset's ability to produce audible bass, treble, and mid-range. I also listened to podcasts, streamed videos, and played video games while evaluating each pair of headphones.

Recent findings suggest that to put the headphones’ noise cancellation through its paces, I wear them on the New York City subway to get to work, in the large open office I share with my colleagues, and on long-distance flights. I make calls, too, carefully observing if their microphones help participants hear me clearly.

In a recent development, I monitor the battery performance of all wireless headphones by tracking how often I have to charge them. I want to ensure that every pick’s battery life at least matches its manufacturer’s claims.

According to recent reports, because you may wear your headphones for long stretches each day, I carefully scrutinize the size, fit, and ergonomics of every pair by using them for hours between breaks. Review: Bowers & Wilkins Px8 S2.

Before we dig into hardware specs and features to keep on your radar, know that spending more on your next Bluetooth or wired headset will get you better audio performance across the board and more onboard features. By audio performance, I mean noise cancellation, support for immersive spatial audio, and superior call quality, among other essentials. These features require sophisticated onboard processors and multiple integrated microphones, which inevitably reflects the retail price.

Many budget cans support lossless audio formats, but you shouldn’t prioritize this unless you have a top-shelf Android phone that supports audiophile-grade LDAC and Qualcomm AptX codecs. Lossless audio also isn't available on Spotify, so make sure your streaming service supports it. Apple Music, Amazon Music, Tidal, and Qobuz are a few that do.

If you’re shopping on a tight budget, I suggest spending $80 to $100 for a good pair. The most feature-packed wireless noise-canceling headphones cost north of $400, so budget accordingly if you want one. You’ll find your investment well worth it when you turn on noise canceling and discover it’s like a mute button for your surroundings.

According to recent reports, due to their lack of Bluetooth chips, batteries, and additional components to control noise cancellation, spatial audio, and other features, wired headphones can treat you to better stereo sound quality than equivalently priced Bluetooth models. Their makers can use more capable, better-tuned audio drivers while keeping the price reasonable without those extra bits, so you can score a high-quality pair from a substantial-name brand for less than $200.

Recent findings suggest that on the other hand, if ultimate high-fidelity and craftsmanship are priorities for you, prepare to spend a hefty four-digit sum to get what you need. Paired with an amplifier and lossless streaming, high-end wired headphones can help you (literally) discover new tones and layers in songs and albums you’ve listened to hundreds of times before. To be clear, though, only the most dedicated audiophiles should even consider something like that.

The headphones’ audio drivers deliver sound to your ears. The materials used in their making and their tuning are more notable than their size. Translation? More expensive headphones feature more sophisticated drivers, resulting in higher-quality sound with a more palpable balance between bass, treble, and mid-range.

Industry observers note that after more than a decade of headphone testing, I can confirm that cheaper models often hide their sonic deficiencies behind heavier bass. A booming low end can affect treble and mid-range production, reducing the quality of the sonic experience even if it still sounds entertaining.

In a recent development, multi-dimensional spatial audio has become a standard feature on most high-end wireless headphones. By making the sound effects feel as if they come from distinct directions instead of just your left, right, and center, headphones with this lifelike functionality will make you feel like you are in the studio with the artist, part of the audience when streaming a live album, or in the onscreen action.

Industry observers note that better yet, the best wireless headphones with spatial audio have sophisticated onboard tech that can process standard audio into immersive multi-channel sound, including the option to add dynamic head tracking for a truly lifelike experience. As its name suggests, this feature shifts the sound source as you move your head for an even more natural listening experience.

This feature is a must for a fresh pair of wireless headphones in 2025—and you no longer have to pay top dollar for it. Once reserved for premium headsets, the functionality is available across the price spectrum, including under-$100 territory. It utilizes microphones and a processor integrated into the headphones to detect ambient sounds and then deliver audio that cancels those sound waves out.Noise cancellation will reduce auditory distractions during your commutes, travels, and workday. Don’t buy Bluetooth headphones that lack it, even if your budget is below $100. Naturally, spending $200 or more will give you superior noise cancellation, often resulting in near-total silence on top-shelf sets.

I typically suggest wireless headphones if you’re looking for an upgrade, not only for offering cable-free convenience but also for desirable features like noise cancellation, spatial audio, and app controls for customizing those. Look for wireless headphones with Bluetooth 5.2 (or higher) on board. These are the most futureproof wireless connectivity standards. Don’t worry if your device doesn’t support them. They are backward-compatible with older Bluetooth standards.

Wired headphones deserve your attention for their rock-solid connection to hardware, which provides instantaneous sound transmission with zero latency. Measured in milliseconds, latency is the time it takes for audio to reach wireless headphones from the source—your phone, tablet, or TV, for example. It’s imperceptible in most cases.That remarked, a zero-latency wired link can come in handy for video-editing projects, where the audio and on-screen content have to stay in perfect sync. The same goes for competitive gaming, where every millisecond counts.

Industry observers note that opting for a cable-toting set of headphones also frees you from charging, companion apps, and firmware updates. By lacking electronic components and degradable batteries, wired headsets also last longer.

Recent findings suggest that don’t settle for a wireless noise-canceling headset that can deliver less than 20 hours of battery life, as it might not be enough to get you through a super-long flight. The over- and on-ear sets I recommend here will last at least 30 hours between charges, and that’s my minimum requirement in 2026.

According to recent reports, still, since superior noise cancellation and fancy spatial audio tax the headphones’ battery, I didn’t mind charging the Sony WH-1000XM6 and Bose QuietComfort Ultra (Gen 2) to get a better experience than what their lower-priced rivals offered. The same goes for the Apple AirPods Max 2.

Sources indicate that if you are shopping for wireless earbuds, a double-digit maximum battery life of at least 10 hours between charges from the bundled charging case is preferable, but not mandatory. Top-tier AirPods and Bose earphones can’t reach this milestone, but they are still easy to recommend for their excellence in other areas.

Sources indicate that except for AirPods and Beats by Dre products, which benefit from Apple’s superb hardware integration, any new pair of wireless headphones must come with a companion app. This includes Beats products, which can play nice with Android phones just as well as they do with an iPhone. It lets you control them and keep them up to date with firmware updates.

And look for a hard-shell storage case when shopping for Bluetooth headphones. It will keep them intact when you toss them in a bag or backpack on your way to work, or stuff them into a carry-on suitcase when traveling. No need to fret if your headphones come with a soft pouch for storage, though; just keep them at the top of your bag while packing to avoid potential (if highly unlikely) damage.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

According to recent reports, I clearly remember the very last time I used one of my reliable old pyrex baking dishes, and it makes me blush. I was making a chicken recipe but had forgotten to add enough liquid to the pan. In the interest of saving time, I took the hot pan out of the oven, opened a carton of chicken stock from the fridge, and tipped a little in. That’s when my pyrex baking dish shattered into three or four large glass shards, mingled with the now ruined chicken. It broke apart the moment the cold stock touched the hot glass.

Recent findings suggest that though I was shocked, I realized what my mistake was—the glass couldn’t bear the sudden temperature change. But it made me wonder: wasn’t pyrex designed specifically to hold its structural integrity under just these kinds of temperature fluctuations? When I started searching, I found that people have been complaining about their pyrex cookware exploding for years. Perhaps they just weren’t reading the instructions. Then, I stumbled across a different reason for my destroyed dinner: there’s pyrex, and then there’s PYREX.

In a recent development, the first experiment to use PYREX for cooking took place more than a century ago, in the kitchen of Corning Glass Works physicist Jesse T. Littleton, whose wife used a sawn-off glass battery jar to bake in the oven. It was made of borosilicate and that was the key. Used today in cookware and lab equipment such as beakers, Corning’s “Nonex” glass was invented for hot, burning-oil railway lanterns that needed to stay intact when exposed to cold weather. Calling it fire-glass, the firm later named it PYREX®, a play on the word “pyro,” meaning “fire” in Greek, and “ex,” from the label that identified its earlier product.

Industry observers note that since then, PYREX has withstood the intense temperatures and harsh chemical onslaughts of laboratory work. It works well for temperatures of up to 425 degrees Fahrenheit in household kitchens.

In a recent development, the secret to the original PYREX’s heat resilience is its borosilicate composition, a glass made of silica and boron trioxide. Glass expands when it’s hot and contracts while cooling. Heat causes its atoms to vibrate and move apart, weakening the glass. However, boron atoms don’t vibrate or separate as much as other elements, making the overall glass more stable.

Around the 1950s, Corning also began making PYREX bakeware out of tempered soda lime glass, according to Smithsonian magazine. In 1998, Corning sold its consumer product operations to Borden, later renamed World Kitchen, then Corelle Brands. Corelle continued to produce the tempered soda lime bakeware in America—this is called “pyrex,” all lowercase. These days, Corning only makes PYREX borosilicate labware products, such as beakers, for scientific use. In Europe, the brand International Cookware still makes borosilicate cookware.

According to recent reports, ✅ To have a more accurate idea of what you're buying, here’s a good rule of thumb: “Pyrex” is a brand name with clear distinctions depending on how it’s written. Only cookware marked “PYREX”—all uppercase—is likely made of borosilicate glass. However, most of this is made in Europe; lowercase pyrex brand cookware made in the U.S. has been tempered soda lime for decades. It’s still possible to locate some Pyrex brand borosilicate cookware in the U.S., but it’s harder to find. If you see the label “pyrex,” it definitely means the glass is made of tempered soda lime.

Despite its deep roots in American kitchens, home cooks have been complaining about pyrex shattering in the oven or during rapid temperature changes since the early 2000s. In 2010, the nonprofit organization Consumer Reports released a warning following a yearlong investigation of pyrex shattering incidents. “When we examined 163 incidents in detail, we discovered at least 42 reports of injuries. While hundreds of millions of dishes are used safely each year, we believe the situation is serious enough that we have asked the Consumer Product Safety Commission to investigate,” according to the report.

During testing, soda lime glass shattered at lower temperatures than “more expensive” borosilicate Pyrex bakeware, the report continued. Consumer Reports found that the iconic glass bakeware produced in America today is of soda lime, while the European-made products investigators tested were borosilicate.

Consumers also complained that the manufacturer’s instructions were confusing. Consumer Reports found that the small print on the back of products containing the necessary precautions is “easy to miss.”.

In a recent development, borosilicate glass can withstand up to three times as much thermal shock as soda lime silicate. “When glass bakeware does shatter, consumers report, it can break into sharp shards that go flying, raising the risks of injuries. This contrasts with claims from one of the manufacturers that its glass bakeware breaks into ‘relatively small pieces generally lacking sharp edges,’” according to the report.

In a recent development, soda lime glass is made of about 60 to 75 percent silica, 12 to 18 percent soda, and 5 to 12 percent lime. Heat-treated and then rapidly cooled on its exterior, the outside of tempered soda lime glass solidifies more quickly than the center. While cooling, the inside pulls at the stiffer exterior layer, creating tension that makes the whole piece more durable. If it does break, tempered glass forms rounded, cube-shaped chunks, instead of the sharp shards of untempered soda lime glass—think about the last time you dropped a drinking glass.

Untempered soda lime glass is used for items that aren’t supposed to be heated, such as drinking glasses and windows. It isn’t safe for either the oven or the microwave oven.

So look for a European provenance, or simply “borosilicate” in the description before you buy your next glass baking dish. I know I will, because I’m pretty sure I’ve only ever owned the soda lime version.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Emily Conover and Kathryn Hulick.

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

A long-sought pinnacle of mathematics has apparently been reached. In a feat that will go down in mathematics history, a human working with AI appears to have solved the most famous puzzle in math, proving the Riemann hypothesis. The problem has foiled repeated and valiant attempts at solution for more than a century.

In a recent development, now, mathematicians are working to understand the proof, posted by Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, on November 20. The Riemann hypothesis, if true, reveals the secrets of prime numbers. In a statement on his website, Alpöge noted he’d developed the proof alongside Anthropic’s AI tool Claude.

In a recent development, by the next day, independent mathematicians had confirmed the result. “We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,” read a joint statement from Lean Focused Research Organization and Mathlib Initiative.

In a recent development, A proof of the Riemann hypothesis is one of the most sought after achievements in mathematics. “As a mathematical landmark, it really doesn’t get bigger than this. I can’t think of a theorem proven not only in my lifetime, maybe in the history of mathematics that is as important as this,” notes mathematician Ken Ono of Axiom Math and the University of Virginia in Charlottesville.

“It’s an historic achievement,” claims Bryna Kra, a mathematician at Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill.

According to recent reports, importantly, this was not the work of AI alone, Kra indicates. First of all, Claude had been trained on the work of thousands of human mathematicians, plus Alpöge was an experienced mathematician himself. He did not just ask for the proof then “push a button and wait,” Kra says.

In a recent development, over six weeks, he worked back and forth with Claude. As an AI agent, Claude can use outside tools to perform tasks. The precise version of Claude that Alpöge used has not been disclosed, but the AI checked its work using Lean, software that converts mathematical arguments into code in order to confirm that a chain of logic holds up. It also had access to Mathlib, a library of known arguments already converted into Lean.

According to recent reports, the result is 250,000 pages of dense, complex math. The world’s mathematicians are still working to translate the proof into a form people can understand. “What’s amazing about this proof is that it involves so many different areas of mathematics,” Ono indicates. “And I don’t know how a single human being could hold all of the ideas in their mind.”.

The Riemann hypothesis, which dates to 1859, is closely linked with prime numbers. Prime numbers seem to be sprinkled randomly along the number line, but the Riemann hypothesis reveals a hidden order. At play is a mathematical enigma called the Riemann zeta function. The zeros of this function — the values that, when plugged into the function, produce a zero — are closely related to prime numbers. The Riemann hypothesis notes that certain zeros — of which there are an infinite number — all sit on a particular line on a graph. If that is true, it would reveal how many primes exist below a given number.

Because so much of mathematics involves prime numbers, many other mathematical statements rest on the correctness of the hypothesis. The latest proof will have wide implications. “It’s an earthquake throughout mathematics,” Ono indicates.

Sources indicate that alpöge claims to have solved not only the Riemann hypothesis itself, but a more general form of it, called the generalized Riemann hypothesis, which extends the idea to related functions. Though he guided the AI, Alpöge wrote that “what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater … Claude far outpaced me near the finish line.”.

In a recent development, AI has been steadily felling major problems of mathematics, and this is the biggest one yet. But according to cognitive scientist Gary Marcus of Latest York University, AI’s genius at math will not carry over to more open-ended types of problems in biology, business or robotics. “In short, it’s not at all obvious that whatever Alpöge did has the generality many people are hoping for,” he wrote in a Substack post.

Industry observers note that and some mathematicians have pushed back against the dominance of AI, disputing the utility of proofs created with the technology. The Association for Human Mathematics wrote in a November 20 statement on their website that no human being can claim to be responsible for the Riemann hypothesis proof, and that no mathematician can “confirm with full certainty that the proof is correct.”.

Sources indicate that kra has been critical of achievements where AI agents worked largely on their own, independent of human intervention. The recent solution, by OpenAI, to a puzzle about the Navier-Stokes equations that describe fluids came about that way. But Alpöge’s approach was different, Kra says. “There is someone to stand behind [the work],” she says. She just hopes that people don’t see this as an end to math. “I think that this is a beginning, this is opening up more questions than it answers. … I think we have to use our imagination and find what’s the next frontier.”.

In a centrally located home in ancient Pompeii’s Via dell’Abbondanza (translated as Street of Abundance), one woman curated a cozy—and intimate—dressing room, obscured by a façade. The identity of the woman is itself now obscured and lost to time, but the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 C.E. froze her personal habits and routines in ash. 2,000 years later, archaeologists found it exactly as it was.

The house in question likely belonged to Cornelius Maxium, based on inscriptions no longer visible but seen during a 1912 excavation. Archaeologists recently ventured behind the home’s façade, and in doing so, opened a wardrobe last opened in 79 C.E.

Recent findings suggest that archaeologists spelled out the find in an online excavation journal from Pompeii Sites, highlighting how the investigation revealed the woman’s personal beauty routine and daily habits. The wardrobe contained cosmetic tools of tweezers and a mixing palette, a glass perfume vial, an incense burner, and a bronze oil lamp. The excavation also revealed vessels and pots of bronze, glass, and ceramic, as well as a small wooden box contained lead weights, which were likely used in trading.

Recent findings suggest that “Pompeii is not just a place of great works of art; it is also a place where the most ordinary objects reveal the human dimension of the past,” Gabriel Zuchtriegel, director of the Pompeii Archaeological Park, said in a translated statement. “The value of this discovery lies in the ability to piece together various traces of a life—personal habits, work, and memories. While we cannot reconstruct the identity of the house’s inhabitant with certainty, these fragments bring us closer to their daily existence.”.

The woman whose wardrobe this was, for example, may have had a great affection for pinecones. In addition to the discovery of a small jug decorated with a pinecone motif, there was also a necklace with at least 24 miniature charms made from faience, bone, glass paste, and rock crystals. Some of those charms also depicted pinecones.

Tucked inside a cloth pouch inside the wardrobe, archaeologists may have found the most personal item of all: a necklace with amulets known as “crepundia,” which literally translates to rattles. Typically worn by children for ritual protection—the amulets were thought to contain spells that offered protection—the items also audibly rattled so adults could better track their children’s movements.

Roman-era experts said adults often kept childhood crepundia as a keepsake. “The Roman world was characterized by a high degree of geographical mobility at every social level, from slaves to wealthy merchants,” according to the statement. “As a result, many people found themselves living far from the parents, relatives, and the places where they had grown up.”.

Amidst the personal items at Via dell’Abbondanza, archeologists may have located the woman’s proto-piggy bank, as excavations revealed a woven container holding 38 bronze coins.

In a recent development, that such deeply personal items, to say nothing of the hoard of bronze coins, were there within the wardrobe to be found centuries later suggests that the owner, whoever she may have been, fled the eruption and subsequent devastation with no time to extract them, and never returned to retrieve them. That, of course, is assuming they survived to even attempt it.

It’s possible the owners were not home at the time of the eruption, as the room housing the wardrobe appeared to be under some level of renovation when the disaster occurred. Even in its mid-reno state, however, the room featured expensive Italian paintings, highlighting the potential wealth of the occupants that match the prime real estate along one of the ancient city’s main thoroughfares. The excavation also uncovered the remains of some of the home’s smaller residents when Vesuvius rained down its devastation. There was a pair of young wood mice skeletons inside an amphora on the home’s mezzanine level, showing that even the finest urban homes in Pompeii clashed with rodents. Evidently, there was no crepundia warding them off.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If hypothetical aliens ever search for technosignatures, thousands upon thousands of satellites orbiting Earth should be an obvious sign that intelligent life exists on this planet. The problem is that an alien spacecraft might be better off keeping its distance. As the spiral into dystopia here on Earth continues, there has been growing concern that someone could take out many of those satellites (and the infrastructure they support) with a nuclear weapon. What would happen in the wake of such an attack is a question keeping scientists from sleeping at night.

In a recent development, when a team of researchers from Princeton and the University of Wisconsin-Madison gauged the theoretical destruction of a nuclear strike in low-Earth orbit, or LEO, the results were grim. There have been over 13,000 satellites at altitudes under 1,242 miles (2,000 km) since early 2026. Many of these fly close together in a region of about 193-232 square miles (500-600 km2), and the use of LEO has only been expanding as the U.S. Department of Defense continues deploying hundreds more for detecting missiles and carrying out military communications, but they have only become more of a target for hostile forces. In an unnerving thought experiment, the researchers worked out the aftermath of detonating a one-megaton nuclear weapon 311 miles (500 kilometers) above the South Atlantic—they found it would easily wipe out about 98% of satellites.

It has been revealed that “Radiation-disabled spacecraft remain in orbit but are assumed to lose maneuverability,” they said in a study recently posted to the preprint server arXiv. “We follow collisions and breakup fragments in altitude bands, retaining mass and allowing fragments to move above and below their birth altitude after a velocity kick. Both intact objects and debris descend under atmospheric drag.”.

This is not the first time a “what if” like has been batted around, in theory or otherwise. Nuclear paranoia decades ago led to an actual experiment that revealed the potential horrors of detonating something in LEO. On July 9, 1962, the the Starfish Prime test saw a 1.4-megaton bomb detonated in the Pacific, around 400 km above Johnston Atoll. An artificial radiation belt was created by clouds of electrons released from radioactive debris scattered by nuclear fission. It caused severe damage to satellites that were either in outfit at the time or launched soon afterward. Radiation continues to be dangerous long after the initial explosion, because spacecraft continue to pass through it as they orbit, experiencing degrading effects that make them more difficult to maneuver. They then end up at increased risk of collision.

Industry observers note that the researchers found that the worst effects from a detonation over the South Atlantic would be from exposure to radiation damage, which would disable 25% of the fleet in not even a day. That would rocket to 78% after three days and 98% after a week. Damaged satellites prone to crashing would collide with each other—or scraps of space junk—and gradually shut down services that rely on them. There would be three collisions within 15 days and double that by 30. Smashing spacecraft would also clog LEO with fragments that would put even more satellites at risk, and at least 19 collisions would occur a year after the detonation. Atmospheric drag would reduce the hazard by removing disabled spacecraft orbiting lower, but those at higher altitudes would remain at the highest risk. Disabled satellites would continue to die off.

Starfish Prime was so disastrous that the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty was signed by the U.S. and the Soviet Union a year later. This enforced an outright ban on testing nuclear weapons anywhere but underground, whether it was on the surface, in the atmosphere, or deep in space. Satellites in LEO have multiplied since the 1960s. How long radioactive ions can keep letting electrons loose above the atmosphere is still uncertain, but satellite breakdowns would be staggering. It would take decades to restore the damaged spacecraft and infrastructure.

“Restoring orbital services would require more than replacing the lost spacecraft,” the researchers said. “Latest satellites would need to survive the remaining radiation and debris. The prospect of rapid infrastructure loss followed by years of disruption reinforces the need to prevent the deployment and use of nuclear weapons in space.”.

Avora Lumina LLC, the manufacturer set to convert the Seven Seas Navigator from Regent Seven Seas Cruises into a residential cruise ship, filed a voluntary Chapter 11 petition in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Florida on Nov. 23, 2026.

The manufacturer stated it its filing that noncontingent liquidated debts are below the $3,424,000 threshold.

In the petition, Avora Lumina estimated its assets at $10 million to $50 million and its liabilities at $1 million to $10 million, with between one and 49 creditors.

The company also remarked that funds will be available for distribution to unsecured creditors.

Sources indicate that the petition was signed by Mikael Petterson, listed as founder and chairman. The company is represented by Bradley S. Shraiberg of Shraiberg Page PA in Boca Raton, Florida.

Navigator Vessel Company LLC, based in Hamilton, Bermuda, was the only creditor listed with a specific claim amount, at $2.5 million.

The remaining entries on the list of the 20 largest unsecured creditors, including the Internal Revenue Service, the Florida Department of Revenue, the Broward County Tax Collector, the Securities and Exchange Commission and federal and state attorneys general offices, were listed “for information purposes” with amounts marked as unknown.

The petition indicated no bankruptcy filings by the firm in the past eight years and no pending cases involving affiliates.

Avora Residences announced in March 2026 that it had acquired the Seven Seas Navigator from Regent Seven Seas Cruises through a nine-year charter with a nominal purchase option from Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings.

The 496-guest ship was set to debut in January 2028 as the Avora Lumina following a full luxury residential conversion, launching from Lisbon on a three-year global circumnavigation.

Aims called for 242 residences, with life-of-ship ownership priced from about $545,000 to $4.2 million and a five-year program starting at around $219,600.

Avora was founded by Petterson and Kathy Villalba, who also founded Villa Vie Residences.

Villa Vie suspended operations of the Villa Vie Odyssey in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, on Oct. 27, 2026, citing sharp increases in fuel costs, and said it was evaluating restructuring and recapitalization alternatives. The Villa Vie Odyssey left Cambodia without residents in early November.
